title: gsea software validation
text:
The usage snippet shows the supported vegas()-to-gsea() mapping. Focused deterministic tests cover each supported dispatcher route.
These recorded simulation results assess selected behavior on ten fixed datasets from the shared design. They do not revalidate the statistical method or cover every setting. The use snippets show the current package interfaces. This report step summarizes retained artifacts and does not rerun analyses. The gsea guide describes current inputs and options.


library(gsea)
evidence <- vegas(statistics, LD_Glist, sets = genes,
                  metadata = metadata,
                  control = list(tail_method = "saddlepoint"))
input <- gsea_input(evidence)
fit <- gsea(input$stat, pathways, method = "preranked")

title: gscore software validation
text:
Current scoring uses gscore::gscore(weights, Glist); weight learning belongs to glma, gbayes or another statistical model owner, and conventional C+T uses gscore::clump_threshold().

title: Shared genomic simulation design
text:
This design fixes the inputs for ten focused software validation runs across glma, gcorr, gbayes, gscore, gmap and gsea. The retained compact results were produced from this fixed design. The current LOCO scan and report driver use the current package interfaces. Website rendering never runs these analyses.


Each seed generates 10,000 unrelated individuals, 50,000 biallelic markers in 500 independent artificial LD regions, and three continuous traits. Disjoint groups of 3,000 supply one GWAS per trait; 1,000 other individuals are reserved for scoring. The pooled 9,000 GWAS individuals supply the matched LD reference. The workflow writes the genotypes blockwise to a packed BED file, then uses gsim to generate phenotypes from declared effects and the prepared panel. It records causal effects, genetic values, residual covariance and sample assignments. Population LD and the generating effects determine the heritability, covariance, correlation and marginal-effect truth; fitted LD does not define truth.
One data-generating process contains three named evaluation patterns:

Distributed effects: effects across regions permit genome-wide GWAS, heritability, genetic correlation, Bayesian regression and prediction checks.
Shared and distinct regional signals: the first two regions have known shared and distinct causal variants for fine-mapping and colocalisation.
Annotation enrichment: causal effects are more frequent in the first 80 regions, with predefined artificial genes and pathways.

These are patterns within each simulated dataset, not three independent phenotype-generating scenarios. Ten fixed seeds are prescribed; failed seeds are recorded and never replaced. The run reuses the established connected workflow and saves compact results by seed, with hashes, package versions, warnings, status and stage timings. Large genotypes, fits and LD resources remain in the ignored build cache. Two R workers process odd and even seeds concurrently; elapsed times describe this machine and workload, not an isolated benchmark.



The code below shows the data-generation part of the connected workflow. Run it from the gsuite repository root with development installations of gsuite and gsim. Change replicate from 1 through 10 to use the prescribed seeds. Genotypes are written one marker at a time to PLINK BED files; gsim then generates the phenotypes from known effects. The recorded design also includes population truth, prepared LD and all six analysis outputs.
.libPaths(c("build/r-library", .libPaths()))
library(gsuite)
library(gsim)

replicate <- 1L
seed <- 20262000L + 100L * replicate
set.seed(seed)
n <- 10000L; m <- 50000L; size <- 100L; nr <- m %/% size
traits <- c("A", "B", "C")
ids <- sprintf("m%05d", seq_len(m))
individuals <- sprintf("id%05d", seq_len(n))
region <- rep(sprintf("region%03d", seq_len(nr)), each = size)
rho <- seq(.2, .8, length.out = nr)
rows <- setNames(lapply(0:2, function(k) k * 3000L + seq_len(3000L)), traits)
holdout <- 9001:10000

out <- file.path("build/examples/simulated-genomics",
                 sprintf("replicate-%02d", replicate))
dir.create(out, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
prefix <- file.path(out, "genotypes")
con <- file(paste0(prefix, ".bed"), "wb")
writeBin(as.raw(c(0x6c, 0x1b, 0x01)), con)
for (j in seq_len(m)) {
  w <- rbinom(n, 2, .3)
  r <- (j - 1L) %/% size + 1L
  if ((j - 1L) %% size) {
    keep <- runif(n) < rho[r]
    w[keep] <- previous[keep]
  }
  previous <- w
  codes <- c(3L, 2L, 0L)[w + 1L]
  writeBin(as.raw(colSums(matrix(codes, 4L) * c(1, 4, 16, 64))), con)
}
close(con)
write.table(data.frame(rep(seq_len(nr), each = size), ids, 0,
                       as.character(rep(seq_len(size) * 1000L, nr)), "A", "G"),
            paste0(prefix, ".bim"), quote = FALSE, row.names = FALSE,
            col.names = FALSE)
write.table(data.frame(individuals, individuals, 0, 0, 0, -9),
            paste0(prefix, ".fam"), quote = FALSE, row.names = FALSE,
            col.names = FALSE)
Glist <- gbase::gprep(bedfiles = paste0(prefix, ".bed"))

active <- runif(m) < ifelse(rep(seq_len(nr), each = size) <= 80, .08, .008)
B <- matrix(0, m, 3, dimnames = list(ids, traits))
correlation <- matrix(.6, 3, 3); diag(correlation) <- 1
B[active, ] <- matrix(rnorm(sum(active) * 3, sd = .035), sum(active), 3) %*%
  chol(correlation)
B[1:200, ] <- 0
B[50, ] <- .5
B[125, 1] <- .5; B[175, 2:3] <- .5

simulation <- gsim::gsim(
  Glist = Glist, nt = 3, architecture = "fixed", beta = B,
  h2 = c(.3, .4, .35), vg = c(.3, .4, .35), re = 0,
  standardize_W = FALSE, scale_effects = TRUE, seed = seed + 1L,
  compute_sumstats = FALSE, chunk_size = 64
)
colnames(simulation$Y) <- colnames(simulation$G) <-
  colnames(simulation$B) <- traits
saveRDS(list(seed = seed, Glist = Glist, simulation = simulation,
             gwas_rows = rows, holdout_rows = holdout, region = region, rho = rho),
        file.path(out, "simulation.rds"))
The first 80 regions have a higher causal-marker probability; the first two regions also contain the declared shared and distinct signals. The GWAS groups, holdout and pooled LD reference are fixed by the row indices above. The saved object includes generating effects and individual genetic values. The connected workflow additionally computes population heritability and genetic-correlation truth from those effects and the known LD construction.



Exact linear GWAS results are checked against selected R ordinary least-squares calculations within \(10^{-9}\). Applying the true marker effects as a score must reproduce centered simulated genetic values within \(10^{-9}\). All requested results, unavailable estimates and numerical statuses are retained. Point estimates, intervals, prediction, posterior diagnostics, causal-marker coverage and pathway results are summarized across the ten attempts without replacing unfavorable outcomes.
The run status and numerical checks list each prescribed seed. The library pages link the compact result tables used in their summaries.
The glma Manhattan and effect plots use per-marker results retained from the prescribed tenth seed. They illustrate one dataset; the ten-run summaries remain the repeated evidence.
The connected 50K-marker BayesC and BayesR fits hold residual variance, effect-variance scale and mixture weights at declared values. They check posterior effects, heritability summaries, chain behavior and held-out scores under that contract. The separate reference-LD parameter-learning checks is the evidence for learning these parameters with a matched independent reference and its prescribed sparse-LD construction.
One additional glma LOCO timing run uses the genotypes and trait A phenotype from seed 2, grouping the 500 artificial regions into 20 artificial chromosomes. It tests all 50,000 markers against a 500-marker background with two operation-local threads. This one run checks execution and timing. The unrelated-individual design and subset background do not qualify mixed-model null-tail calibration or heritability estimation. LOCO is not part of the ten repeated library comparisons.
Ten replicates support descriptive truth comparisons, not precise coverage, power, false-positive-rate or method-ranking claims. The LD reference overlaps the GWAS individuals. Binary traits, population structure, ancestry mismatch, independent external LD panels and complete package/platform validation are outside this design.

title: Gene and pathway analysis with gsea
text: gsea analyses gene-level evidence and named collections of genes. It re-exports glma::vegas() for the preceding marker-to-gene step, then offers over-representation, preranked, competitive, MAGMA-style and Bayesian pathway methods. pops() separately ranks genes using their features. This tutorial continues the shared 20K/50K analysis. Run the overview’s loading block and the glma VEGAS step first to define gene_sets and gene_results.

title: Gene and pathway analysis with gsea
text:
From markers to genes
VEGAS has already converted aligned marker statistics and reference LD into one gene table per trait. gsea_input() checks that all traits have available p-values and the same genes in the same order, then renames the gene identifier for pathway analysis.
library(gsea)

input <- gsea_input(gene_results)
gene_stat <- input$stat
names(gene_stat)
head(gene_stat$A[c("gene", "score", "p_value",
  "marker_count", "sample_size")])
VEGAS sets contain marker names. The pathway sets below contain gene names. The simulated enriched set includes genes drawn from the first 80 regions; background and mixed provide comparisons.
pathway_sets <- list(
  enriched = names(gene_sets)[1:160],
  background = names(gene_sets)[401:560],
  mixed = names(gene_sets)[seq(1, 999, by = 5)]
)

title: Gene and pathway analysis with gsea
text:
Fit the MAGMA-style competitive model
The public MAGMA route consumes calibrated gene p-values and gene metadata such as marker count, effective parameters, GWAS sample size and minor-allele count. The VEGAS result carries those fields from the preceding stage. Gene dependence must be declared; the saved example deliberately uses an independent working gene covariance.
pathways <- gsea(gene_stat, pathway_sets, method = "magma",
  sampling = list(gene_covariance = "independent"))

pathways$pathways
pathways$preparation

title: Gene and pathway analysis with gsea
section: Rank genes from features with PoPS
text:
Rank genes from features with PoPS
PoPS-style ranking is a different question: which genes receive high feature-based priority scores? Features are numeric columns in a gene-by- feature matrix. A chromosome-held-out model scores each gene using a fit that excluded its chromosome from the training response.
gene_names <- names(gene_sets)
region_index <- rep(seq_len(500), each = 2L)
set.seed(20260932)
features <- matrix(rnorm(length(gene_names) * 100L),
  nrow = length(gene_names),
  dimnames = list(gene_names, sprintf("feature%03d", 1:100)))
features[, 1] <- as.numeric(gene_names %in% pathway_sets$enriched)

pops_stat <- data.frame(
  gene = gene_names,
  chromosome = as.character(ceiling(region_index / 25L)),
  score = gene_stat$A$score
)

ranking <- pops(pops_stat, features,
  sampling = list(gene_covariance = "independent"),
  control_features = "feature001")

head(ranking$predictions[order(ranking$predictions$genome_rank), ])
ranking$folds

title: Gene and pathway analysis with gsea
text:
Select another pathway question








Method
Required gene evidence
Main output




ora
A logical selected flag over the complete gene background.
Over-representation and fold enrichment.


preranked
A finite signed gene score.
Enrichment score, normalized score and permutations.


competitive
A finite gene score and declared gene covariance.
Joint or separate regression effects for pathways.


magma
Gene p-value and required gene metadata.
Corrected competitive pathway statistics.


bayesc, bayesr
Gene score, explicit priors and gene covariance.
Posterior pathway effects and inclusion probabilities.



For a simple selected-gene or ranked-gene analysis on the same evidence:
selected <- transform(gene_stat$A, selected = p_value < 0.05)
ora <- gsea(selected, pathway_sets, method = "ora",
  control = list(adjustment = "BH"))

ranked <- gsea(gene_stat$A, pathway_sets, method = "preranked",
  control = list(replicates = 999L, seed = 2401L))
The selected threshold, permutation count and adjustment are analysis choices. These alternative fits were not used to create the displayed MAGMA table. For joint Bayesian traits, the gsea guide shows the required effect covariance prior and fixed residual trait covariance. It also describes the package’s deterministic marker-level gsea_preranked() route.
Download pathway results · download the leading PoPS genes

title: Regional fine-mapping with gmap
text: gmap works at a declared set of regions rather than fitting the complete genome at once. It offers regional multi-effect, BayesC and BayesR fits, posterior sets, Bayesian FDR summaries and colocalisation. It can also interpret regions from an existing individual-level gbayes fit. This page uses the A and B summaries and the LD resource from the shared simulation. Run the overview’s loading block first for statistics, reference_Glist, Y and regions; the glma page defines the named gwas_ids.

title: Regional fine-mapping with gmap
text:
Prepare the regional likelihood
gmap_stat() converts ordinary intercept-only linear GWAS b and seb into score and information inputs using the observed phenotype variance. It checks exact marker and allele order against the complete Glist LD reference. Provide the sample variance of the phenotype in each GWAS cohort, with R’s usual n - 1 denominator.
library(gmap)

phenotype_variance <- c(
  A = var(Y[gwas_ids$A, "A"]),
  B = var(Y[gwas_ids$B, "B"])
)
prepared <- gmap_stat(statistics[c("A", "B")], reference_Glist,
  phenotype_variance = phenotype_variance)

head(prepared$A[c("rsids", "ea", "nea", "score", "information")])
The conversion assumes ordinary linear regression with a common sample size within each trait. It is not an automatic conversion for mixed-model or logistic GWAS statistics. See the full mapping guide for the individual-level route and input checks.

title: Regional fine-mapping with gmap
text:
Fit 20 marker-defined regions
The simulated regions each contain 100 marker names in LD-reference order. The multi-effect fit below requests one effect per region and uses a sequence of retained positive eigenvalue mass targets. If a fit needs another target, its successful target and retained rank are saved in diagnostics.
fit <- gmap(prepared, reference_Glist,
  regions = regions[1:20], method = "multi_effect",
  prior = list(residual_variance = 1, effect_variance = 0.04),
  control = list(
    effects = 1L, max_sweeps = 200L,
    eigen = list(retained_positive_mass = c(0.995, 0.99, 0.95))
  ))

head(fit$estimates[c("region", "trait", "marker", "mean", "pip")])
pip is a posterior inclusion probability. mean is the posterior mean effect in the prepared regional model. The leading markers in the saved run are:

title: Regional fine-mapping with gmap
text:
Summarize sets and Bayesian FDR
gmap_sets() returns ordinary set-level and marker-level data frames. The meaning of set mass depends on the fitted method; read the meaning column rather than treating every set as the same type of credible set.
posterior_sets <- gmap_sets(fit)
head(posterior_sets$summary)
head(posterior_sets$members)

fdr <- gmap_bfdr(fit, target = 0.05)
head(fdr[c("region", "trait", "selected_markers",
  "expected_false_discoveries", "bfdr")])
Bayesian FDR averages 1 - PIP among selected markers under the fitted posterior. It does not provide a frequentist FDR guarantee.

title: Regional fine-mapping with gmap
section: Compare traits and reuse saved fits
text:
Compare traits and reuse saved fits
Component-pair colocalisation can use the saved multi-effect fits without refitting the regional models. The two simulated GWAS cohorts are disjoint; the complete 100-marker regions and reference are shared by both traits.
coloc <- gmap_coloc_components(fit, fit, reference_Glist,
  trait1 = "A", trait2 = "B", regions = "region001",
  control = list(complete_region_coverage = TRUE,
                 non_overlapping_samples = TRUE))
summary(coloc)
coloc$estimates
The colocalisation call illustrates a supported follow-on analysis; its probabilities were not included in the displayed run. Priors and eligibility checks are recorded in the returned result. For a global individual-level BayesC/BayesR fit, gmap_bed() instead groups its saved marker posterior within named regions using LD from the same fitted samples; those groups are not regional refits.
Download the top marker PIPs · download all fit diagnostics

title: Bayesian genomic regression with gbayes
text: gbayes fits marker effects from aligned summary statistics and the shared Glist LD reference. It also supports individual BED phenotypes, multivariate fits, annotation-informed priors and several focused summary engines. This page interprets the BayesC fit from the 20K/50K simulation; alternative calls below show other available routes without attaching the displayed BayesC numbers to them. Load statistics, reference_Glist, Y and panel from the linked study overview and gbase preparation, or run the complete driver there to regenerate the saved fit.

title: Bayesian genomic regression with gbayes
text:
Fit one summary trait
Trait A contributes 6,000 GWAS individuals. Its aligned table has effect estimates b, standard errors seb and sample size n for every marker. The fixed BayesC prior used in the saved run expects roughly 2% of markers to be active.
library(gbayes)

prior <- list(
  residual_variance = 1,
  effect_variance = 0.3 / (50000 * 0.02),
  inclusion_probability = 0.02
)
control <- list(
  burnin = 500L,
  sampling_sweeps = 700L,
  seeds = c(11, 29, 47, 71),
  threads = 4,
  residual_policy = "fixed"
)

fit <- gbayes(statistics$A, reference_Glist,
  method = "bayesc", trait = "A",
  prior = prior, control = control)
The fit returns one row per marker in fit$estimates, a portable allele-labelled fit$weights table, posterior parameter summaries and chain diagnostics. These are the saved parameter summaries:

title: Bayesian genomic regression with gbayes
section: Choose the model and data route
text:
Choose the model and data route








Route
Example call
When it is useful




Summary BayesR
gbayes(statistics$A, reference_Glist, method = "bayesr", prior = bayesr_prior)
Mixture of several nonzero effect scales.


Annotation-informed eigen blocks
gbayes(statistics$A, reference_Glist, method = "sbayesrc", annotation = component_annotation)
Verified independent LD blocks and marker annotations.


Individual-level BayesC/R
gbayes(data = phenotype_table, Glist = panel, method = "bayesc", trait = "A", prior = prior)
Fit directly to selected BED genotypes and named phenotypes.


Focused summary approximations
gbayes(statistics$A, reference_Glist, method = "variational")
Deterministic variational or shrinkage analyses with their own controls.


One regional effect
gbayes_single_effect(region_stat)
Posterior assignment probabilities under a one-effect model.



For individual-level fitting, supply a data frame with unique character id and a finite pre-adjusted phenotype column:
phenotype_table <- data.frame(id = rownames(Y), A = Y[, "A"])
bed_fit <- gbayes(data = phenotype_table, Glist = panel,
  method = "bayesc", trait = "A", prior = prior)
sbayesrc requires the verified block partition from gbase::define_ld_blocks() and a marker-aligned component annotation. Block eigensystems are prepared once per fit and reused by its chains. The Bayesian workflow guide gives the full annotation structure and describes BayesR, BayesS scaling, multivariate traits, study-specific references and method-specific approximation controls.

title: Bayesian genomic regression with gbayes
text:
Continue or request posterior quantities
Long chains can resume from an exact saved continuation state when the model definition and marker order are unchanged. posterior can request genetic covariance/correlation from a declared LD reference, heritability with an explicit phenotype variance, marker partitions or predictions for selected individuals with posterior uncertainty.
fit_with_quantities <- gbayes(statistics$A, reference_Glist,
  method = "bayesc", trait = "A", prior = prior, control = control,
  posterior = list(reference = reference_Glist,
                   phenotype_variance = c(A = 1)))

fit_with_quantities$quantities
Those quantities are separate from the fixed BayesC run displayed above; use the phenotype variance of your actual trait rather than the illustrative value in the snippet.
Download posterior summaries · download the top marker estimates

title: Prepare genotypes and LD with gbase
text: gbase owns the data boundary shared by the analysis packages. Its Glist records the selected samples and markers, physical BED locations, allele labels and marker summaries. When LD is requested, the same object also carries the sparse-LD identity, sample and marker provenance, and LD scores. This page uses the shared 20K/50K simulation.

title: Prepare genotypes and LD with gbase
text:
Prepare the panel
Start with a SNP-major PLINK BED file and matching BIM/FAM files. gprep() infers the companion paths from the BED name. Sample IDs and marker IDs are selected by name and retain their documented Glist order.
library(gbase)

prefix <- "path/to/genotypes"  # replace with your PLINK prefix
individuals <- sprintf("id%05d", 1:20000)
marker_ids <- sprintf("m%05d", 1:50000)
reference_ids <- individuals[1:18000]
regions <- split(marker_ids,
  rep(sprintf("region%03d", 1:500), each = 100))

panel <- gprep(bedfiles = paste0(prefix, ".bed"), nthreads = 4)
reference_Glist <- gprep(bedfiles = paste0(prefix, ".bed"),
  ids = reference_ids, nthreads = 4)

stopifnot(sum(lengths(panel$rsids)) == 50000)
stopifnot(length(reference_Glist$study_ids) == 18000)
The selected-reference summaries, including allele frequencies and genotype counts, come from those 18,000 people. panel retains all 20,000 people for later association scans and held-out scoring.

title: Prepare genotypes and LD with gbase
section: Review marker quality before LD construction
text:
Review marker quality before LD construction
gfilter() returns marker names in file order. It can screen MAF, missingness, exact Hardy–Weinberg p-values, imputation INFO when supplied, allele ambiguity, indels and the assembly-specific MHC interval. The returned names can be fed back into gprep(); filtering the Glist after building LD would leave an inconsistent reference.
retained <- gfilter(reference_Glist,
  maf = 0.01, missing = 0.05, hwe = 1e-12,
  ambiguous = TRUE, indels = TRUE, verbose = TRUE)

# For a study that applies this filter:
filtered_reference <- gprep(bedfiles = paste0(prefix, ".bed"),
  ids = reference_ids, rsids = retained, nthreads = 4)
The saved 20K/50K run used all 50,000 simulated markers in its LD resource; filtered_reference above illustrates the optional QC route and is not the source of the tables below.

title: Prepare genotypes and LD with gbase
text:
Compute and reuse sparse LD
The simulation has 500 independent 100-marker regions. Its full within-region LD is retained with r2 = 0; the 100-variant window bounds the calculation. For real data, choose windows and thresholds appropriate to the intended method and report them with the reference.
dir.create("analysis", showWarnings = FALSE)
reference_Glist <- gprep(Glist = reference_Glist, task = "sparseld",
  out_prefix = "analysis/reference-LD",
  max_distance_bp = 0, max_distance_variants = 100,
  r2 = 0, block_size = 128, nthreads = 4,
  overwrite = TRUE)
reference_Glist$assembly <- "artificial-20k-50k"

block_table <- data.frame(
  block_id = names(regions),
  first_marker = vapply(regions, `[`, character(1), 1L),
  last_marker = vapply(regions, function(x) tail(x, 1L), character(1))
)
reference_Glist <- define_ld_blocks(reference_Glist, block_table)
verify_ld(reference_Glist)
saveRDS(reference_Glist, "analysis/reference-Glist.rds")
define_ld_blocks() verifies that the named, ordered partition is exhaustive and that retained LD does not cross blocks. verify_ld() explicitly scans the complete resource after construction or transfer. Routine readers use the lightweight Glist identity check when opening the same immutable LD files. Keep the Glist RDS together with its referenced LD files.

title: Prepare genotypes and LD with gbase
section: Inspect LD and compute annotation scores
text:
Inspect LD and compute annotation scores
Ordinary LD scores are already stored in the Glist. ld_region() returns a named dense matrix for a small ordered marker set; ld_eigen() returns its complete verified eigensystem. Use these for inspection or methods that need a regional matrix rather than repeatedly reading the whole reference.
reference_Glist <- readRDS("analysis/reference-Glist.rds")
validate_Glist(reference_Glist)
scores <- ld_scores(reference_Glist)
R_region1 <- ld_region(reference_Glist, regions$region001)
eigen_region1 <- ld_eigen(reference_Glist, regions$region001)

ld_markers <- unlist(reference_Glist$rsidsLD, use.names = FALSE)
annotation <- matrix(as.numeric(ld_markers %in% regions$region001), ncol = 1,
  dimnames = list(ld_markers, "region001"))
annotation_scores <- ld_scores(reference_Glist, annotation = annotation)
An annotation score at marker j accumulates squared LD from j to the annotated markers, including LD crossing the annotation boundary. This is the input needed for standard stratified LDSC in gcorr.

title: Prepare genotypes and LD with gbase
text:
Align GWAS statistics
checkStat() maps a reported GWAS table to the reference’s marker IDs, coordinates and effect-allele direction. It returns an ordinary data frame in reference order. In the simulated run, the following explicit options retain all 50,000 markers so the methods share the same marker universe:
aligned <- checkStat(reference_Glist, raw_stat,
  excludeMAF = NULL, excludeMAFDIFF = NULL, excludeINFO = NULL,
  excludeCGAT = FALSE, excludeINDEL = FALSE, excludeDUPS = TRUE,
  excludeMHC = FALSE, excludeMISS = NULL, excludeHWE = NULL)

head(aligned[c("rsids", "chr", "pos", "ea", "nea", "b", "seb", "p", "n")])
raw_stat is assembled from the glma association result. For a real GWAS, choose QC thresholds deliberately; do not infer alleles or sample sizes from the LD reference. The aligned table is used by gbayes, gcorr, gmap and VEGAS.
Download the reference summary

title: Association analysis with glma
text: This tutorial uses the artificial PLINK panel distributed with gsuite: 96 individuals, 48 markers and six chromosome-local regions. gsim creates two continuous traits from declared marker effects. The small example is intended to explain the interface and results; it is not a power, calibration or performance study.

title: Association analysis with glma
text:
Prepare the genotype panel
library(gbase)
library(glma)
library(gsim)

example_dir <- system.file("extdata", "summary-statistic", package = "gsuite")
bed <- file.path(example_dir, "reference.bed")
Glist <- gprep(bedfiles = bed)

length(Glist$ids)
sum(lengths(Glist$rsids))
Glist fixes the selected people, markers, alleles and source-file order used by every individual-level analysis below.

title: Association analysis with glma
text:
Simulate two quantitative traits
Declare a few nonzero effects, then let gsim generate phenotypes from the existing genotype panel.
markers <- unlist(Glist$rsids, use.names = FALSE)
traits <- c("trait_A", "trait_B")
effects <- matrix(0, length(markers), length(traits),
  dimnames = list(markers, traits))
effects[c(3, 11, 27, 35), "trait_A"] <- c(.45, -.30, .35, .25)
effects[c(3, 19, 27, 43), "trait_B"] <- c(.30, .40, -.25, .35)

simulation <- gsim(
  Glist = Glist,
  nt = 2,
  architecture = "fixed",
  beta = effects,
  h2 = c(.45, .35),
  vg = c(.45, .35),
  re = .15,
  standardize_W = FALSE,
  scale_effects = TRUE,
  seed = 20260929,
  compute_sumstats = FALSE,
  chunk_size = 16
)

set.seed(20260930)
covariates <- matrix(rnorm(length(Glist$ids)), ncol = 1,
  dimnames = list(Glist$ids, "batch"))
phenotypes <- simulation$Y + .25 * covariates[, 1]
rownames(phenotypes) <- Glist$ids
colnames(phenotypes) <- traits
Named phenotype rows and covariate rows are aligned to the selected Glist individuals. An intercept is added by glma; do not include one in covariates.

title: Association analysis with glma
section: Scan one or several quantitative traits
text:
Scan one or several quantitative traits
linear <- glma_linear(
  phenotype = phenotypes,
  Glist = Glist,
  covariates = covariates,
  block_size = 16
)

linear
The phenotype matrix produces one glma_fit per named trait while BED reading and genotype decoding are shared:
<glma_multi_fit> 2 quantitative traits: trait_A, trait_B
The principal result is an ordinary data frame:
association_A <- linear$trait_A$associations
head(association_A[c("marker", "chromosome", "a1", "a2",
  "beta", "se", "statistic", "p", "status")])

successful_A <- subset(association_A, status == "ok")
successful_A[order(successful_A$p), ][1:5, ]
For a linear scan, beta is the allele-1 dosage effect, se its standard error, and statistic the t statistic. Every selected marker remains in the table. A marker that cannot be tested has a non-ok status and unavailable estimates rather than being silently removed.

title: Association analysis with glma
text:
Condition on selected markers
condition_on uses 1-based positions in selected Glist marker order. The specified genotypes enter the fixed-effect design together.
conditional <- glma_linear(
  phenotype = phenotypes[, "trait_A"],
  Glist = Glist,
  covariates = covariates,
  condition_on = 3L,
  block_size = 16
)

conditional$method
conditional$diagnostics
head(conditional$associations)
This answers whether each tested marker contributes after adjustment for the conditioning marker. It is not a multi-marker omnibus test.

title: Association analysis with glma
text:
Analyse a binary trait
Create a reproducible binary outcome from the first simulated genetic value and the same covariate.
probability <- plogis(
  -.4 + as.numeric(scale(simulation$G[, 1])) + .25 * covariates[, 1]
)
binary <- rbinom(length(probability), 1, probability)
names(binary) <- Glist$ids

logistic <- glma_logistic(binary, Glist, covariates, block_size = 16)
logistic

head(logistic$associations[c("marker", "case_n", "control_n",
  "beta", "se", "statistic", "p", "status")])
Here beta is an allele-1 log-odds effect and statistic is a Wald z statistic. Separation, sparse outcomes and convergence failures are reported in status. This route is ordinary logistic regression, not binary mixed-model association.

title: Association analysis with glma
section: Account for a genomic background with LOCO
text:
Account for a genomic background with LOCO
The infinitesimal route estimates a genomic background and refines it after excluding each chromosome. Small stochastic controls keep this teaching example quick; larger analyses should choose precision controls deliberately.
loco_controls <- list(
  simulation_count = 4L,
  rhe_probes = 8L,
  calibration_count = 6L,
  loco_batch_size = 2L,
  seed = 20260931
)

infinitesimal <- glma_infinitesimal_loco(
  phenotypes[, "trait_A"],
  Glist,
  covariates,
  algorithm = "chunk_ridge",
  block_size = 16,
  controls = loco_controls
)

infinitesimal
infinitesimal$fit[c("genetic_variance", "residual_variance")]
infinitesimal$fit$loco
infinitesimal$diagnostics
The association table contains calibrated one-degree-of-freedom chi-square statistics and p-values. beta and se are intentionally unavailable because this score route does not label approximate effects as exact mixed-model GLS estimates.
The alternative prior-selected background chooses among native prediction priors and returns marker effects after the selected global and LOCO refits:
prior_selected <- glma_prior_selected_loco(
  phenotypes[, "trait_A"],
  Glist,
  covariates,
  algorithm = "decoded_full",
  block_size = 16,
  controls = list(
    scaling_factor = 1,
    validation_fraction = .2,
    split_seed = 20260932,
    maximum_sweeps = 200L
  )
)

prior_selected$fit
prior_selected$diagnostics
head(prior_selected$associations)
The explicit scaling_factor = 1 keeps this tiny example deterministic and bypasses automatic structure calibration. It is not a general recommendation for real datasets.

title: Association analysis with glma
text:
Aggregate marker evidence with VEGAS
VEGAS uses checked summary statistics and sparse LD from the same Glist. Prepare the LD resource once and derive aligned effect/standard-error summaries from the linear scan.
ld_prefix <- tempfile("glma-tutorial-ld-")
LD_Glist <- gprep(
  Glist = Glist,
  task = "sparseld",
  out_prefix = ld_prefix,
  max_distance_bp = 0,
  max_distance_variants = 8,
  r2 = 0,
  block_size = 16,
  nthreads = 1
)

statistics <- data.frame(
  rsids = association_A$marker,
  ea = association_A$a1,
  nea = association_A$a2,
  b = association_A$beta,
  seb = association_A$se
)

sets <- split(markers, rep(paste0("region", 1:6), each = 8))

evidence <- vegas(
  statistics,
  LD_Glist,
  sets = sets,
  threads = 4,
  verbose = TRUE
)

evidence
evidence$stat$trait[c("set", "marker_count", "statistic",
  "score", "p_value", "p_available")]
Each marker set defines one region. The one-call form opens one sparse-LD reader and prepares eigenvalue spectra in bounded batches across marker sets. For repeated analyses, prepare the spectra once and reuse the ordinary serializable R object for any number of checked traits:
prepared <- prepare_vegas(LD_Glist, sets, threads = 4)
saveRDS(prepared, "vegas-reference.rds")

evidence_A <- vegas(statistics, prepared = prepared)
evidence_B <- vegas(statistics_B, prepared = prepared)
Evaluation does not reopen the LD resource or repeat the eigendecompositions. Memory remains bounded by the preparation thread count rather than the total number of sets. gsea::prepare_vegas() and gsea::vegas() re-export the same interfaces for pathway workflows.
For full within-gene LD computed directly from BED, prepare once through gbase and reuse the stored spectra in glma:
eigen_Glist <- gbase::gprep(Glist, task = "eigen", sets = sets, nthreads = 4)
prepared_BED <- prepare_vegas(eigen_Glist)
# Align checked statistics to prepared_BED$markers, including both alleles.
saveRDS(prepared_BED, "vegas-bed-reference.rds")
Each trait supplied to vegas(stat, prepared = prepared_BED) must contain every row of prepared_BED$markers in its exact marker and allele order. This metadata is the union of the requested gene markers. The saved spectra retain full gene membership; removing a marker requires preparation again. Constant positive weights within each gene can rescale the stored spectrum; nonuniform weights require sparse-LD preparation. Sparse-LD cutoffs and windows do not apply to the BED spectra. Tail defaults remain glma’s existing approximations; this route does not assert identical P-values to qgg’s different tail evaluator.
Remove the temporary sparse-LD files when the example is finished:
unlink(unlist(LD_Glist$sparseLD$paths, use.names = FALSE))

title: Association analysis with glma
text:
Save and report results
All results are ordinary R lists and data frames:
saveRDS(list(linear = linear, conditional = conditional,
  logistic = logistic, infinitesimal = infinitesimal,
  prior_selected = prior_selected, vegas = evidence),
  "glma-analysis.rds")

write.csv(association_A, "trait-A-associations.csv", row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(evidence$stat$trait, "trait-A-marker-sets.csv", row.names = FALSE)
For real analyses, inspect the complete status column, method-specific fit information and diagnostics before filtering by p-value. Multiple-testing correction, Manhattan/QQ plotting and scientific interpretation remain explicit analysis decisions rather than automatic transformations of the native output.
The larger connected genomic analysis shows linear GWAS and VEGAS results for 10,000 simulated individuals and 50,000 markers. The glma validation page records the focused numerical comparisons and their limits.

title: Preparing summaries, fitting Bayesian models and scoring
text: These interfaces connect existing native components. Preparation is explicit; estimators do not silently align alleles or change the marker universe. Current examples are shown below.

title: Preparing summaries, fitting Bayesian models and scoring
section: Prepare once, then choose the analysis
text:
Prepare once, then choose the analysis
For already aligned input, no preparation call is necessary. Otherwise, gbase::checkStat() maps user columns to an ordinary qgg-style checked data frame, validates values, harmonizes against Glist alleles and applies explicit QC thresholds:
stat <- gbase::checkStat(Glist = Glist, stat = raw)
Here raw contains explicitly mapped marker, coordinate, allele and analysis columns. checkStat() preserves the ordinary data-frame contract with canonical names such as rsids, chr, pos, ea, nea, eaf, b, seb, stat, p, n and info. Exact and swapped alleles can be harmonized explicitly; ambiguous or incompatible records are rejected or removed according to the requested policy. It does not standardize effects or infer the generating model. Task packages validate the subset and scale they require.

title: Preparing summaries, fitting Bayesian models and scoring
text:
Association evidence for marker sets
gbase::checkStat() can perform explicit mapping and Glist harmonisation; the association input remains an ordinary checked data frame. glma::vegas() calculates marker-set evidence against sparse LD attached by gbase::gprep(task = "sparseld"):
evidence <- glma::vegas(statistics, Glist, sets = marker_sets)
evidence$stat
Sets may represent genes, regions or annotations. This reuses native glma quadratic tests, with LD-aware null distributions and between-set score dependence. It is not enrichment or a claim of executable/RNG equivalence with historical VEGAS software. See the GWAS-to-pathway example for the connection to gsea() and its assumptions.

title: Preparing summaries, fitting Bayesian models and scoring
text:
Construct and apply genomic scores
weights <- gscore::clump_threshold(statistics, reference_Glist,
  p_threshold = 5e-8, r2_threshold = 0.1, window_bp = 250000)
scores <- gscore::gscore(weights, target_Glist)
scores$scores
clump_threshold() is the only scoring-specific weight construction route. Its sparse-LD reference must cover the whole clumping rule: no variant-count window (max_distance_variants = 0), a base-pair window at least as wide as window_bp, and an LD construction r2 threshold no larger than r2_threshold. The bounded reference in the package tutorial is not suitable for its 250 kb C+T example; the scoring tutorial shows a separate reference construction. Other weights come from their statistical model owner, for example gbayes_fit$weights, including method = "sbayesrc". The portable weight frame declares marker coordinates, effect and other alleles, allele frequency, and one or more numeric score columns. gscore() aligns exact or swapped alleles to every active Glist BED component, preserves selected sample order, and records omitted weighted markers. It supports standardized or raw mean-imputed dosage coding and applies multiple score columns in one call.
Bayesian posterior means can be applied genome-wide or by supplied marker sets:
fit <- gbayes::gbayes(
  checked, reference_Glist, method = "bayesr",
  control = list(burnin = 1000, sampling_sweeps = 5000,
                 seeds = c(11, 29))
)

scores <- gscore::gscore(
  fit$weights, target_Glist,
  sets = marker_sets,
  include_total = TRUE
)
sets is a uniquely named list of marker names. The target Glist resolves each name to its BED component and physical column, so callers do not split sets by chromosome or calculate file offsets. Sets may overlap and span BED files. The native scorer decodes each required marker once per file and accumulates all set scores from sparse membership, without constructing a dense marker-by-set coefficient matrix. scores$coverage, scores$set_membership and scores$missing_set_markers record the resolved contract. By default only set scores are returned; include_total=TRUE also retains the original score columns. Optional named set_weights are applied after score standardization.
gscore does not fit ridge, L1 or mixture models and does not select models on validation summaries. Those are statistical-learning tasks, not genomic scoring.

title: Preparing summaries, fitting Bayesian models and scoring
text:
Additional Bayesian inference engines
checked <- gbase::checkStat(Glist=Glist, stat=reported)
vb <- gbayes::gbayes(checked, Glist, method="variational",
                     prior=list(p=.01, h2=.4))
mixture <- gbayes::gbayes(checked, Glist, method="mixture_variational",
                  prior=list(variances=c(0,.01), weights=c(.9,.1)))
gibbs <- gbayes::gbayes(checked, Glist, method="point_normal",
                prior=list(p=.01, h2=.4),
                control=list(seed=17, burnin=500, sampling_sweeps=1000))
summary(vb)
These routes accept one trait and a Glist containing prepared sparse LD, and return the common gbayes_fit contract with method-specific estimates and diagnostics.

Point-normal Gibbs: p and h2 determine the initial prior. Controls include burnin=500, sampling_sweeps=200, seed=1, sparse=FALSE and auto_update=FALSE. Native parameter paths remain visible. Marker variances are not supplied by this engine and remain unavailable.
Point-normal / mixture variational: fixed priors, maximum_iterations=200 and tolerance=1e-8. Optional windows is a two-column matrix of one-based inclusive ranges. Windows may overlap; a single ordered window pass does not establish whole-panel convergence. Objective/drift/window diagnostics remain available; posterior variances are variational approximations.
Continuous shrinkage: prior=list(global_scale=1); controls burnin=500, sampling_sweeps=500, thinning=5, seed=1, learn_global_scale=FALSE, maximum_block_dimension=2048 and required block_offsets=c(0,...,M). This is an explicitly zero-based boundary vector, not marker IDs. Native checks reject retained cross-block LD. LD must be materialized. Local/global/residual-scale summaries are returned; this continuous prior has no inclusion PIP, and marker variances remain unavailable.

These bindings use one chain/fit (threads=1). They do not inherit BayesC/BayesR multitrait, annotation, parameter-learning or posterior-summary controls. They do not manufacture ESS, R-hat or uncertainty absent from the native result. Independent reruns and appropriate statistical qualification remain necessary.

title: Preparing summaries, fitting Bayesian models and scoring
section: Reuse GNOVA annotations for grouped covariance models
text:
Reuse GNOVA annotations for grouped covariance models
library(gcorr)
grouped <- gcorr_grouped_covariance(source_fit, continuous = TRUE,
  units = setNames(rep("standardized genetic covariance", 3),
                   c("A", "B", "C")))
sem <- gcorr_grouped_sem(grouped, sem_model)
ggm <- gcorr_grouped_ggm(grouped, edges)
gcorr accepts a coordinated continuous-trait GNOVA or SumHer fit that retains full cross-group jackknife covariance. It returns joint SEM or fixed-graph GGM estimates and exposes explicit cross-group test functions. See the covariance guide and the deterministic example. Regional LAVA partial-correlation and regression analyses remain separate workflows.

title: Genetic covariance models
text:
gcorr_covariance() requires a finite labelled continuous-trait covariance matrix, compatible named units and, for model fitting, the full joint sampling covariance of lower-column moments.
library(gcorr)

traits <- c("A", "B", "C")
G <- matrix(c(1, .3, .2, .3, 1, .4, .2, .4, 1), 3,
  dimnames = list(traits, traits))
labels <- c("A|A", "B|A", "C|A", "B|B", "C|B", "C|C")
V <- diag(.001, 6)
dimnames(V) <- list(labels, labels)
input <- gcorr_covariance(G, V, continuous = TRUE,
  units = setNames(rep("standard deviations", 3), traits))

title: Genetic covariance models
text:
gcorr_covariance() requires a finite labelled continuous-trait covariance matrix, compatible named units and, for model fitting, the full joint sampling covariance of lower-column moments.
library(gcorr)

traits <- c("A", "B", "C")
G <- matrix(c(1, .3, .2, .3, 1, .4, .2, .4, 1), 3,
  dimnames = list(traits, traits))
labels <- c("A|A", "B|A", "C|A", "B|B", "C|B", "C|C")
V <- diag(.001, 6)
dimnames(V) <- list(labels, labels)
input <- gcorr_covariance(G, V, continuous = TRUE,
  units = setNames(rep("standard deviations", 3), traits))

title: Genetic covariance models
text:
Structural models
gcorr_sem() consumes an explicit recursive model with variables, parameter starts/bounds and directed or disturbance entries. gcorr_sem_test() tests named linear constraints using the fitted joint parameter covariance.
model <- list(
  variables = c(traits, "F"),
  parameters = data.frame(name = c("lA", "lB", "lC", "vA", "vB", "vC"),
    start = c(rep(.5, 3), rep(.7, 3)),
    lower = c(rep(-Inf, 3), rep(1e-8, 3)), upper = rep(Inf, 6)),
  entries = data.frame(
    matrix = c(rep("directed", 3), rep("disturbance", 4)),
    row = c(traits, traits, "F"), column = c(rep("F", 3), traits, "F"),
    parameter = c("lA", "lB", "lC", "vA", "vB", "vC", ""),
    value = c(rep(0, 6), 1)))
sem <- gcorr_sem(input, model)

title: Genetic covariance models
text:
Graphical models
gcorr_ggm_network() reports the descriptive all-trait conditional network. gcorr_ggm() fits an explicitly allowed fixed graph; it performs no graph search. gcorr_ggm_test() tests selected fitted free edges.
edges <- matrix(c("A", "B", "B", "C"), ncol = 2, byrow = TRUE)
network <- gcorr_ggm_network(input)
graph <- gcorr_ggm(input, edges)
edge_test <- gcorr_ggm_test(graph, edges[1, , drop = FALSE])

title: Genetic covariance models
text:
Grouped models
gcorr_grouped_covariance() extracts GNOVA categories, SumHer architecture components or transformed SumHer categories with their full cross-group jackknife covariance. gcorr_grouped_sem() and gcorr_grouped_ggm() apply one prespecified model across groups; their test functions propagate cross-group uncertainty. Marginal standard errors are never substituted for the required joint covariance.

title: From GWAS results to fine-mapping and colocalisation
text:
There are two routes. A saved individual-level BED gbayes::gbayes() fit can be interpreted by region using LD from the same people and markers. This reuses the global posterior and does not refit it. Alternatively, start with aligned GWAS results and a Glist augmented with sparse LD. Prepare the statistics, fit each region and trait, inspect marker support, then compare fitted multi-effect components with gmap_coloc_components().
This example requires development installations of gbase, gbayes, gmap and gsim. The website displays saved results and does not run models. The current calls are shown below; a refreshed end-to-end script remains separate work.

title: From GWAS results to fine-mapping and colocalisation
text:
There are two routes. A saved individual-level BED gbayes::gbayes() fit can be interpreted by region using LD from the same people and markers. This reuses the global posterior and does not refit it. Alternatively, start with aligned GWAS results and a Glist augmented with sparse LD. Prepare the statistics, fit each region and trait, inspect marker support, then compare fitted multi-effect components with gmap_coloc_components().
This example requires development installations of gbase, gbayes, gmap and gsim. The website displays saved results and does not run models. The current calls are shown below; a refreshed end-to-end script remains separate work.

title: From GWAS results to fine-mapping and colocalisation
text:
Familiar summary-statistic calls
For statistics computed from the selected BED people, regional BayesC/BayesR can use full LD directly in memory:
G <- gbase::gprep(bedfiles="cohort.bed")
sets <- list(locus=c("marker1", "marker2", "marker3"))
fit <- gmap::gmap(Glist=G, stat=stat, sets=sets, method="bayesC",
  algorithm="mcmc", nit=1000, nburn=100, seed=10, output="full")
head(fit$stat)       # bm: native posterior effect mean; dm: PIP
head(fit$post)      # one row per region: ve, vg, vb, pi, pip, marker/range summaries
head(fit$conv)      # native R-hat, ESS, MCSE and diagnostic statuses by region
fit$cs              # marginal-PIP/LD groups by region
fit$timings         # decoding, LD product, preparation and sampling phases
gbase::mapSets(sets, Glist=G) maps named marker sets to prepared marker IDs or indices; unknown members are dropped and empty sets stay visible. gbase::getLD(G, rsids=sets$locus) returns full regional correlation in requested marker order without writing an LD file. Missing dosages are mean-imputed. Local nthreads controls decoding; the dense product uses R’s configured BLAS.
algorithm="mcmc" requires positive-definite LD, applies no PSD repair or truncation, and does not require sparse LD. algorithm="mcmc-eigen" retains the sparse-LD eigen route and its explicit retained-mass controls. Existing regions and score/information calls retain their advanced defaults.
Familiar calls default to one chain, 1000 post-burn sweeps, 100 burn-in sweeps, h2=.5, mc=5000, BayesC weights c(.99,.01), and learned slab/residual variances and mixture weights. Residual learning asserts in-sample LD and rejects a likelihood dimension exceeding the selected reference sample count. nit, nburn, nthin, nrun, seed, pi, gamma, vb, ve and updateB/updateE/updatePi adapt to native controls; conflicting explicit aliases and nested settings are rejected. post$vg is the posterior mean of the joint-effect quadratic b' C b / n, evaluated from the sampler’s cached residual; it is not qgg’s separate genetic-variance hyperparameter draw. post$pi is the total non-null mixture probability, pi0, pi1, … retain each mixture weight, and post$pip sums marker PIPs (expected active count). conv has rhat_*, ess_*, mcse_* and status_* columns for these quantities; these are native diagnostics, rather than qgg Geweke z scores. Fixed quantities, missing traces and single-chain limitations remain explicit. ntrials and cutoff record selected eigen attempts and retained mass. One-chain fits remain provisional. Original native tables and details remain available.
BayesC/BayesR accept the same optional LD-swap controls as gbayes() on both dense and eigen routes:
fit <- gmap::gmap(Glist=G, stat=stat, sets=sets, method="bayesC",
  algorithm="mcmc", nit=1000, nburn=100, nrun=4, seed=10,
  control=list(ld_swap=list(probability=.05, minimum_r2=.8,
    maximum_friends=50L, moves=1L)))
fit$ld_swap
The sampler proposes relocating an active effect to an inactive LD neighbour, using its native Metropolis-Hastings acceptance rule. probability selects a sweep for up to moves proposals; minimum_r2 and maximum_friends bound the neighbour list. LD is defined by the fitted cross-products, including retained eigen truncation. The result has one row per selected region/trait fit, with attempted and accepted counts and an acceptance rate; per-chain counts are in details. Counts include burn-in. Without an attempted move the rate is NA. These counts describe proposal activity, not convergence. The native neighbour list is prepared once per region/trait likelihood and shared across its chains; LD is not recomputed from genotypes for each swap.
Probability defaults to zero in both packages; zero moves also disables swaps and neighbour preparation. Optional neighbour preparation adds cost, particularly for eigen operators. Existing manuscript timings used swaps disabled and are preserved. The multi-effect variational method does not accept LD-swap controls.
Saved regional or genome-wide PIPs can be grouped without refitting:
groups <- gmap::getCredibleSets(Glist=G, fit=fit, sets=sets,
  cs_threshold=.8, cs_r2=.5, cs_method="CS2")
This standalone native helper reproduces qgg CS2/CS3 ordering and strict LD^2 > r2 neighborhoods. Its grouping target is marginal-PIP mass (expected active-marker count), not guaranteed component credible coverage. It has no qgg runtime dependency. Multi-trait results require an explicit trait.

title: From GWAS results to fine-mapping and colocalisation
section: From an individual-level BED fit to regional marker support
text:
From an individual-level BED fit to regional marker support
First fit the whole selected marker panel using pre-adjusted phenotypes, as in the Bayesian regression guide. Then prepare sparse LD from that same Glist and use it to interpret the saved posterior in named regions:
G <- gbase::gprep(bedfiles="cohort.bed", ids=phenotypes$id)
fit <- gbayes::gbayes(data=phenotypes, Glist=G, trait="height", method="bayesr",
  prior=list(residual_variance=.8, effect_variance=.2),
  control=list(burnin=1000, sampling_sweeps=4000, seeds=c(31,97)))

G <- gbase::gprep(Glist=G, task="sparseld", out_prefix="build/ld/cohort",
  r2=0, max_distance_bp=0, max_distance_variants=49)
regions <- list(locus=G$sparseLD$marker_metadata$marker_id[101:150])
mapped <- gmap::gmap_bed(fit, G, regions)
summary(mapped)
plot(mapped, region="locus", trait="height")
The 101:150 marker range is illustrative; choose a biological region in reference order. Here r2=0 and the 49-marker window retain every pair in that contiguous 50-marker region. Set the window to span the largest region you intend to interpret. gmap_bed() checks the saved fit against the Glist’s selected people, physical BED marker offsets, alleles and frequencies. It rejects incomplete within-region LD unless control=list(allow_incomplete_ld=TRUE) is explicitly supplied; those groups are then labelled approximate. Regions are bounded to 2048 markers by default.
The returned PIPs and effect summaries are from the global BED fit. Native gmap groups these marginal PIPs using within-region LD. These groups are not component credible sets, do not carry guaranteed coverage and are not regional refits. Inspect chain behavior and parameter summaries on fit itself. The same call accepts a saved joint-trait BED BayesC/BayesR fit and returns separate labelled regional views for each trait.

title: From GWAS results to fine-mapping and colocalisation
text:
Prepare summary statistics
Each trait has an ordinary data frame with marker, allele1, allele2, beta, se and n. allele1 is the effect/counting allele. Marker rows and alleles must already match the entire reference in order. Alignment is a separate task; this helper never flips, reorders or drops markers.
library(gmap)
G <- readRDS("build/examples/gmap-workflow/Glist.rds")
example <- readRDS("build/examples/gmap-workflow/workflow.rds")
gwas <- example$gwas
head(gwas$A)
stat <- gmap_stat(gwas, G,
                 phenotype_variance = example$phenotype_variance)
regions <- example$regions
The helper supports continuous outcomes analysed by ordinary linear regression with an intercept and conventional standard errors: a separate y ~ marker regression for each marker, without other covariates. All markers within a trait must use the same individuals. Supply the sample phenotype variance, not the residual variance or an assumed value of one.
For centered genotype \(x_j\) and outcome \(y\), the OLS identities give:
\[
d_j=x_j^\mathsf{T}x_j
= \frac{(n-1)s_y^2}{(n-2)\operatorname{SE}(\hat\beta_j)^2+\hat\beta_j^2},
\qquad x_j^\mathsf{T}y=d_j\hat\beta_j.
\]
gmap_stat() returns marker_ss = d and score = d * beta. The native model combines these with the regional LD correlation matrix \(R\):
\[
X^\mathsf{T}X \approx D^{1/2} R D^{1/2},\qquad D=\operatorname{diag}(d_j).
\]
The marginal conversion is exact under the stated OLS contract. The full matrix is exact only with matching in-sample LD, apart from storage precision. This example uses an independent panel, so its off-diagonal entries are approximations. The SuSiE summary-statistic documentation also explains the role of in-sample LD in recovering an individual-data fit.
Covariate-adjusted, mixed-model, logistic, robust-SE, meta-analysis and varying-sample-size summaries are outside this helper’s contract. It cannot recognise the generating analysis from numbers alone. Supplying equal n does not prove identical samples. Correctly prepared cross-products can still be passed directly to gmap(); z-only conversion is deferred.

title: From GWAS results to fine-mapping and colocalisation
section: A small simulation with known truth
text:
A small simulation with known truth
The complete script generates binomial dosages with correlated neighbours and uses gsim() for continuous phenotypes. The artificial coordinates have no biological interpretation.







Setting
Value




GWAS cohorts
Two disjoint cohorts of 10,000 individuals each


LD reference
Independent 4,000-individual panel from the same generator


Regions
Two artificial chromosomes, 20 markers each


Genotype construction
Allele frequency 0.3; adjacent copy probability 0.8


Shared region
m08 affects both traits


Distinct region
m25 affects A; m36 affects B


Effects
0.12 and 0.14 per standardized dosage; converted to raw-dosage units


Residual variance
Known simulation value 1, fixed during fitting


Seeds
Genotypes 20260915; gsim 20260916 and 20260917



The LD reference retains all within-region correlations, is prepared once, and caches one eigensystem per region. Each call reuses that preparation across traits. The script fits traits separately; it is not a joint multivariate Bayesian model. Marginal GWAS results are calculated separately in each cohort.
By default, gmap() first retains 99.5% of the positive regional LD eigenvalue mass, then tries 99% and 95% only when the earlier likelihood does not meet the method’s convergence rule. The eigendecomposition is not repeated. For a region with several traits, one threshold is accepted only when every trait passes. Multi-effect fits use their native convergence flag; BayesC and BayesR use the configured maximum between-chain PIP range. The selected threshold, achieved mass, retained rank and score-projection change are in diagnostic_summary; eigen_attempts retains one lightweight row per attempted trait and threshold.
fit$diagnostic_summary
fit$eigen_attempts

# Exact full-rank likelihood, without fallback
full <- gmap(stat, G, regions, method = "multi_effect", prior = prior,
  control = list(effects = 3,
                 eigen = list(retained_positive_mass = 1)))
If no attempted likelihood passes, the last complete fit is returned with status = "provisional" and a warning; the threshold is therefore never hidden. Only positive directions are retained, materially indefinite LD is rejected, and every truncated likelihood explicitly projects the score into the retained space. Residual-variance learning currently requires the full-rank setting.

title: From GWAS results to fine-mapping and colocalisation
text:
Fit the three methods
prior <- list(residual_variance = 1, effect_variance = .04)
mc <- list(burnin = 1000, sampling_sweeps = 5000,
           seeds = c(31, 97), retain_diagnostics = TRUE)

bayesc <- gmap(stat, G, regions, method = "bayesc",
  prior = c(prior, list(inclusion_probability = .05)), control = mc)
bayesr <- gmap(stat, G, regions, method = "bayesr",
  prior = c(prior, list(weights = c(.95, .01, .01, .03))), control = mc)
multi <- gmap(stat, G, regions, method = "multi_effect", prior = prior,
  control = list(effects = 3, max_sweeps = 500,
                 estimate_effect_variance = TRUE,
                 eigen = list(retained_positive_mass = 1)))
These deliberately specified priors differ between methods; the example is not a ranking experiment. effect_variance is on the original GWAS effect scale. BayesR uses its default variance multipliers. Multi-effect can reduce unneeded component variances to zero. Residual variance is fixed in this example; the known simulation value is not a general recommendation for data. A regional fit also omits the other region’s small genetic contribution, so fixing the residual variance at one is a deliberate working approximation. The multi-effect fit uses full rank because its saved components are used for colocalisation below; component colocalisation does not accept a truncated likelihood.

title: From GWAS results to fine-mapping and colocalisation
text:
Learn parameters when needed
The default keeps the supplied variances and mixture weights fixed. To learn BayesC/BayesR effect variance and mixture weights, enable the native updates and supply explicit hyperpriors. For example, using the external-panel inputs above:
learned <- gmap(stat, G, regions, method = "bayesr",
  prior = list(residual_variance = 1, effect_variance = .04,
               effect_variance_prior = list(df = 6, scale = .04),
               weight_prior = c(95, 1, 1, 3)),
  control = c(mc, list(estimate_effect_variance = TRUE,
                      estimate_weights = TRUE)))
learned$parameters
These hyperpriors illustrate the syntax; they are not universal settings. The variance prior is scaled inverse chi-square (df, scale), and scale is not its mean. weight_prior contains Dirichlet concentrations, null component first. BayesR variance multipliers remain fixed. The parameter table distinguishes fixed values from pooled MCMC posterior means or multi-effect variational estimates. Per-chain parameter means and optional traces remain in details.
Residual learning needs in-sample LD, so it is not enabled for this example’s independent reference panel. With a separately prepared complete G_in_sample and statistics from the same individuals and centered design, the pattern is:
# Template: y, stat_in_sample and G_in_sample must describe the same data.
normalization <- list(A = list(response_ss = sum((y - mean(y))^2),
                               likelihood_dimension = length(y) - 1,
                               in_sample_ld = TRUE))
learned_multi <- gmap(list(A = stat_in_sample), G_in_sample, regions,
  method = "multi_effect", prior = prior,
  control = list(effects = 3, estimate_effect_variance = TRUE,
                 estimate_residual_variance = TRUE),
  normalization = normalization)
learned_multi$parameters
For an intercept-only model the likelihood dimension is n - 1, not the n - 2 used by each marginal regression’s standard error. Covariate-adjusted inputs require the corresponding residualized design and response. The function cannot verify sample identity; in_sample_ld=TRUE is an explicit assertion. Thresholded or incomplete regional LD is rejected for residual learning, and control$eigen$retained_positive_mass must be 1.
BayesC/BayesR additionally require residual_variance_prior = list(df=..., scale=...) when estimate_residual_variance=TRUE. Multi-effect uses variational updates without that hyperprior and reports its residual trace and convergence flag. Normalization applies to every selected region for its trait. A regional residual includes effects omitted from that region; it is not automatically the whole-genome environmental variance. Subsequent colocalisation uses fitted parameter values, without integrating parameter uncertainty.

title: From GWAS results to fine-mapping and colocalisation
text:
Inspect estimates, sets and chains
summary(bayesr)
head(bayesr$estimates)
posterior_sets <- gmap_sets(bayesr)
posterior_sets$summary
posterior_sets$members
gmap_bfdr(bayesr, threshold = c(0.8, 0.9, 0.95))
gmap_bfdr(bayesr, target = 0.05)
bayesr$details$shared$A$chain_agreement
plot(bayesr, region = "shared", trait = "A", quantity = "chains")
summary(multi)
multi$sets$shared$A
plot(multi, region = "shared", trait = "A", quantity = "objective")



Marker support for the three methods; vertical dotted lines mark the causal variants.


For this fixed simulation, all methods selected the causal marker first:

The top-marker PIPs exceed 0.99999. Each fit returned one complete set. All four multi-effect fits converged in two sweeps. The largest BayesR PIP range between the two chains was 0.014. These strong signals make an easy workflow demonstration, not a demanding fine-mapping evaluation.
BayesC/BayesR report PIPs pooled over the two chains. Chain-specific PIPs and ranges are available; agreement alone does not certify convergence. Their sets group marginal PIP mass within LD neighbourhoods. Multi-effect sets represent component assignment probabilities. These set probabilities are not interchangeable, and this one simulation does not establish coverage. The sum of PIPs is the expected number of active markers, not necessarily the number of independent signals.
gmap_sets() keeps the native interpretation in its meaning column: marginal_pip_mass for BayesC/BayesR neighbourhood groups and component_assignment for multi-effect credible sets. Its summary table also retains completeness, pairwise LD purity, incomplete-LD, duplicate and fit-status fields. The member table gives the markers, posterior weights and LD to the lead.
gmap_bfdr() uses only marker PIPs. At threshold \(t\), its expected number of false discoveries is \(\sum_{j:PIP_j\ge t}(1-PIP_j)\) and BFDR is that value divided by the number selected. With target, it returns the largest marker group defined by a PIP threshold whose BFDR is no larger than the target. This posterior summary does not provide a frequentist FDR guarantee.

title: From GWAS results to fine-mapping and colocalisation
text:
Compare the traits without refitting
shared <- gmap_coloc_components(
  multi, multi, G, trait1 = "A", trait2 = "B",
  control = list(complete_region_coverage = TRUE,
                 non_overlapping_samples = TRUE)
)
summary(shared)
shared$estimates
shared$component_status
plot(shared, region = "shared")
plot(shared, region = "distinct")



Component-pair colocalisation probabilities in the shared and distinct regions.


H0 means neither trait is associated; H1/H2 mean only one is associated; H3 means distinct causal variants; H4 means a shared causal variant. These are component-pair probabilities, not a single region-wide posterior. The defaults are per-variant priors \(p_1=p_2=10^{-4}\) and \(p_{12}=10^{-5}\). In this run, shared-region H4 was 0.999999999991; distinct-region H3 rounded to 1, with H4 about \(3.24\times10^{-45}\). These values reflect this strong, artificial example and its specified priors, not general performance. Changing these priors reuses the saved evidence. No eligible component pairs means there is no eligible comparison; it is not evidence for H0.

title: From GWAS results to fine-mapping and colocalisation
text:
Numerical checks and saved results
The script compares the converted scores and diagonals against direct cross-products from the simulated individuals. It also fits all three methods from both routes, with the same LD and seeds, and checks PIPs and posterior means. That validates the conversion; it does not validate the external-LD approximation or establish calibration. The LD file checksums are checked before and after fitting.
The run on 15 September 2026 used gsuite 0.43.0, gsim 0.9.0 and R 4.4.1. The largest score/diagonal discrepancy was \(1.82\times10^{-12}\); the largest posterior-mean discrepancy was \(1.11\times10^{-16}\). PIPs agreed to numerical precision. Approximate observed times for four region/trait fits per method were 0.69 s (BayesC), 6.16 s (BayesR) and 0.36 s (multi-effect). The whole script took 17.91 s, including preparation, repeat fits for verification, colocalisation and figures. These are illustrative elapsed times on one laptop, not a benchmark; another package-build process was also active.

example$equivalence

workflow.rds contains the summaries, prepared statistics, truth, fitted objects and checks. report.txt records summaries and package versions. The directory also contains two figures and compact CSV tables. Saved fits can be plotted without the LD files; a new gmap_coloc_components() call requires the reference files so that eligibility and reference checks can run.

title: From GWAS results to fine-mapping and colocalisation
text:
ABF colocalisation
For at most one causal variant per trait, compare the aligned GWAS tables directly. This route uses native gmap ABFs; it does not require an LD object, gmap_stat() or a Bayesian fine-mapping fit. The example’s two cohorts are disjoint, and each selected region contains one generating causal variant per trait, so it is suitable for illustrating this model.
markers <- regions$shared
first <- gwas$A[match(markers, gwas$A$marker), ]
second <- gwas$B[match(markers, gwas$B$marker), ]
abf <- gmap_coloc(
  first, second, region = "shared",
  phenotype_sd1 = sqrt(example$phenotype_variance[["A"]]),
  phenotype_sd2 = sqrt(example$phenotype_variance[["B"]]),
  p1 = 1e-4, p2 = 1e-4, p12 = 1e-5)
abf$shared_variant_probability
Each table requires rsids, chr, pos, ea, nea, b and seb. Rows and alleles must match exactly. ea is the effect allele; effects and standard errors are on the phenotype scale per allele. Phenotype standard deviations are supplied here, unlike the variances passed to gmap_stat(). The effect-prior SD is the specified fraction of each phenotype SD. Binary/log-odds, z-only and p-value-only inputs are not supported, and phenotype SD is never inferred.
H0 means neither trait is associated, H1/H2 one trait alone, H3 distinct causal variants and H4 a shared causal variant. Here these are regional probabilities under the single-causal model. The earlier multi-effect results instead apply to individual component pairs; they must not be added into a regional posterior. Marker probabilities are conditional on H4, not marginal fine-mapping PIPs.
Use separate calls to examine alternative association priors. Regional coverage and sample independence are scientific assumptions of this model and must be established by the caller. Selected MR instruments alone do not provide complete regional data. Evidence for shared association is not by itself evidence for a causal effect of one trait on another.

The small script supplies correlated genotypes to gsim(W = ...); gsim generates the effects and phenotypes. This artificial LD construction is not a demographic simulation. It provides differing LD scores without reference data downloads. Marginal regressions are calculated separately in the two disjoint GWAS samples. Their t statistics are supplied as z statistics, using the large-sample approximation. All marker identities and allele directions are aligned by construction; no harmonization is needed for this generated example.
The reference is prepared once as a separate LDlist, saved and reloaded. All three regional methods reuse its cached eigensystems. LD files remain unchanged during fitting. Every within-region correlation is retained; regions are treated as independent chromosomes for LD preparation.

title: gcorr method comparison: simulated results
text:
What counts as truth?
The effect draw does not have to reproduce its generating correlation exactly. For this draw, the population h2 values are 0.299 and 0.395, and the genetic correlation is 0.540, rather than the generating value of 0.60.
Truth is calculated from the realized gsim effects and the known population covariance of the genotype generator, not from the estimated reference LD. After converting standardized effects to raw-dosage effects, for region \(r\):
\[
G_r = B_r^\mathsf{T}\Sigma_r B_r,
\qquad (\Sigma_r)_{jk}=2(0.3)(0.7)\rho_r^{|j-k|}.
\]
The regions are independent, so \(G=\sum_r G_r\). Total phenotypic variances combine its diagonal with gsim’s residual variances. Regional covariance is scaled by the square root of the two total phenotypic variances; it is not a within-region genetic correlation. The script also checks that the effect conversion reproduces gsim’s individual genetic values.

title: Genetic correlation from summary statistics
text:
Genetic-correlation analysis uses the gcorr R package.


Every trait is an ordinary data frame using the qgg column names rsids, chr, pos, ea, nea, stat, and n. Here stat is the signed Z statistic. Use gbase::checkStat() when a Glist reference is available and alignment or QC is required. Marker order, coordinates and allele orientation must already agree across traits. The package never intersects, flips or rescales traits. The high-level ldsc() workflow obtains LD scores, annotation scores and reference metadata from a Glist; the focused interfaces also accept those quantities explicitly. A single data frame uses the label "trait"; pass a uniquely named list for multiple traits.
library(gbase)
library(gcorr)

markers <- paste0("rs", 1:20)
one <- data.frame(rsids = markers, chr = "1", pos = 1:20,
  ea = "A", nea = "G", stat = rep(2, 20), n = 10000)



The recommended LDSC interface uses the same stat contract as glma::vegas():
ordinary <- ldsc(stat = one, Glist = Glist, what = "h2")

multiple <- ldsc(
  stat = list(height = height_stat, bmi = bmi_stat),
  Glist = Glist,
  what = "rg"
)

partitioned <- ldsc(stat = one, Glist = Glist,
  sets = list(coding = coding_markers, regulatory = regulatory_markers),
  residual = TRUE, what = "h2")

grouped <- ldsc(stat = one, Glist = Glist,
  sets = list(region1 = region1_markers, region2 = region2_markers),
  set_model = "grouped", residual = TRUE, what = "h2")
Marker sets are named marker-ID vectors and may overlap. The default set_model = "stratified" uses standard annotation-specific LD scores and accounts for LD crossing set boundaries. set_model = "grouped" instead fits the qgg-style grouped construction by masking the stored ordinary LD-score vector with focal-marker membership; it avoids a sparse-LD scan and is most appropriate when cross-boundary LD is limited. Glist supplies the ordinary and annotation-specific LD scores and reference sample size. Deterministic contiguous delete blocks are generated when blocks is omitted. The result records the selected set model, retains the full fit, and adds convenient h2 and rg components.
The explicit focused functions are:

gcorr_ldsc() and gcorr_ldsc_partitioned();
gcorr_gnova() for ordinary or binary-annotation GNOVA;
gcorr_sumher() for architecture components and optional categories.

The package-owned gcorr(..., method=) dispatcher also selects the focused methods but has no task selector or control list.
scores <- setNames(seq(1, 2, length.out = 20), markers)
blocks <- setNames(rep(paste0("b", 1:5), each = 4), markers)

explicit <- gcorr_ldsc(one, scores, blocks, marker_count = 50000)
gnova <- gcorr(one, blocks = blocks, ld_scores = scores, method = "gnova")
Partitioned LDSC requires annotation LD scores, weighting LD scores and annotation sums. Annotated GNOVA additionally requires the matching binary annotation matrix and reference-panel sample size. SumHer requires uncorrected architecture LD scores, component weight sums and separate tagging values. These quantities are not inferred from one another.



gcorr_prepare_regions() reads named marker regions directly from Glist sparse LD through one native reader. It validates each complete eigensystem once; the resulting session-bound preparation is accepted by:

gcorr_hess() and gcorr_rho_hess();
gcorr_supergnova();
gcorr_lava(), gcorr_lava_partial() and gcorr_lava_regression();
gcorr_hdll().

regions <- gcorr_prepare_regions(Glist,
  regions = list(locus = markers[1:4]))
regional <- gcorr_hess(one, regions, maximum_components = 0,
  minimum_eigenvalue = 0)
Named signed-LD matrices plus their reference sample sizes remain supported when a Glist is not available.
The summary data frame must contain every regional marker. LAVA sampling correlations, binary-trait metadata and simulation seeds are explicit. SUPERGNOVA exposes covariance rather than correlation. HDL-L accepts exactly two continuous traits per fit. Joint HESS/rho-HESS requires disjoint prepared regions and reports its correction explicitly.

title: Development status and evidence
text:
gsuite remains in private development. gsim and gact are already public and retain their existing repositories and releases. See Downloads.



The capability overview separates native components from the current R workflows. Focused checks cover summary-statistic, covariance-model, MR, mapping, Bayesian and longitudinal integrations; they do not establish broad calibration or biobank-scale performance. Full R CMD check remains pending.
The model catalog records support for particular model, backend and inference combinations. Scoped evidence does not establish a complete pass for every package or platform.
formula and formulas are aliases in gfit(); their spelling does not select a fitting route. The retained compiled route is selected explicitly with control = gs_fit_control(...) and requires explicit gvc() components with complete starts and no separate pedigree argument. See the pedigree tutorial and formula reference. A catalog label must be interpreted within its stated scope, not as a blanket guarantee for any composition.



The 50K pedigree comparison with DMU publishes covariance estimates, selected prediction comparisons and descriptive single-run timings. It does not establish general speedups, compare likelihood constants, or qualify all current routes and platforms.
Other local-data and solver qualification campaigns are referenced in the technical guides. Their full development reports are not included in this publication. References to those reports lead here so that the limits of the available public evidence remain explicit.



Implementation, integration tests, internal reviews and build instructions remain in the private development repositories. This site provides public method descriptions and tutorial code, not private implementation source.
Website publishing is separate from software release approval. No software release or new licence grant is implied by this publication.
