title: From a scientific question to a supported model
text:
An assistant can help identify a missing interface, component combination or numerical capability, implement it and assemble validation evidence.
Code that runs becomes a supported model only after its statistical meaning and numerical behavior have been checked.
This tutorial illustrates the development workflow through example requests. It does not implement or qualify a new model. It complements analysis with an assistant, which describes working with existing gsuite interfaces.
crumbs: Developing a model with an assistant

title: From a scientific question to a supported model
section: 1. Begin with an analysis that needs more
text:
1. Begin with an analysis that needs more
You might ask:

I have repeated body-weight measurements. I want to distinguish additive genetic variation from persistent environmental differences between animals. Can my current gsuite workflow express that model? Check the existing machinery before proposing an implementation.

A candidate repeatability model is
\[
y = X\beta + Z_a a + Z_p p + e,
\]
with mutually independent random components
\[
\operatorname{Var}(a)=\sigma_a^2 A,\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(p)=\sigma_p^2 I,\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(e)=\sigma_e^2 I.
\]
Here \(a\) is the additive genetic animal effect, \(p\) is a permanent-environment animal effect shared across that animal’s observations, and \(e\) is the record-specific residual. The fixed design \(X\) must also reflect the study, including time effects where appropriate. This model does not by itself describe changing genetic trajectories or residual serial correlation.
This model already has an explicit gvc() workflow: the repeatability example uses separate grouping columns for animal and permanent-environment effects. It records the optimizer tolerance needed for that dataset and the stricter stopping limitation. The model catalog also lists specialized and component routes. For this request, use the existing workflow; the development steps below apply when a further requirement reveals a gap.
The assistant first inspects the installed interface, implementation and evidence. If an existing supported route meets the request, the next step is an analysis script using that route. Development begins only for an identified gap, such as exposing an existing composition through a particular interface.
crumbs: Developing a model with an assistant

title: From a scientific question to a supported model
text:
2. Classify the missing piece
You might ask:

Explain exactly what is missing. Is this an R-interface change, a combination of existing components, or new numerical work? Identify what can be reused.









Gap
Typical work
Evidence needed




Missing R interface
Add validation and translate R inputs into an existing model contract
Equivalent inputs produce the same model and results as the established route


Missing composition
Connect existing relationships, covariance blocks and record mappings
The assembled covariance and fitted results agree with an independent small reference


Missing numerical capability
Implement an operator, derivative, inference step or solver capability in its owning library
Mathematical checks, numerical reference comparisons and tests of the supported parameter domain



The qgtools-style specification separates formulas, record identities, relationship kernels, covariance descriptors and the fitting task. For the example, the two animal effects share grouping IDs but have different relationships: pedigree for genetic effects and identity for permanent environment. The internal representation must preserve that distinction.
The architecture guide identifies ownership: R validation and integration belong in gsuite, mixed-model inference in greml, and numerical solvers in gsolve. Genomic data operations remain with their existing owners. The primitive registry and model reductions help identify reusable machinery.
crumbs: Developing a model with an assistant

title: From a scientific question to a supported model
text:
3. Agree on the statistical contract
Before writing code, the assistant records what the model means and which cases the proposed extension will support.
For the repeatability example, this includes the definition of an observation, the animal ID mapping, pedigree coverage, repeated-record handling, fixed effects, covariance assumptions and prediction targets. It also includes missing-data behavior, starting values and supported variance boundaries.
The study must contain information to distinguish the components. For example, with one observation per animal, a permanent-environment identity effect and an independent residual cannot be separated by their covariance contributions. A more general syntax does not resolve identifiability.
You might ask:

Write down the model assumptions, input contract and supported domain. Explain which components the data can distinguish, and identify unsupported cases before implementing the extension.
crumbs: Developing a model with an assistant

title: From a scientific question to a supported model
text:
4. Implement a small, reusable extension
You might ask:

Implement the identified gap using existing public interfaces. Preserve current behavior, keep the change within the owning libraries, and make unsupported combinations fail clearly. Include focused validation.

Develop a reviewable patch. Where possible, translate new R syntax into an existing model description and reuse its fitting algorithm.
Keep the first supported scope explicit. Missingness, covariance boundaries, prediction and uncertainty each need their own contract; successful fitting does not automatically establish support for all of them.
crumbs: Developing a model with an assistant

title: From a scientific question to a supported model
text:
5. Establish statistical and numerical evidence
For a small deterministic repeatability example, independently assemble
\[
V = \sigma_a^2 Z_a A Z_a^{\mathsf T}
  + \sigma_p^2 Z_p Z_p^{\mathsf T}
  + \sigma_e^2 I.
\]
This dense calculation is a small reference, not the production execution strategy. It lets the assistant check the model independently of the new interface or assembly code.







Check
What it establishes




Covariance and record mapping at fixed parameters
The implementation represents the stated statistical model


Likelihood and fixed-covariance predictions against the small reference
Numerical calculations agree under matched conventions


Scores and information, where applicable
Optimization quantities match independent calculations; derivative checks use appropriate interior points


REML estimates and convergence against a trusted route
The supported fitting path reaches a consistent solution within declared tolerances


Reordered IDs, repeated records and supported missingness
Input representation does not silently change the model


Invalid inputs, unidentified designs and unsupported boundaries
Failures are explicit and do not silently substitute another model


Existing affected workflows
The extension preserves supported behavior



Tolerances and pass criteria should be chosen before interpreting results. Likelihood comparisons must reconcile constants and parameter conventions. Simulation is useful, but a fitted estimate need not equal its generating parameter in a finite sample. Agreement between two wrappers over the same engine checks integration; it is not an independent numerical reference.
You might ask:

Show me the validation evidence, including failures and untested cases. Separate evidence for model correctness, numerical accuracy and performance.

Larger workloads and repeated timings are a separate qualification step. A successful small example establishes only its tested scope; it does not establish production-scale performance or support on other platforms.
crumbs: Developing a model with an assistant

title: From a scientific question to a supported model
text:
6. Make support explicit and reproducible
The extension becomes a supported workflow only when its declared statistical contract and relevant numerical checks are satisfied. Update the model catalog and qualification evidence for the exact model, backend and inference combination, recording remaining limitations. Follow the repository’s required build and package checks as well as focused model tests.
The completed work should contain a reviewable implementation, deterministic reference checks, updated interface documentation, and a small tutorial users can run. Record the versions used for qualification. An implemented but unqualified route must retain that distinction in its documentation.
You might ask:

Summarize what is now supported, which checks passed, what remains outside scope, and how another user can reproduce the example.
crumbs: Developing a model with an assistant

title: From a scientific question to a supported model
text:
Grow capabilities through scientific use
Prefer extensions that other analyses can reuse: covariance structures, relationship mappings and inference capabilities. Scientific review and validation determine which resulting workflows gsuite can support.
crumbs: Developing a model with an assistant

title: Canonical LMM architecture
text:
This section defines the LMM architecture. Current dependency versions are recorded in package metadata; the original architecture baseline used greml 0.66.0. Capability status belongs in the model catalog, reusable machinery in the primitive registry, evidence in model qualification, and established equivalences in model reductions. Historical development notes do not supersede the current capability catalog.


Current public headers and R exports define what is implemented. Focused tests and committed qualification evidence determine whether a specific model/backend/inference combination is qualified. The catalog uses exactly:

qualified: implemented, publicly reachable where claimed, and covered by focused numerical or contract evidence for that combination;
implemented_unqualified: code exists, but the complete claimed combination lacks focused qualification;
unsupported: the combination rejects explicitly or has no implementation;
not_applicable: the concept does not apply to the route.

Code presence alone never establishes qualified. A limitation on one route must not be generalized to the suite.



The backend-independent specification contains caller-ordered observed records and stable record IDs; response values; compact fixed-coefficient references; random component, level, channel/trait, and basis references; deterministic external domains and coefficient order; relationship covariance or precision contracts; typed covariance layouts; residual blocks and groups; prediction targets; uncertainty requests; and separate resource/execution policy.
Caller record order may change only record-shaped output order. Scientific domains, parameter positions, likelihoods, active sets, coefficients, and uncertainty results are deterministic after alignment by external identity. Production stores short record-level coefficient-reference lists and never materializes a global fixed- or random-effect incidence matrix, dense or sparse. Pedigree routes reuse the committed ordering, inbreeding, Henderson precision, relationship diagonal, and determinant.




Component LMM coefficients are component-major, then level-major, then channel-major.
Pedigree random-regression coefficients are animal-major, then basis axis.
Pedigree multitrait coefficients retain declared trait order for every external animal.
Fixed effects retain validated caller column order.
Structured residual values use canonical variance-group order followed by rho or phi; they are not packed SPD matrices.
SPD covariance values retain declared channel/trait order and use explicit natural and log-Cholesky transformed layouts.

Every public result returns identities or names; callers do not infer them from undocumented offsets.



Scientific syntax is independent of PCG, CHOLMOD, PARDISO, batching, threading, and memory budgets. Gsolve owns numerical sessions and selected inversion; greml owns model assembly, likelihoods, derivatives, optimization, BLUP, and uncertainty; gsuite owns R validation, lowering, typed serialization, and external-order restoration.
Backend and trace method are distinct. CHOLMOD and PARDISO consume the same sparse MME, but only CHOLMOD supplies selected inversion. Coordinate traces are an exact bounded route. Retained-factor selected_solve target-block uncertainty is another exact bounded route and is not selected inversion. PCG has no retained direct factor. Stochastic Hutchinson/SLQ routes exist only where the catalog identifies them; they are never silent fallbacks for exact sparse-direct fits.
Incomplete-multitrait pedigree stochastic REML constructs deterministic counter-Rademacher trace and determinant banks once per fit and retains common probe identities across accepted and trial covariance states. Greml inference owns phase-aware precision: finite raw trace and score standard errors are diagnostics; nonstationary step resolution is assessed on curvature/Newton scales; convergence requires score compatibility with zero and adequate dimensionless log-Cholesky-scale uncertainty. Natural and transformed AI are validated and canonically symmetrized at the greml inference boundary before one identical matrix is used for rank diagnostics and the gsolve moment solve.
Stochastic covariance convergence, approximate likelihood availability, and BLUP finalization are distinct states. Final SLQ imprecision does not revoke an accepted score/AI optimum or prevent retained-response BLUP, but it makes the restricted likelihood unavailable for reporting or model comparison. Solver diagnostics likewise separate logical PCG systems from attempts, recovered warm-start retries, and unrecovered failures.
Successful direct optimization retains the accepted likelihood, factor, response, score, AI state, and relevant selected-inverse values. BLUP reuses the retained response. Exact coefficient PEV is the random-effect block of the inverse of the complete MME, conditional on fitted covariance parameters. Existing CHOLMOD selected inversion, pedigree trace contractions, longitudinal pedigree uncertainty, and component-LMM uncertainty are current capabilities. Exact PARDISO selected_solve PEV is qualified for the three sparse pedigree routes; PCG exact PEV and PARDISO selected inversion remain unsupported.



The component LMM’s opt-in active-set policy supports an exact zero scalar random component and rank-one two-channel covariance with KKT checks and reactivation. Larger covariance blocks and all residual parameters remain positive-interior. AR(1) and continuous exponential residual blocks share one typed residual-block abstraction; this does not imply ARMA, heterogeneous temporal scales, spatial covariance, or mixtures of residual structures.

title: Canonical LMM architecture
Canonical LMM architecture
text:
The backend-independent specification contains caller-ordered observed records and stable record IDs; response values; compact fixed-coefficient references; random component, level, channel/trait, and basis references; deterministic external domains and coefficient order; relationship covariance or precision contracts; typed covariance layouts; residual blocks and groups; prediction targets; uncertainty requests; and separate resource/execution policy.
Caller record order may change only record-shaped output order. Scientific domains, parameter positions, likelihoods, active sets, coefficients, and uncertainty results are deterministic after alignment by external identity. Production stores short record-level coefficient-reference lists and never materializes a global fixed- or random-effect incidence matrix, dense or sparse. Pedigree routes reuse the committed ordering, inbreeding, Henderson precision, relationship diagonal, and determinant.

title: Canonical LMM architecture
text:
Component LMM coefficients are component-major, then level-major, then channel-major.
Pedigree random-regression coefficients are animal-major, then basis axis.
Pedigree multitrait coefficients retain declared trait order for every external animal.
Fixed effects retain validated caller column order.
Structured residual values use canonical variance-group order followed by rho or phi; they are not packed SPD matrices.
SPD covariance values retain declared channel/trait order and use explicit natural and log-Cholesky transformed layouts.

Every public result returns identities or names; callers do not infer them from undocumented offsets.

title: Canonical LMM architecture
text:
Scientific syntax is independent of PCG, CHOLMOD, PARDISO, batching, threading, and memory budgets. Gsolve owns numerical sessions and selected inversion; greml owns model assembly, likelihoods, derivatives, optimization, BLUP, and uncertainty; gsuite owns R validation, lowering, typed serialization, and external-order restoration.
Backend and trace method are distinct. CHOLMOD and PARDISO consume the same sparse MME, but only CHOLMOD supplies selected inversion. Coordinate traces are an exact bounded route. Retained-factor selected_solve target-block uncertainty is another exact bounded route and is not selected inversion. PCG has no retained direct factor. Stochastic Hutchinson/SLQ routes exist only where the catalog identifies them; they are never silent fallbacks for exact sparse-direct fits.
Incomplete-multitrait pedigree stochastic REML constructs deterministic counter-Rademacher trace and determinant banks once per fit and retains common probe identities across accepted and trial covariance states. Greml inference owns phase-aware precision: finite raw trace and score standard errors are diagnostics; nonstationary step resolution is assessed on curvature/Newton scales; convergence requires score compatibility with zero and adequate dimensionless log-Cholesky-scale uncertainty. Natural and transformed AI are validated and canonically symmetrized at the greml inference boundary before one identical matrix is used for rank diagnostics and the gsolve moment solve.
Stochastic covariance convergence, approximate likelihood availability, and BLUP finalization are distinct states. Final SLQ imprecision does not revoke an accepted score/AI optimum or prevent retained-response BLUP, but it makes the restricted likelihood unavailable for reporting or model comparison. Solver diagnostics likewise separate logical PCG systems from attempts, recovered warm-start retries, and unrecovered failures.
Successful direct optimization retains the accepted likelihood, factor, response, score, AI state, and relevant selected-inverse values. BLUP reuses the retained response. Exact coefficient PEV is the random-effect block of the inverse of the complete MME, conditional on fitted covariance parameters. Existing CHOLMOD selected inversion, pedigree trace contractions, longitudinal pedigree uncertainty, and component-LMM uncertainty are current capabilities. Exact PARDISO selected_solve PEV is qualified for the three sparse pedigree routes; PCG exact PEV and PARDISO selected inversion remain unsupported.

title: Longitudinal sparse-pedigree REML and BLUP
text:
Longitudinal sparse-pedigree REML and BLUP
gs_longitudinal_pedigree_records() stores only observed scalar longitudinal records. Each row supplies an animal, phenotype, reporting time, fixed-design row, caller-supplied random-regression basis row, and residual-group label. Missing occasions are absent rows. Records may be irregular, repeated, arbitrarily ordered, and uneven across animals; pedigree-only animals remain in the fitted domain. Character residual groups use deterministic lexical order and integer groups use deterministic numeric order, so record permutation does not change covariance-parameter positions.
ped <- gs_pedigree_data(
  individual = c("dam", "sire", "offspring", "relative"),
  sire = c(NA, NA, "sire", "sire"),
  dam = c(NA, NA, "dam", "dam")
)
animal <- c("dam", "dam", "sire", "offspring", "offspring")
time <- c(0, 1.4, 0.2, 0.7, 2.1)
y <- c(1.1, 1.8, 0.9, 1.4, 2.2)

records <- gs_longitudinal_pedigree_records(
  ped, animal, y, time,
  basis = cbind(intercept = 1, time = time),
  fixed = cbind(intercept = 1, time = time),
  residual_group = ifelse(time < 1, "early", "late")
)
start <- gs_longitudinal_pedigree_start(records)
control <- gs_longitudinal_pedigree_reml_control(
  linear_solver = "sparse_direct", direct_backend = "pardiso",
  requested_threads = 8,
  exact_trace_method = "coordinate",
  maximum_direct_coefficient_dimension = 5000,
  max_exact_trace_systems = 5000
)
fit <- gs_longitudinal_pedigree_fit(
  records, start, covariance = "optimized", control = control,
  prediction = list(
    animal = c("offspring", "relative"), time = c(1.5, 1.5),
    basis = cbind(1, c(1.5, 1.5)),
    fixed = cbind(1, c(1.5, 1.5))
  )
)
The deterministic non-RHE start fits the supplied fixed design, calculates \(s_r^2=\frac{\mathrm{RSS}}{N-\operatorname{rank}(X)}\) and mean basis magnitude \(m_b=\frac{1}{N}\sum_j\lVert b_j\rVert^2\), then sets \(Q_0=\frac{s_r^2}{2m_b}I\) and each residual-group variance to \(s_r^2/2\). User-supplied SPD Q and positive residual starts override it.
Both solvers use one canonical animal-major sparse MME. linear_solver = "pcg" is portable and is the large fixed-covariance BLUP route. "sparse_direct" is an optional moderate-problem route with one reused PARDISO or CHOLMOD symbolic analysis, exact retained-factor likelihood, and bounded complete coordinate traces. Automatic selection prefers PARDISO; CHOLMOD and support work are serial. Explicit direct selection never falls back: an unavailable backend returns not_supported and the gsolve message. PCG factors the bounded fixed-effect preconditioner block and one basis-rank block per pedigree animal, and verifies the true MME residual.
Coordinate traces remain the default. Explicit CHOLMOD supernodal selected inversion replaces only the exact coordinate trace systems. Deterministic positive-definite planning compiles derivative support once, then reuses one trace plan, derivative mapping, and selected-inverse workspace across covariance states. The result reports calls, selected and filled-factor entries, workspace/request/output and projected peak bytes, systems avoided, and serial selected-inverse support threads. AI derivative-response systems, exact determinant work, optimizer acceptance, and retained BLUP finalization are unchanged. CHOLMOD orchestration and support remain serial, while selected-inverse dense kernels use an independently requested oneMKL thread count. PARDISO selected inversion, including automatic when it resolves to PARDISO, is explicitly not_supported without fallback after symbolic capability resolution and before numerical factorization. PCG remains a separate fixed-covariance route with zero direct work.
The result reports starting/final covariance, fixed effects, animal-by-basis latent coefficients, observed genetic trajectories, fitted values, residuals, Py, optional prediction trajectories, covariance/optimizer diagnostics, and complete factorization/trace/AI work. Successful optimization reuses the accepted response coefficients for one BLUP finalization and performs no additional response solve. The shared typed serializer translates these diagnostics without numerical work. In the direct diagnostics, sparse_direct$requested is a logical direct-route flag, whereas requested_backend and resolved_backend are backend strings.
Resource preflight bounds coefficient dimension, coordinate systems, RHS batch width, workspace, and factor memory. Construction and PCG diagnostics expose the single record pass, zero optimizer record revisits, stored sparse-statistic values/nonzeros, fixed and animal preconditioner blocks, RHS width, and true residual. CHOLMOD selected-inverse trace and retained-factor prediction-error paths are available through this API. Exact PEV/reliability requires retained selected-inverse state.
PARDISO selected inversion, MUMPS, covariance boundaries, RHE, serial residual correlation, multiple relationship components, genomic models, marker effects, and ssGBLUP are not supported by this interface. The prediction-error contract supports bounded PARDISO selected_solve coefficient and trajectory uncertainty from retained factors. This does not add PARDISO selected inversion or PCG exact PEV.

title: gmat integration
text:
The R workflow has one owner at each layer:
gbase Glist → gbase sparse-LD preparation → gmat disk resource → task packages
gbase::gprep() owns genotype preparation and augments a Glist with sparse-LD identity, marker and sample selections, paths, settings, and provenance. gbits owns BED decoding. gmat owns panel mappings, sparse-LD computation, the disk format, validation, and readers. Task packages accept the Glist and use installed public gmat interfaces from C++.

title: gmat integration
text:
Serializable bridge objects
Root gsuite retains only the BED resource and panel objects needed by its own internal genotype integration:

gsuite_bed_resource retains canonical BED/BIM/FAM paths, physical counts, and literal ordered BIM/FAM metadata.
gsuite_bed_panel retains component resources, exact selections, selected metadata, and zero-based native source mappings.

These list-style S3 objects have no external pointers. Sparse-LD preparation and access are not duplicated in root gsuite.

title: gmat integration
text:
Identity and ordering
Component order is list order. Components must have identical ordered (family_id, individual_id) pairs before selection. Sample identities and per-component marker IDs are resolved exactly, and requested order is preserved. Global marker order concatenates component selections. Duplicate or missing identities are errors. Nothing silently sorts chromosomes, positions, markers, samples, or alleles.
The gbase::gprep(task = "sparseld") contract, numerical conventions, and Glist fields are specified in sparse-LD preparation.

title: gmat integration
text:
Limitations
The integration does not harmonize alleles, flip dosage, convert genome builds, or parse summary statistics. All five files in a persistent gmat sparse-LD resource must remain available together.
See the gmat method catalogue for the complete native contracts.

title: Marker-QC contract
text:
gbase::gfilter() is the summary-only marker-selection operation. It accepts the strict serializable c("gs_genotypes", "Glist") descriptor produced by gbase::gprep(task = "prepare") and returns a plain marker-ID vector. It does not mutate the descriptor, read packed BED genotype bytes, write BED or CSR files, decode a genotype matrix, or construct sparse LD. gmat and gbits remain unchanged owners of metadata/LD and packed-genotype operations respectively.
Marker identity is canonical chromosome/file/BIM order. Every required chromosome-wise field is checked for the same shape, and IDs must be complete and globally unique. The existing preparation validator also reopens the BIM/FAM/BED descriptors and verifies source mappings. Genotype counts must be nonnegative integers whose sum equals the exact summary population recorded by sample_source_indices_0based and provenance$summary_samples. MAF must agree with n0, n1, and n2. Thus a study-sample preparation uses that selected population rather than the complete FAM count.



Each enabled rule creates a full-length exclusion mask; the final mask is their union. NULL disables a numeric rule and FALSE disables a logical rule.

MAF excludes \(\mathrm{maf}_j\leq\texttt{maf}\); equality is excluded.
Missingness is \(\frac{n_{\mathrm{miss}}}{n_0+n_1+n_2+n_{\mathrm{miss}}}\) and excludes values strictly greater than missing; equality is retained.
HWE excludes exact-test p-values strictly less than hwe; equality is retained.
INFO excludes values strictly less than info; equality is retained.
Ambiguity excludes the exact allele pairs A/T, T/A, C/G, and G/C.
The indel/non-SNP rule retains only exact uppercase single-base A, C, G, or T for both alleles. It therefore rejects multi-base, symbolic, and lowercase encodings without silently normalizing alleles.
MHC excludes a closed interval, including both endpoints, on stored chromosome labels 6 and chr6: GRCh37 [28,477,797, 33,448,397], or GRCh38 [28,510,120, 33,480,577]. The assembly must be explicitly GRCh37 or GRCh38, supplied as an argument or in Glist$assembly; it is never guessed.

All numeric thresholds are finite scalars in [0,1]. Logical controls are nonmissing scalars. A marker-aligned INFO field is required only when INFO filtering is enabled. It may be a named numeric vector or list, but its names must be a duplicate-free exact set of prepared marker IDs. Values are reordered by identity into canonical order before the mask is calculated.



For each biallelic marker, gbase conditions on the observed sample count and minor-allele copy count and enumerates every feasible heterozygote count with the same allele total. The two-sided p-value is the sum of conditional genotype probabilities no greater than the observed genotype probability. Probabilities within relative tolerance 1e-12 are treated as ties. This is the conventional probability-ordering exact test. Monomorphic markers receive p-value 1. All-missing or structurally invalid counts are descriptor errors; any otherwise nonfinite HWE result is conservatively excluded when HWE filtering is enabled.
qgg 1.1.6 instead uses a one-degree-of-freedom Pearson chi-square calculation. The tested version’s gfilter() also has disabled-mask hazards, relies on incomplete positional/name alignment, and subsets its combined mask incorrectly during INFO filtering. gsuite deliberately uses the exact test, complete identity validation, independent full-length masks, and an explicit default HWE threshold of 1e-12. It also freezes the documented inclusive MAF boundary.



Glist <- gbase::gprep(
  study = "Reference",
  bedfiles = bedfiles,
  task = "prepare",
  nthreads = 4
)

rsids <- gbase::gfilter(
  Glist,
  maf = 0.01,
  missing = 0.05,
  hwe = 1e-12,
  ambiguous = TRUE,
  indels = TRUE
)

Glist <- gbase::gprep(
  Glist = Glist,
  task = "sparseld",
  rsids = rsids,
  out_prefix = "reference_ld",
  nthreads = 4
)
Preparation computes reusable summaries once. The same unchanged descriptor can be filtered under several policies, and sparse LD is subsequently built only for the selected markers.

title: Marker-QC contract
text:
gbase::gfilter() is the summary-only marker-selection operation. It accepts the strict serializable c("gs_genotypes", "Glist") descriptor produced by gbase::gprep(task = "prepare") and returns a plain marker-ID vector. It does not mutate the descriptor, read packed BED genotype bytes, write BED or CSR files, decode a genotype matrix, or construct sparse LD. gmat and gbits remain unchanged owners of metadata/LD and packed-genotype operations respectively.
Marker identity is canonical chromosome/file/BIM order. Every required chromosome-wise field is checked for the same shape, and IDs must be complete and globally unique. The existing preparation validator also reopens the BIM/FAM/BED descriptors and verifies source mappings. Genotype counts must be nonnegative integers whose sum equals the exact summary population recorded by sample_source_indices_0based and provenance$summary_samples. MAF must agree with n0, n1, and n2. Thus a study-sample preparation uses that selected population rather than the complete FAM count.

title: Marker-QC contract
text:
Each enabled rule creates a full-length exclusion mask; the final mask is their union. NULL disables a numeric rule and FALSE disables a logical rule.

MAF excludes \(\mathrm{maf}_j\leq\texttt{maf}\); equality is excluded.
Missingness is \(\frac{n_{\mathrm{miss}}}{n_0+n_1+n_2+n_{\mathrm{miss}}}\) and excludes values strictly greater than missing; equality is retained.
HWE excludes exact-test p-values strictly less than hwe; equality is retained.
INFO excludes values strictly less than info; equality is retained.
Ambiguity excludes the exact allele pairs A/T, T/A, C/G, and G/C.
The indel/non-SNP rule retains only exact uppercase single-base A, C, G, or T for both alleles. It therefore rejects multi-base, symbolic, and lowercase encodings without silently normalizing alleles.
MHC excludes a closed interval, including both endpoints, on stored chromosome labels 6 and chr6: GRCh37 [28,477,797, 33,448,397], or GRCh38 [28,510,120, 33,480,577]. The assembly must be explicitly GRCh37 or GRCh38, supplied as an argument or in Glist$assembly; it is never guessed.

Values are reordered by identity into canonical order before the mask is calculated.

title: gbase
text:
gbase
gbase contains small, task-neutral R data contracts shared by the gsuite ecosystem. It performs no statistical fitting. Its genotype preparation contract uses the installed public gmat, gbits, and gsolve interfaces, with a qualified native prefix checked during compilation and native versions and ABIs checked again when the package loads. gsolve supplies dense products and regional eigensystems or eigenvalues; the portable binary disables CHOLMOD, MKL and PARDISO while retaining OpenMP support.
Summary statistics use the established qgg workflow: checkStat() maps and aligns an ordinary data frame to Glist, applies explicit QC, and returns an ordinary data frame with familiar short column names:
library(gbase)

stat <- checkStat(Glist = Glist, stat = raw_stat)
The result has no special summary-statistics class, constructor or accessor. Each task function validates the columns it uses, and statistical work belongs to the task package.
PLINK genotype resources are prepared once and remain serializable:
Glist <- gprep(bedfiles = c("chr1.bed", "chr2.bed"))
Glist <- gprep(
  Glist = Glist,
  task = "sparseld",
  out_prefix = "reference",
  max_distance_bp = 1000000,
  max_distance_variants = 1000,
  r2 = 0.01
)
The second call returns the same Glist contract augmented with its sparse-LD descriptor; it does not introduce a separate genotype or LD owner.
The same Glist is the input to task-neutral marker and LD utilities:
markers <- gfilter(Glist)
scores <- ld_scores(Glist)
region <- ld_region(Glist, markers = markers[1:100])
spectrum <- ld_eigen(Glist, markers = markers[1:100])

blocks <- data.frame(block_id = "chr1", first_marker = markers[1],
  last_marker = markers[length(markers)])
Glist <- define_ld_blocks(Glist, blocks)
Sparse-LD construction and metadata stay on the Glist returned by gprep(task = "sparseld").
Full regional LD eigenvalues can also be prepared directly from BED without first making sparse LD:
regionSets <- list(region1 = Glist$rsids[[1]][1:100])
Glist <- gprep(Glist, task = "eigen", sets = regionSets, nthreads = 4)
values <- Glist$eigen$values$region1
saveRDS(Glist, "Glist-with-regional-eigenvalues.rds")
Each region is a named marker set from one chromosome. Membership is retained in reference order, and the prepared sample IDs are stored with the spectra. Missing genotypes are mean-imputed; constant markers are rejected by ID. Only eigenvalues are computed, with no clipping or truncation. When markers outnumber samples, the smaller sample-space Gram matrix is used and the full marker spectrum is recovered by padding its null eigenvalues with zeros. Regions are processed sequentially; nthreads controls local BED decoding. The existing gsolve Eigen backend performs dense products and decomposition without a mandatory OpenBLAS dependency. Sparse-LD cutoffs and windows do not apply. glma::prepare_vegas(Glist) reuses these stored spectra for VEGAS without repeating LD computation or decomposition. It returns a serializable prepared object with the required marker and allele order for subsequent traits. Constant positive weights within each gene are supported; nonuniform weights continue to use the sparse-LD route. Statistical evaluation remains owned by glma.
mapSets(sets, Glist) resolves named marker memberships to prepared marker IDs or indices. Unknown members are dropped; empty sets remain visible. getLD(Glist, rsids=region) computes full regional BED correlation in requested marker order using the selected people, installed gmat decoding and R’s configured BLAS. Missing genotypes are mean-imputed and constant markers are rejected. It writes no files and applies no sparse-LD windows or cutoffs. The returned matrix records sample count and decoding/product timings. Statistical priors, sampler controls and posterior sets remain with task packages.

title: R package boundaries
text:
The R layer is divided by user task instead of placing every interface in one large gsuite package. The root gsuite package remains the ecosystem identity, website and integration surface. Independently distributed task capabilities are R/native pairs: an R package owns the user contract and its corresponding native library owns the implementation. Each task package can be installed and used without the root package.


The dependency direction is:
gbase <- gcorr, glma, gbayes, gscore, gmap, gsea

task packages do not import gsuite
task packages depend on each other only for an explicit scientific workflow
gbase must not depend on a task package. Its public source distribution builds task-neutral gbits/gmat and bounded gsolve-core/greml-core source into a reusable static archive. A task package must not depend on the root gsuite package. This prevents dependency cycles and lets users install one task without installing the complete suite.



This is the canonical map of R/native distribution units. Method details belong in the capability overview; native transitive dependencies belong in the build manifests.

Code belongs in gbase only when it is stable, task-neutral and needed by more than one task package. The package contains or will own:

one-trait, allele-labelled summary-statistics data frames;
checkStat() mapping, harmonization and explicit QC of reported statistics against a Glist reference;
validation of marker identity, positions, alleles and supplied numerical columns;
explicit allele-oriented variant keys;
gbase::gprep() preparation and sparse-LD publication plus the serializable Glist contract shared by individual-level task packages;
gbase::define_ld_blocks() one-time verification and serialization of an exhaustive independent-block partition tied to the sparse-LD identity;
summary-based marker filtering and Glist-owned LD scores, regional matrices, complete verified regional eigensystems, and reusable eigenvalues-only full regional BED spectra through gprep(task = "eigen", sets = ...).

checkStat() follows the established qgg workflow and returns an ordinary data frame. Its canonical columns are rsids, chr, pos, ea, nea, with the available analysis columns among eaf, b, seb, stat, p, n and info. Downstream functions validate the subset they require. Gbase does not require a public summary-statistics class, constructor, accessor or print method.
The following do not belong in gbase:

automatic strand inference or downstream LD-model fitting;
genotype, LD or matrix storage;
statistical fitting, priors or sampler controls;
scoring, correlation or association algorithms;
orchestration across tasks.

Those responsibilities remain with gmat/data preparation, the relevant task package or the gsuite umbrella.

title: From conversation to a reproducible analysis
text:
You bring the scientific question and study knowledge. An assistant can help inspect data, run R code, examine diagnostics and prepare a report using gsuite.
This illustrative conversation uses the single-trait pedigree example; it is not a completed analysis. To run it, the assistant needs access to your files, R and an installed gsuite. Website rendering does not execute the code.

title: From conversation to a reproducible analysis
section: 1. Start with the question and data
text:
1. Start with the question and data
You might ask:

I have body-weight records, sex, cohort and herd, plus a pedigree. Help me estimate additive genetic variation and predict animal effects. First inspect the data and explain any issues that affect the analysis.

The assistant checks the column meanings and measurement units with you, then inspects missing values, duplicated records, factor levels and phenotype distributions. It checks that observation IDs match the pedigree, parent IDs are represented consistently, and pedigree relationships are valid. Repeated measurements require particular attention: several records per animal may need a different model from one observation per animal.
For a reproducible demonstration, use the Prepare ordinary data frames section and the data preparation at the start of Single trait in the pedigree tutorial. That supplies pedigree and data, including BW, sex, cohort, herd and id. For your study, use your own data frames instead.
str(data)
summary(data)
colSums(is.na(data))
anyDuplicated(pedigree$id)
setdiff(data$id, pedigree$id)
table(table(data$id))
These are initial checks, not a complete data-validation procedure. The assistant records issues and proposed changes in a data-check summary. Decisions such as excluding records or recoding missing parents belong in the analysis script, with an explanation you can review.

title: From conversation to a reproducible analysis
section: 2. Translate the question into a model
text:
2. Translate the question into a model
You might ask:

Treat sex, cohort and herd as fixed effects. Use the pedigree for additive genetic animal effects. Explain the assumptions and show me the model code.

For the tutorial’s single-trait model:
\[
y = X\beta + Za + e,\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(a)=\sigma_a^2 A,\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(e)=\sigma_e^2 I.
\]
Here \(A\) is the pedigree relationship matrix. The model assumes independent animal and residual effects and a common residual variance. Whether herd should be fixed, and whether additional environmental effects are needed, depends on the study design and your scientific question.
The qgtools-style separation of effects, relationships and covariance components makes each decision explicit:



Model decision
gsuite specification




Fixed effects and animal grouping
Formula


Observations and explanatory variables
data


Relationships between animals
Pedigree kernel


Genetic and residual variance components
gvc() descriptors


Estimate covariance parameters
task = "reml"



library(gsuite)

PED <- gs_pedigree(pedigree, id = "id", sire = "sire", dam = "dam")
vcs <- list(
  animal = gvc(variable = "id", traits = "BW", kernel = PED),
  residual = gvc(variable = "residual", traits = "BW")
)
Starting variances are omitted here: gsuite uses its existing deterministic initializers. The pedigree tutorial also shows the short form, which expresses the same model with fewer arguments. The assistant checks the supported model combinations before suggesting an extension; a general specification does not imply that every model is implemented.

title: From conversation to a reproducible analysis
text:
3. Run and examine the fit
You might ask:

Run this model, retain the script and fit, and check convergence before interpreting the estimates. Explain any failures rather than silently changing the model.

fit <- gfit(
  formula = BW ~ sex + cohort + herd + (1 | id),
  data = data,
  vc = vcs,
  task = "reml"
)

summary(fit)
fit_diagnostics <- diagnostics(fit)
fit_diagnostics$status
fit_diagnostics$converged
fit_diagnostics$initialization
stopifnot(isTRUE(fit_diagnostics$status$ok),
  isTRUE(fit_diagnostics$converged))
coef(fit)
head(gs_ranef(fit)$animal)
This data-frame route defaults to CHOLMOD selected inversion and requires a build with CHOLMOD support. The check above stops the example before prediction plots and reporting if status or convergence is unsuccessful.
After checking status and convergence, examine estimates and residual patterns for unusual values or possible confounding.
plot(fitted(fit), residuals(fit),
     xlab = "Fitted value", ylab = "Residual")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)
Record failures and unavailable diagnostics alongside the results.

title: From conversation to a reproducible analysis
section: 4. Turn the analysis into a report
text:
4. Turn the analysis into a report
You might ask:

Create a Quarto report with the data checks, model and assumptions, convergence diagnostics, variance estimates, animal predictions and residual plots. Explain what the results support and what remains uncertain.

The report uses the actual saved results. It identifies the data used, exclusions, software versions and analysis settings, and links conclusions to tables and figures. It separates predicted animal effects from observed phenotypes and avoids presenting a failed fit as a completed analysis.
The working directory can remain small:







File
Purpose




analysis.R
Data preparation, checks and model fitting


results.rds
Extracted estimates, predictions and diagnostics for reporting


report.qmd
Methods, results, figures and interpretation


session-info.txt
R and package versions



Save the reporting values rather than relying on an in-memory fit to survive between R sessions:
results <- list(
  summary = summary(fit),
  diagnostics = diagnostics(fit),
  fixed_effects = coef(fit),
  animal_effects = gs_ranef(fit)$animal,
  record_mapping = fit$record_mapping,
  fitted = fitted(fit),
  residuals = residuals(fit)
)
saveRDS(results, "results.rds")
writeLines(capture.output(sessionInfo()), "session-info.txt")
The conversation helps develop the analysis. The scripts, extracted results and report preserve the work so you or a colleague can inspect and reproduce it without reconstructing the conversation.

title: From conversation to a reproducible analysis
text:
Continue with more complex models
The same collaboration applies to multitrait and longitudinal analyses: discuss the question, inspect the record structure, specify effects and covariances, run a supported model and assess the results. gsuite remains an R package with explicit interfaces; no conversational service is required inside the package.

Architecture
text: gsuite is organised by user task. Shared data preparation lives in gbase; analysis methods live in independently installable R packages; numerical and statistical computation remains in the corresponding native libraries. The root gsuite package provides the mixed-model and solver interfaces and serves as the ecosystem documentation and integration point.

title: Architecture
text:
Native capabilities and R availability









Native library
Capability
Immediate boundary
Standalone R package

Does not own genomic resource metadata, general solvers or statistical models
No; used through gbase and root gsuite

gbase is the standalone shared R package for task-neutral genotype, summary statistics and LD preparation. gsim is the standalone R package for simulation. The root gsuite package contains the mixed-model and solver integration and the suite-level version and documentation interfaces.
The capability overview lists the analyses available through each package. The package-boundary guide records the dependency rules.

title: Architecture
text:
Shared genomic resources
Glist is the serializable contract connecting data preparation with analysis. gbase::gprep() validates a PLINK panel and can attach sparse LD computed by gmat from gbits-backed genotypes. The same Glist can then be passed to analysis packages without copying the genotype or LD data into R.
gprep(task = "eigen", sets = regionSets) also prepares full regional LD eigenvalues directly from BED. gmat supplies centred unit-norm columns through gbits, gsolve supplies dense products and eigenvalues-only decomposition, and gbase attaches the named spectra and sample identities to Glist$eigen. The smaller sample-space Gram matrix is used when markers outnumber samples. This route is independent of sparse-LD cutoffs and does not fit a gene test. Analysis packages still require an explicit consumer interface for this resource.
flowchart LR
    bed["PLINK BED / BIM / FAM"] --> gprep["gbase::gprep()"]
    gprep --> glist["Glist"]
    glist --> glma[glma]
    glist --> gbayes[gbayes]
    glist --> gscore[gscore]
    glist --> gmap[gmap]
    glist --> gcorr[gcorr]
    glist --> gsea[gsea]
The Glist fields ldfiles, idsLD and rsidsLD identify the stored LD resource, its reference samples and its marker order. validate_Glist() checks the lightweight descriptor used by ordinary calls. verify_ld() performs the full sparse-LD integrity scan when a resource crosses a trust boundary.
Native consumers open one gmat LD reader per high-level call and reuse it across regions, traits, chains or marker sets. Regional matrices, independent blocks and eigensystems remain tied to the same Glist identity. This avoids repeated payload checks and unnecessary dense copies.

title: Architecture
text:
Analysis flow
Each R package validates task-specific inputs, calls its native implementation and returns labelled R results. Shared preparation does not blur statistical ownership:

glma fits association models and produces marker- or set-level evidence;
gbayes fits Bayesian regression models and produces posterior quantities;
gscore applies prepared weights, including Glist-resolved marker-set scores, while model fitting remains with the model owner;
gmap performs regional fine-mapping, posterior-set and Bayesian-FDR interpretation, and colocalisation;
gcorr fits summary-statistic correlation, covariance and MR models; and
gsea performs enrichment or PoPS-style gene ranking after gene or feature evidence has been prepared.

A connected association-to-enrichment workflow therefore follows:
flowchart LR
    stats["Checked association statistics"] --> vegas["glma::vegas()"]
    ld["Glist sparse LD or regional BED spectra"] --> vegas
    vegas --> genes["Gene-level evidence"]
    genes --> enrichment["gsea::gsea()"]
The VEGAS step processes the supplied marker sets directly. One sparse-LD reader prepares eigenvalue spectra in bounded parallel batches; the resulting ordinary R object can be reused across traits and sessions without reopening LD or repeating decompositions. Cross-gene covariance, when required by a downstream enrichment model, is a separate explicit input. Alternatively, glma reuses the full within-region spectra stored by gbase::gprep(task="eigen"); constant weights require no new decomposition. Nonuniform weights continue to use the sparse-LD route. gbase owns preparation and identity validation; glma owns the statistic and tail evaluation.
Method-specific controls, outputs and qualification limits belong in the method catalogue and the linked workflow guides, rather than on this architecture page.

title: Architecture
text:
Mixed models and numerical methods
The root gsuite package exposes the mixed-model integration. R formulas or explicit covariance components are prepared for greml, which owns model semantics, estimation, prediction and uncertainty. greml delegates general factorization and solving to gsolve. gbits supplies packed genotype operations, and gmat owns reusable genotype-panel and matrix resources.
flowchart LR
    input["Formula or covariance components"] --> gsuite["gsuite R interface"]
    gsuite --> greml["greml: model and inference"]
    greml --> gsolve["gsolve: numerical methods"]
    gbits["gbits: packed genotypes"] --> gsuite
    gmat["gmat: genomic resources"] --> gsuite
    greml --> result["Labelled fit, prediction and diagnostics"]
The mixed-model guide explains this boundary, and the model catalogue records the supported model and backend combinations.

title: Architecture
text:
Dependency rules

Task packages may depend on gbase; gbase does not depend on a task package.
Task packages do not import the root gsuite package.
A task package may use another task package only for an explicit scientific workflow, such as the gsea re-export of glma::vegas().
Packed genotype decoding and algebra belong to gbits; panel identity, matrices and LD resources belong to gmat.
General numerical methods belong to gsolve; mixed-model semantics belong to greml; each other statistical method belongs to its task library.
New dependencies must follow this direction and must not introduce cycles.

gsim is separate from the analysis dependency graph. It creates ordinary R data that can be passed into examples and analysis packages.
Regional dense MCMC follows the same ownership boundaries: gbase maps marker sets and exposes full BED LD through installed gmat decoding and R’s BLAS; native gmap validates and binds the region, then reuses native gbayes sampling. Familiar argument adapters remain in the gmap and gbayes R packages. Native gmap owns qgg-compatible marginal-PIP grouping; it does not require qgg at runtime. Standalone gbayes binds verified Glist LD blocks to native factorized BayesC/BayesR for mcmc-eigen, independently of the annotated SBayesRC model. Native gbayes owns retained joint-effect genetic variance and chain diagnostics; the R task packages arrange these into familiar post and conv tables. When the genetic reference is the fitted operator, accumulation reuses the cached residual quadratic. Both task R interfaces pass optional scalar-summary LD-swap controls to the existing native gbayes sampler; no sampler is duplicated in the R layer or native gmap. Native gbayes prepares the LD-neighbour graph once per fit and shares it across chains. Sparse-LD operators scan existing stored correlations; factorized operators derive neighbours from their fitted cross-products. The R packages expose pooled and per-chain proposal counts. Probability defaults to zero, preserving the existing sampler and timing evidence.

title: Source-package repository
text:
The public distribution unit consists of exactly seven R source packages: gbase, gbayes, gcorr, glma, gmap, gscore, and gsea. The root gsuite package, gshare, and the complete gsolve and greml libraries are not part of this repository.
Users install from the conventional R repository:
options(repos = c(
  gsuite = "https://psoerensen.github.io/gtools/gsuite/repository",
  CRAN = "https://cloud.r-project.org"
))

install.packages("gbase")
install.packages(c("gbayes", "gcorr", "glma", "gmap", "gscore", "gsea"))
The first public source release is version 0.1.0.


gbase builds the task-neutral gbits and gmat implementation together with bounded gsolve-core and greml-core source sets. It installs their public headers and one position-independent static archive for the task packages. The cores exclude sparse direct factorization, selected inversion, CHOLMOD, oneMKL, PARDISO, and the pedigree, longitudinal, and full mixed-model surfaces.
gbayes contains its R/Rcpp layer and Bayesian native implementation. In addition to its package DLL, it installs the public headers and a second static archive needed by glma, gmap, gscore, and gsea. Those packages therefore compile only their own native implementation instead of recompiling the large Bayesian source set. gcorr needs only the gbase archive.
Every task package links the installed archives declared by its R package dependencies, so no preinstalled gsuite SDK is needed. Native files in release packages are generated from the canonical sibling repositories. They are not maintained as copied source inside this repository.
The ordinary source-build requirements are:

Linux or HPC: R’s configured C++17 compiler;
Windows: the Rtools version matching R;
macOS: Xcode Command Line Tools or another compiler configured for R;
R packages Rcpp and RcppEigen.

OpenMP is used when the R toolchain supplies it and otherwise the same source build remains available without OpenMP.



From the gsuite checkout, with the canonical native repositories beside it:
Rscript --vanilla tools/build/build_source_repository.R
The command stages generated package sources, extracts source lists from the owners’ CMake declarations, builds and checks packages in dependency order, installs them into an isolated library, and writes the seven archives plus PACKAGES, PACKAGES.gz, PACKAGES.rds, and SHA256SUMS under repository/src/contrib. Release assembly requires the R package openssl to calculate SHA-256 checksums; end users do not need it unless another dependency requires it.
Use --stage-only to inspect generated source, --build-only to assemble the archives without compiling them, and --skip-check for an installation smoke build. --from=<package> resumes an interrupted ordered run. Those modes are partial validation.
Approved contents under repository/ are tracked as release artifacts. All staging, check, object, and installation outputs remain generated and ignored. The build command itself never deploys, pushes, or changes GitHub Pages.



Before each publication, review package versions, source-check results on release platforms, licence notices, archive contents and checksums, absence of private source, and the website wording. Running the documented website publisher copies the approved release into site/gsuite/repository in the public gtools checkout. Pushing that reviewed snapshot activates the gtools GitHub Pages deployment workflow.

title: Formula and variance-component compiled-MME REML
text:
For the new data-frame shorthand, optional starts, fixed solves and genetic random regression, begin with Pedigree analysis. Both formula and formulas now use the same general adapter. This page documents the specialized compiled-MME route, explicitly requested with a gs_fit_control() object, complete explicit covariance starts, and task = "reml" (or greml() with those same controls). Its result layout remains specialized and does not support the gsolve(fit) handoff. Supplying starts alone does not select it. General fits accept named controls for the selected pedigree or component fitter. Compiled controls now default to CHOLMOD selected inversion.
The data-frame gs_pedigree() constructor described here is distinct from gs_model_pedigree(), the ordered-parent constructor used by the persistent-model API. The two signatures are not interchangeable and do not dispatch implicitly.
greml() is the estimation entry point; gfit() remains available with task = "reml". Model incidence comes from formulas, pedigree relationships come from gs_pedigree(), and explicit positive-interior covariance starts come from named gvc() components. The interface lowers one immutable model to greml’s public compiled-MME plan, creates one numerical session, optimizes, and finalizes BLUPs from the retained accepted response state.
PED <- gs_pedigree(pedigree, id = "id", sire = "sire", dam = "dam")

fit <- gfit(
  BW ~ sex + batch + (1 | id),
  records,
  list(
    animal = gvc("id", "BW", PED, start = 1),
    residual = gvc("residual", "BW", start = 1)
  ),
  control = gs_fit_control(direct_backend = "cholmod")
)
For multiple traits, formulas is a named list and each component start is an SPD matrix in the declared trait order. Each trait has a separate fixed-effect block. Scalar records are ordered by formula-list order and original data-row order. An NA response is absent; observed traits from the same data row form one complete or incomplete patterned residual unit. Missing fixed covariates, nonfinite observed responses, and missing pedigree identifiers are errors.


From the repository root, with gsuite installed, run:
source("tools/examples/run_single_trait_pedigree_example.R")
The complete example starts with two ordinary data frames: data has one observation per row (id, BW, factor sex, continuous covariate x); pedigree has one animal per row (id, sire, dam). It reuses the small deterministic BW formula-test illustration, not a random draw from the fitted pedigree model. Its artificial sex labels vary across records of an animal; real data should use consistent animal sex. These toy values illustrate the API, not biological inference or variance recovery.
The formula BW ~ sex + x + (1 | id) supplies fixed effects and animal incidence. A separate gs_pedigree() relationship and named animal and residual components supply covariance structure and positive starting variances. Under this model, animal covariance is the pedigree relationship times the animal variance; residuals are independent with a common variance. Repeated observations share the animal effect, with no additional permanent environment effect. Starts are not fixed variances.
IDs, not row positions, align the tables. Pedigree rows may be reordered; unknown parents use NA, while known parents must be listed. Observation IDs absent from the pedigree are errors. Animal a8 has no observations but remains in the pedigree and receives a conditional animal prediction from relatives.
summary(fit) displays covariance estimates and convergence, coef(fit) returns fixed effects, and the public fit$random_effects$animal table contains IDs and animal BLUPs (not full predicted body weights). fit$converged and fit$convergence_reason expose the stopping result. Prediction tables follow pedigree order, so compare them by ID. Prediction for new data and prediction uncertainty are not supported on this formula route.
For development verification only, select the existing isolated installation before sourcing the same example:
.libPaths(c(file.path("build", "r-library"), .libPaths()))
source("tools/examples/run_single_trait_pedigree_example.R")



The only random grammar is exactly (1 | variable). A scalar formula has one or two distinct terms, with at most one pedigree component and one independent identity component. Multitrait formulas retain one shared pedigree term. Random slopes, more than two terms, duplicate terms, ||, nesting, crossing, functions, interactions, and expressions on the grouping side are rejected. After removing the random terms, base R model.frame() and model.matrix() build the fixed design and preserve coefficient names, contrasts, factor levels, and the formula environment.
Random incidence is never materialized as an R matrix. Each observed scalar record supplies a pedigree entity ID, trait/member ID, residual unit and coordinate, and a unit random-intercept weight directly to the compiled-MME specification. This first version may materialize a dense R fixed-effect model.matrix() and therefore targets moderate in-memory data frames.



Scalar fits accept one identity component, one pedigree component, or one of each, plus one homogeneous residual component. Formula order determines the random coefficient blocks and covariance-parameter order. Pedigree levels use external pedigree order, including unphenotyped animals. Identity levels use the sorted observed character or integer domain. Every record contributes a unit weight directly to each present component, including the data-induced pedigree/identity cross block; no R incidence matrix is built.
For example, repeatability and a common-environment model use the same bounded composition rule:
ID <- gs_identity()
repeatability <- gfit(
  y ~ sex + (1 | animal_id) + (1 | permanent_id), records,
  list(
    animal = gvc("animal_id", "y", PED, start = 0.8),
    permanent = gvc("permanent_id", "y", ID, start = 0.4),
    residual = gvc("residual", "y", start = 0.3)
  ),
  control = gs_fit_control(direct_backend = "cholmod")
)

common_environment <- gfit(
  y ~ sex + (1 | animal_id) + (1 | environment), records,
  list(
    animal = gvc("animal_id", "y", PED, start = 0.8),
    environment = gvc("environment", "y", ID, start = 0.4),
    residual = gvc("residual", "y", start = 0.3)
  ),
  control = gs_fit_control(direct_backend = "cholmod")
)
Starts remain mandatory finite positive scalars or finite symmetric positive-definite matrices. Covariance boundaries and automatic rank repair are not attempted.
gs_fit_control() maps backend, direct/support threads, exact trace route, optimizer bounds, coefficient dimension, factor memory, selected-inverse workspace, exact trace systems, RHS workspace, and linear-solve controls directly to the public greml session. A failed preflight does not silently change backend, trace route, batch width, or solver. Diagnostics report the required and configured RHS bytes, peak RHS width, resident coefficient vectors, workspace category, limit result, overflow result, and zero numerical work after rejection.
PARDISO uses its own requested internal thread count and coordinate-exact traces. CHOLMOD uses serial support work and selected inversion. Generic support execution remains independent; an unsupported request is returned as not_supported before solver work. No GNU OpenMP layer is introduced.
The returned gs_fit owns covariance estimates, fixed effects, animal BLUPs in external pedigree order, caller-record mappings, optional fitted values, residuals and Py, score/standard-AI diagnostics, optimizer history, resource preflight, work counters, and retained-state diagnostics. print(), summary(), coef(), fitted(), residuals(), logLik(), and nobs() are provided. Record methods fail clearly when record values were omitted.
Genomic relationships, random slopes, correlated random components, more than one pedigree or identity component, multitrait repeatability, heterogeneous or serial residual covariance, covariance boundaries, PEV/reliability, prediction from new data, disk-backed data, formula dependencies, Bayesian tasks, JSON, Python, and R-side public plan/session objects remain deliberately outside this compiled-MME formula interface.

Its artificial sex labels vary across records of an animal; real data should use consistent animal sex. These toy values illustrate the API, not biological inference or variance recovery.
The formula BW ~ sex + x + (1 | id) supplies fixed effects and animal incidence. A separate gs_pedigree() relationship and named animal and residual components supply covariance structure and positive starting variances. Under this model, animal covariance is the pedigree relationship times the animal variance; residuals are independent with a common variance. Repeated observations share the animal effect, with no additional permanent environment effect. Starts are not fixed variances.
IDs, not row positions, align the tables. Pedigree rows may be reordered; unknown parents use NA, while known parents must be listed. Observation IDs absent from the pedigree are errors. Animal a8 has no observations but remains in the pedigree and receives a conditional animal prediction from relatives.
summary(fit) displays covariance estimates and convergence, coef(fit) returns fixed effects, and the public fit$random_effects$animal table contains IDs and animal BLUPs (not full predicted body weights). fit$converged and fit$convergence_reason expose the stopping result. Prediction tables follow pedigree order, so compare them by ID. Prediction for new data and prediction uncertainty are not supported on this formula route.

.libPaths(c(file.path("build", "r-library"), .libPaths()))
source("tools/examples/run_single_trait_pedigree_example.R")

title: Formula and variance-component compiled-MME REML
text:
The only random grammar is exactly (1 | variable). A scalar formula has one or two distinct terms, with at most one pedigree component and one independent identity component. Multitrait formulas retain one shared pedigree term. Random slopes, more than two terms, duplicate terms, ||, nesting, crossing, functions, interactions, and expressions on the grouping side are rejected. After removing the random terms, base R model.frame() and model.matrix() build the fixed design and preserve coefficient names, contrasts, factor levels, and the formula environment.
Random incidence is never materialized as an R matrix. Each observed scalar record supplies a pedigree entity ID, trait/member ID, residual unit and coordinate, and a unit random-intercept weight directly to the compiled-MME specification. This first version may materialize a dense R fixed-effect model.matrix() and therefore targets moderate in-memory data frames.

title: Formula and variance-component compiled-MME REML
text:
Scalar fits accept one identity component, one pedigree component, or one of each, plus one homogeneous residual component. Formula order determines the random coefficient blocks and covariance-parameter order. Pedigree levels use external pedigree order, including unphenotyped animals. Identity levels use the sorted observed character or integer domain. Every record contributes a unit weight directly to each present component, including the data-induced pedigree/identity cross block; no R incidence matrix is built.
For example, repeatability and a common-environment model use the same bounded composition rule:
ID <- gs_identity()
repeatability <- gfit(
  y ~ sex + (1 | animal_id) + (1 | permanent_id), records,
  list(
    animal = gvc("animal_id", "y", PED, start = 0.8),
    permanent = gvc("permanent_id", "y", ID, start = 0.4),
    residual = gvc("residual", "y", start = 0.3)
  ),
  control = gs_fit_control(direct_backend = "cholmod")
)

common_environment <- gfit(
  y ~ sex + (1 | animal_id) + (1 | environment), records,
  list(
    animal = gvc("animal_id", "y", PED, start = 0.8),
    environment = gvc("environment", "y", ID, start = 0.4),
    residual = gvc("residual", "y", start = 0.3)
  ),
  control = gs_fit_control(direct_backend = "cholmod")
)
Starts remain mandatory finite positive scalars or finite symmetric positive-definite matrices. Covariance boundaries and automatic rank repair are not attempted.
gs_fit_control() maps backend, direct/support threads, exact trace route, optimizer bounds, coefficient dimension, factor memory, selected-inverse workspace, exact trace systems, RHS workspace, and linear-solve controls directly to the public greml session. A failed preflight does not silently change backend, trace route, batch width, or solver. Diagnostics report the required and configured RHS bytes, peak RHS width, resident coefficient vectors, workspace category, limit result, overflow result, and zero numerical work after rejection.
PARDISO uses its own requested internal thread count and coordinate-exact traces. CHOLMOD uses serial support work and selected inversion. Generic support execution remains independent; an unsupported request is returned as not_supported before solver work. No GNU OpenMP layer is introduced.
The returned gs_fit owns covariance estimates, fixed effects, animal BLUPs in external pedigree order, caller-record mappings, optional fitted values, residuals and Py, score/standard-AI diagnostics, optimizer history, resource preflight, work counters, and retained-state diagnostics. print(), summary(), coef(), fitted(), residuals(), logLik(), and nobs() are provided. Record methods fail clearly when record values were omitted.
Genomic relationships, random slopes, correlated random components, more than one pedigree or identity component, multitrait repeatability, heterogeneous or serial residual covariance, covariance boundaries, PEV/reliability, prediction from new data, disk-backed data, formula dependencies, Bayesian tasks, JSON, Python, and R-side public plan/session objects remain deliberately outside this compiled-MME formula interface.

title: gs_genotypes preparation contract
text:
gbase::gprep() implements the bounded "prepare", "sparseld", and "eigen" tasks. For preparation, gbase owns argument validation, orchestration, and the returned R descriptor; gmat owns strict BIM/FAM parsing and exact ordered multi-file identity; gbits owns BED header, size, offset, packed-code, and threaded count logic. The existing SNP-major PLINK BED files remain the sole persistent genotype representation. qgg is a read-only behavioural and scientific reference and is not a runtime dependency.
Sparse-LD orchestration is specified separately in sparse-LD preparation. gbase::gprep() does not add separate LD-score tasks: gbase::ld_scores(), ld_region(), and ld_eigen() consume the augmented Glist directly. Genetic-map import, GRMs, association, scoring, and other qgg tasks are not implemented by gbase::gprep(). Marker filtering is provided separately by gbase::gfilter(). Unknown preparation tasks fail explicitly.



Every BED/BIM/FAM vector is nonempty and has identical length. Omitted companions are derived by replacing only a final case-insensitive .bed suffix. Every path is normalized and must name an existing regular file. gbits requires the exact header 6c 1b 01 and exact size \(3+M\lceil N/4\rceil\); individual-major, truncated, and trailing-byte inputs fail.
The first FAM supplies ids and the complete physical sample order. Individual IDs are nonempty and globally unique. gmat requires every component to have the same exact ordered (family_id, individual_id) sequence; no set-only check or positional permutation is used. With ids = NULL, all samples contribute and study_ids is NULL. A supplied vector is nonempty, unique, nonmissing, fully resolved, retained in caller order, and used only as the summary sample set; ids remains complete.
Every BIM row has six fields, a nonempty chromosome and marker ID, finite nonnegative map position, positive physical position, and distinct nonempty alleles. Source marker IDs are globally unique across every supplied BIM, including unselected rows. BIM order is canonical. A supplied rsids vector is validated completely, then filtered in file/BIM order; caller order is intentionally not retained because the public descriptor remains a file-partitioned physical view. source_marker_indices_0based records every original BIM/BED index, including noncontiguous selections. BED is never rewritten.



a1 is BIM field 5 and a2 BIM field 6. Counts and frequencies always refer to copies of a1:



PLINK code
Copies of a1
Count




00
2
n2


10
1
n1


11
0
n0


01
missing
nmiss



For \(N_{\mathrm{obs}}=n_0+n_1+n_2\), the returned values are \(\mathrm{af}=\frac{2n_2+n_1}{2N_{\mathrm{obs}}}\), \(\mathrm{af}_1=\mathrm{af}\), \(\mathrm{af}_2=1-\mathrm{af}\), \(\mathrm{maf}=\min(\mathrm{af},1-\mathrm{af})\), \(\mathrm{hom}=(n_0+n_2)/N_{\mathrm{obs}}\), and \(\mathrm{het}=n_1/N_{\mathrm{obs}}\). All-missing selected markers fail with their marker ID. Empirical frequencies are not clipped: monomorphic values are exactly zero or one. This deliberately differs from the tested qgg 1.1.6 reference, whose summaryBED() clips frequencies to [0.00001, 0.99999] and substitutes 0.5 for all-missing markers.



The result is a plain list with class c("gs_genotypes", "Glist"). It carries study, normalized bedfiles/bimfiles/famfiles, complete ids, optional study_ids, n, nchr, m, chromosome/file-wise rsids, mchr, chr, pos, map, a1, a2, cpra, af, af1, af2, maf, nmiss, hom, het, n0, n1, n2, assembly = NULL, physical sample/marker mappings, format and ordering labels, and provenance. It contains neither dense genotypes nor a mandatory external pointer and therefore survives an exact saveRDS()/readRDS() round trip.
gsim has a native bounded BED reader for Glist-backed simulation. It resolves selected sample and marker IDs against FAM/BIM files, checks allele orientation, and reads selected BED blocks. A custom deterministic getG_fun remains an explicit alternative. Check the installed gsim version before use.



regionSets <- list(region1 = Glist$rsids[[1]][1:100])
Glist <- gprep(Glist, task = "eigen", sets = regionSets, nthreads = 4)
Glist$eigen$values$region1
saveRDS(Glist, "Glist-with-spectra.rds")
sets is a nonempty uniquely named list of marker-ID vectors. All markers must exist in Glist, duplicates are rejected, and each set must belong to one chromosome. Sets may overlap and need not be contiguous. Marker membership is stored in reference/BIM order. The samples default to study_ids when present, otherwise all ids; an explicit ids argument selects and records another reference sample set. At least two samples are required.
gmat reads unit-norm centred regional dosage columns through gbits. Missing calls are imputed to the observed marker mean; constant or all-missing markers fail with their ID. gsolve computes dense products and eigenvalues only. The spectrum is that of full within-set correlation, without sparse-LD thresholds or distance windows. No eigenvectors, clipping, statistical test, or persistent LD files are produced.
For N selected samples and M markers, the smaller Gram matrix is used. When M exceeds N, the sample-space spectrum is padded with M-N exact zeros and sorted to retain the full M-value spectrum. Floating-point null eigenvalues can differ from a full marker-space decomposition at rounding level. The default eigen_control$maximum_dimension = 2048 applies to min(N, M), not M. One region is processed at a time with O(NM + min(N,M)^2) scratch storage; only O(M) values and region identities remain on Glist. nthreads controls gbits decoding, while the current portable gsolve product and Eigen spectrum backends are serial and do not require OpenBLAS. No global thread setting is changed.
Glist$eigen records named sets, descending values, native diagnostics, selected sample IDs and offsets, controls, and provenance. It survives ordinary RDS persistence. validate_Glist() checks its identities and spectrum shape; it does not recompute the eigenvalues. If a downstream analysis removes markers or changes the reference samples, prepare matching spectra again. glma::prepare_vegas(Glist) reuses the stored spectra; sets may select named regions but must preserve their full membership. Its prepared$markers holds the union of requested markers in reference order. Align all trait rows and alleles to that metadata before calling glma::vegas(stat, prepared=prepared). Constant positive weights within each set are supported. For nonuniform weights, use glma’s existing sparse-LD preparation on a Glist without the unweighted eigen resource. Save the prepared object to evaluate subsequent traits without reopening the original BED files. gsea re-exports both functions.



gbits scans packed marker records directly. Selected original offsets are checked with 64-bit arithmetic. Threaded execution assigns deterministic static marker partitions and never calls R from workers. Temporary native storage is \(O(T\lceil N/4\rceil)\) packed bytes for T workers plus \(O(M)\) counts and selection mappings; preparation does not build an \(O(NM)\) decoded matrix. The separate regional eigen task uses the bounded regional scratch described above.
