title: Numerical and mixed-model routes
text:
This guide explains route choice and scaling. The model catalog owns capability status, the primitive registry owns reusable mechanism mappings, and architecture owns package dependencies. A native primitive does not establish a qualified public R route.


greml() estimates variance components; gsolve() holds them fixed and returns fixed effects and random-effect predictions. Both use the same formula/data/pedigree and explicit gvc() specifications as gfit().
fit <- greml(formula = BW ~ sex + (1 | id),
             data = data, pedigree = pedigree)
summary(fit)
fit$variance_components

# The same model/data specification, now with fixed covariance values.
solved <- gsolve(formula = BW ~ sex + (1 | id), data = data,
                 pedigree = pedigree, vc = c(id = 1, residual = 1))

# Optional shortcut: reuse the prepared model and its fitted covariance values.
resolved <- gsolve(fit)
resolved_pcg <- gsolve(fit, control = list(linear_solver = "pcg"))
Starting values are optional for greml(). Direct gsolve() calls require all covariance values. For gsolve(fit), the default is to use the fitted values, requiring successful status and REML convergence. A complete named vc list/vector can override them; names identify components, and matrix coordinates retain the fitted trait/basis order. Such an override solves the stated fixed model and does not turn a failed REML fit into a successful one.
The handoff reuses prepared records, sparse design and ID mappings. It supports saving/reloading the fit with saveRDS() / readRDS(). Numerical factors are rebuilt for the new solve. Fits therefore retain their analysis data; consider this when sharing saved objects. Supplying a new control replaces the route-specific controls; omitting it inherits the fit’s controls.
Single-trait, multitrait and longitudinal pedigree formulas support the existing PCG and sparse-direct routes. CHOLMOD is the default direct backend. The explicit single-response component route, including correlated channels and grouped/AR(1)/exponential residuals, uses its existing direct solvers. Backend availability depends on the installed build. General gs_model workflows and low-level numerical gsuite_solve() retain their own APIs.
gfit(task = "reml") and gfit(task = "solve") remain available. The compiled route selected by gs_fit_control() is REML-only: greml() can use it, but its fit cannot be handed to gsolve(). This interface change adds no new numerical algorithms or qualification claims. The pedigree tutorial shows the three main data-frame workflows. REML fits already include predictions, so a second solve is optional.



gsolve owns checked column-major matrix views, leading dimensions, caller-owned workspaces, square and rectangular operators, dense/sparse SPD factors, PCG, preconditioners, deterministic probes, SLQ, and numerical diagnostics. Its operator contracts declare symmetry, definiteness, concurrency, and available diagonals. Rectangular operators provide forward/transpose application and bounded column materialization.
greml owns covariance models, fixed-effect projection, likelihood, score, standard average information (AI), optimization, prediction, and uncertainty. gsuite validates explicit R inputs and translates installed public results. Packed genotype operations belong to gbits; resource identity and LD belong to gmat. The optional gbits adapter supplies numerical operators without a reverse dependency from gsolve or greml to genotype libraries.



For single-trait covariance components, \(V = \sum_c \theta_c K_c\) and
\[
P=V^{-1}-V^{-1}F(F^{\mathsf T}V^{-1}F)^{-1}F^{\mathsf T}V^{-1}.
\]








Route
Computation and storage
Practical boundary




Exact dense
Factors observation covariance V; quadratic storage
Small reference models; prepared genomic BED terms are rejected


Matrix-free covariance
PCG applies inverses/projections; common Hutchinson probes estimate traces and SLQ estimates log determinants
Operator and bounded \(O(nk)\) Krylov/probe storage; solver and stochastic precision must both be adequate


Sparse MME
Assembles coefficient-space statistics and uses a retained sparse factor or a qualified coefficient operator
Fill and resource limits matter; backend, trace, inference, and uncertainty support depend on the specific API


Hybrid covariance
Uses structured sparse terms as a state-matched preconditioner for separately declared matrix-free terms
Components enter once; a pedigree plus genomic sum is not automatic single-step GBLUP


Iterative large-p projection
Nested PCG avoids retaining \(V^{-1}F\) and the full fixed-normal matrix; fixed determinant uses SLQ
Selected contrasts may be available while full fixed-effect covariance is unavailable



The low-level gs_model() sparse/hybrid interface is distinct from the specialized pedigree and component-MME interfaces. Its limitations do not apply to all sparse-direct APIs. CHOLMOD selected inversion and PARDISO selected_solve target uncertainty are documented in prediction error. PARDISO selected inversion is unsupported.
Unbalanced multivariate covariance uses the observed principal submatrix of a trait-by-unit covariance: scatter, base-operator application, trait mixing, and gather. Random regression uses supplied basis columns. Neither operation requires a dense production incidence or Kronecker matrix. Selected prediction uncertainty computes only requested target blocks.



Prepared packed BED storage trades preparation work and memory for repeated applications; genomic production routes form no dense GRM. Sparse MME cost depends on coefficient dimension and fill. Matrix-free memory is dominated by operators and bounded Krylov/probe buffers. Nested fixed-effect solves add their own tolerance and determinant-precision requirements.
Independent multiple-RHS PCG solves columns independently. Explicit true block PCG shares a block Krylov recurrence and reports rank compression, deflation, restarts, and each original RHS’s true residual. Its orchestration owns one outer thread. A two-level preconditioner uses a caller-supplied, copied, rank-compressed coarse basis tied to one covariance state; it does not discover a basis automatically. Outer RHS/probe parallelism and operator-local OpenMP must not be nested. Requested and resolved execution are reported separately.
Route selection is API-specific. Low-level model routes are explicit; pedigree direct controls may resolve automatic to an available backend according to their documented policy. An explicit unsupported request does not silently change the statistical route.



The persistent R interface specifies handles, lifetime, ordering, controls, and low-level examples. The formula interface is a separate bounded lowering API. The package qualification limits remain; that page also records the focused constructor naming repair.
Model qualification, qgdata evidence, and the DMU workflow retain scoped numerical evidence and negative outcomes. They do not establish general biobank readiness or universal performance. Build and packaging commands belong in development and binary distribution.

A two-level preconditioner uses a caller-supplied, copied, rank-compressed coarse basis tied to one covariance state; it does not discover a basis automatically. Outer RHS/probe parallelism and operator-local OpenMP must not be nested. Requested and resolved execution are reported separately.
Route selection is API-specific. Low-level model routes are explicit; pedigree direct controls may resolve automatic to an available backend according to their documented policy. An explicit unsupported request does not silently change the statistical route.

title: Numerical and mixed-model routes
text:
The persistent R interface specifies handles, lifetime, ordering, controls, and low-level examples. The formula interface is a separate bounded lowering API. The package qualification limits remain; that page also records the focused constructor naming repair.
Model qualification, qgdata evidence, and the DMU workflow retain scoped numerical evidence and negative outcomes. They do not establish general biobank readiness or universal performance. Build and packaging commands belong in development and binary distribution.

title: Methods
text:
Catalog authority. This page contains route-specific method descriptions and qualification notes. The current suite-wide LMM status is defined by the canonical model catalog, with evidence in model qualification. An exclusion below applies only to the workflow and version being described; it is not a global gsuite capability statement.
This catalogue maps development capabilities to their owning repository. Implemented means the capability is implemented in development code and exercised by relevant repository validation; it does not claim production-scale qualification. Experimental identifies a present but deliberately provisional integration surface. Planned identifies work with no current implementation. Availability through R is stated separately; gsuite has no public software release yet.
The connected genomic example exercises representative routes across six modules using one 10K-individual, 50K-marker simulation. Its qualification record distinguishes execution checks and truth comparisons from untested capabilities.

title: Methods
text:
Capability overview
Reviewed against the development interfaces on 30 September 2026. These are available workflows, not claims of full upstream-software parity or broad statistical calibration. Each guide records its supported inputs and limits. See the estimate/solve contract for the mixed-model entry points. | Analysis or resource | Native owner | Current R access and guide | | — | — | — | | Pedigree, multivariate and longitudinal mixed models | greml, gsolve | greml() for variance estimation, gsolve() for fixed-covariance solving, gfit() and persistent model interfaces; pedigree tutorial, LMM catalog | | Genotypes, marker QC, sparse LD, independent blocks, LD scores and regional eigenvalues/eigenpairs | gmat, gbits, gsolve | gbase::gprep() prepares and augments Glist resources; task = "eigen" prepares reusable full regional BED eigenvalues through the smaller sample/marker Gram matrix; validate_Glist() checks their lightweight descriptor and verify_ld() performs explicit full integrity verification; define_ld_blocks() verifies a block partition once; gbase::gfilter(), ld_scores(), ld_region() and ld_eigen() consume the same Glist; genotype preparation, LD resources | | LDSC, GNOVA, SumHer, HESS/rho-HESS, SUPERGNOVA, LAVA and HDL-L | gcorr | ldsc(stat, Glist, ...) provides the checked single- or multi-trait Glist workflow, including standard stratified and qgg-style grouped marker-set models; explicit focused functions remain selectable directly or through gcorr(method=...). Task and uncertainty coverage. Grouped interfaces extract GNOVA categories and SumHer components/categories with full cross-group jackknife covariance for joint SEM/GGM contrasts. See covariance models. | | GSMR, GSMR2, IVW, Egger and weighted-median MR | gcorr | gcorr_prepare_mr() plus focused method functions and thin gcorr(..., method=) dispatch consume aligned ordinary summary-statistics data frames, explicit effect units and signed LD. See the MR workflow. | | BayesC/BayesR from individual BED or aligned summaries, annotation-informed block-eigen regression, several traits or independent studies | gbayes | Learned scalar and multivariate summary/BED BayesC/BayesR, verified block-eigen scalar BayesC/BayesR through mcmc-eigen, plus single-trait sbayesrc over verified Glist LD blocks with retained eigensystems and component annotations. Shared-LD or independent sampling, study-specific references, covariance learning, posterior capture and continuation, genetic covariance, reporting partitions, selected-individual score uncertainty and four focused summary engines are available; Bayesian regression. | | Regional Bayesian mapping and posterior sets | gbayes, gmap | gmap::gmap() fits regional multi-effect, BayesC or BayesR models using full BED LD for dense MCMC or explicit sparse-LD eigen preparation; familiar iteration/prior arguments, regional post/conv/stat/cs outputs and standalone getCredibleSets() are available; gmap_bed() interprets a saved individual-BED posterior without refitting. gmap_sets() presents labelled set/member tables and gmap_bfdr() summarizes PIP-threshold Bayesian FDR. Mapping workflow. Marginal-PIP groups and component sets have different meanings | | ABF and component-pair colocalisation | gmap | gmap_coloc() provides the single-causal ABF route; gmap_coloc_components() compares saved multi-effect components without refitting. Colocalisation has method-specific assumptions | | Linear/logistic GWAS and quantitative-trait LOCO association | glma | glma::glma() provides ordinary, conditional, batched linear, logistic, infinitesimal LOCO and prior-selected LOCO scans over gbase Glist inputs. Binary logistic tests do not adjust for relatedness | | Genomic scoring and posterior prediction | gscore, model-fitting packages | gscore(weights, Glist) applies portable allele-labelled weights and can accumulate overlapping, cross-file marker-set scores from Glist-resolved marker names. clump_threshold(stat, Glist) constructs conventional C+T weights from reported association effects and prepared sparse LD. glma, gbayes and other model owners fit their statistical effects. Selected-individual score uncertainty is available through gbayes::gbayes(); guide | | Genotype, pedigree and phenotype simulation | gsim | Separate public R package; gsim documentation | | Marker-set association evidence | glma, gsea, gsolve | gsea::vegas() re-exports glma::vegas(). It consumes ordinary checked summary-statistics data frames and Glist sparse LD and provides LD-aware weighted quadratic tests. prepare_vegas() computes eigenvalue-only spectra in bounded parallel batches and returns a serializable object reusable across traits and sessions; gsea_input() validates the gene-labelled enrichment handoff. ACAT remains native-only. Default tails are approximate except for equal positive eigenvalues; the controlled positive-series evaluator reports accuracy and term-budget failures | | Gene-set, genomic-feature and gene-prioritization analysis | gsea | gsea() provides ORA, preranked GSEA, competitive GLS, bounded MAGMA and optional scalar/multitrait Bayesian pathway regression. pops() fits chromosome-held-out marginal selection plus ridge regression and returns feature-based gene rankings. Explicit universe/set preparation, native aggregate/block resampling and optional BH/BY adjustment remain available. Pathway and gene-ranking workflow |
The native MAGMA comparison covers SNP-wise mean gene evidence and competitive pathway analysis with MAGMA 1.10 preprocessing. A small pinned comparison checked 40 genes and two pathways. This is not complete MAGMA equivalence: other gene models, rare-variant preprocessing, missing-data handling and singular-matrix pruning remain outside the route. Its controlled tail evaluator may return unavailable for difficult spectra or tails rather than use a silent fallback. Scalar and joint multitrait Bayesian pathway analysis is exposed through gsea(), reusing gbayes for sampling and parameter learning. PoPS-style gene ranking is exposed separately through gsea::pops(). It repeats marginal feature selection and ridge fitting after excluding each target chromosome, accepts explicit blockwise gene covariance, and returns ranked predictions plus fold and feature diagnostics. It is a focused PoPS-style model rather than a claim of output equivalence to every upstream PoPS preprocessing and locus-reporting step.
Selected native operations remain outside the R bindings, including gscore pseudo-summary generation and the single-effect Bayesian entry point. Checks cover independent small calculations, pinned ACAT comparison and a connected native example, not broad GWAS calibration. glma::vegas() implements native LD-aware quadratic gene evidence from aligned GWAS Z statistics. prepare_vegas() reuses one validated sparse-LD reader and prepares eigenvalue-only gene spectra in bounded parallel batches. Its ordinary R result can be saved and reused across traits, with explicit tail status during evaluation. It also consumes the full regional BED spectra stored by gprep(task="eigen") without repeating decomposition, for constant positive within-set weights. Statistics must follow the prepared union’s complete marker and allele order. The sparse-LD route retains nonuniform weighting. Existing tail defaults and accuracy limits are unchanged. The gsea package re-exports both interfaces and gsea_input() validates the gene-statistic handoff to gsea() without automatic harmonization or inferred cross-gene dependence. Methods that require gene covariance need it supplied separately. ACAT and other gene-evidence combinations remain native-only. Competitive GLS uses supplied gene-covariance blocks; its Student-t inference is a working approximation for non-Gaussian gene scores. It does not claim full MAGMA or Pascal equivalence. Python interfaces remain planned. Multivariate sampling covariance can be learned only for the shared-LD route with an explicit response cross-product; arbitrary sampling overlap across different LD references remains outside the interface. See the current qualification limits before interpreting capability as validated use.
The gbayes::gbayes() choices include point_normal, continuous_shrinkage, variational and mixture_variational. These retain method-specific controls/results, rather than inheriting all BayesC/BayesR features. gbase::checkStat() provides the shared ordinary summary-statistics preparation step. See the summary interface guide.

title: Methods
text:
Pedigree formula workflows
The pedigree tutorial demonstrates the data-frame interface on 10,000 simulated animals. It reuses existing numerical engines:







Formula model
Scope




Pedigree animal model
One or multiple traits; missing responses omitted trait by trait


Genetic random regression
One response, one pedigree effect and homogeneous residuals


Independent components
Multiple pedigree/identity intercepts, including permanent environment and common groups


Correlated channels
One response with named channels under a shared kernel, such as direct/maternal effects


Structured residuals
Grouped variances, integer-gap AR(1), or continuous-time exponential correlation



Short and explicit forms share normalization. formula and formulas are aliases; starts do not select the engine. REML initializes omitted starts, while supplied values remain authoritative. Fixed solves require complete covariance values. The tutorial gives the route-specific initialization rules.
Distinct descriptors are independent. Correlated channels must be declared explicitly and have known IDs for observed responses. Correlated residual blocks require unique positions within one variance group. Multi-component multitrait/random regression, multi-response residual descriptors, nuggets and unknown-time imputation remain outside this adapter. Covariance boundaries and unsupported combinations are not silently repaired. These examples do not extend workload or platform qualification.

title: Methods
text:
Association mapping
Association mapping belongs in native glma and the Glist-based glma() R interface; fine-mapping and colocalisation remain in gmap. The current quantitative-trait methods are exact linear regression, calibrated infinitesimal LOCO testing, and prior-selected LOCO offset testing with automatic structure-dependent scaling or a manual override. The LOCO methods can fit on a selected subset of Glist markers while testing every marker in that Glist; the subset must cover every tested chromosome. Association scans also accept a phenotype matrix with named traits and return one association result per trait. Exact linear scans share genotype reads and dosage decoding. LOCO traits share immutable genotype preparation but each retains its own variance fit, prior selection and calibration. Exact linear scans can include selected marker genotypes as fixed covariates through condition_on; this is a complete-case conditional test and does not reuse the LOCO null model. Binary traits can use the distinct logistic method for ordinary covariate-adjusted per-marker log-odds Wald tests. Sparse case/control counts, separation and non-convergence have explicit statuses. This baseline does not adjust for relatedness or claim LOCO binary calibration. glma provides linear, logistic, infinitesimal LOCO and prior-selected LOCO functions plus the glma(..., method=) dispatcher. vegas() consumes validated gbase summaries and Glist sparse LD. These methods are separate from gmap_stat() summary-statistic preparation.

Bayesian workflow



The connected gcorr validation checks genotype-derived LD scores and fits against dense references. A shared unit floor on marginal working means keeps all prescribed draws finite on the fixture. The floor changes variance weights without clamping raw estimates, and activation is reported in native diagnostics. See the weighting contract. The subsequent statistical calibration study completes all fits and passes parameter-recovery screens, but flags undercoverage for 15 primary quantities. Uncertainty qualification remains incomplete. An independent trait-1 QR diagnostic agrees with the native fixed-weight procedure; re-estimating weights during block deletion improves coverage but does not fully resolve it. These capabilities have not been broadly qualified on real GWAS. The coordinated reliability study finds better coverage with known weights and analytical SEs, supporting an uncertainty-procedure limitation in the tested setting. Matched full LD gives stable estimates in the fixture; short windows and mismatched references cause bias. Current normal/jackknife intervals remain experimental; broad confidence-interval qualification is still open.
Detailed equations, layouts, ownership, and limitations remain in each repository’s local catalogue and linked design documents. The actual local dataset campaign is summarized separately in qgdata qualification.

title: Methods
text:
Sparse-direct pedigree methods
The three pedigree APIs use the same canonical lower-CSC MME for their supported direct backends. Retained factors supply exact determinants and bounded coordinate traces or CHOLMOD selected-inverse traces. Rejected likelihood-only trials omit trace/AI work; accepted response coefficients finalize BLUP without another response solve. Backend factor-memory limits are preflight bounds, not strict allocator quotas.
Use the model catalog for backend/inference status, multitrait workflow and longitudinal workflow for record contracts, and prediction error for complete-MME PEV, CHOLMOD selected inversion, and bounded PARDISO retained-factor target solves. PARDISO selected inversion remains unsupported. Direct and support thread domains and requested/resolved methods remain distinct diagnostics.

title: Methods
text:
Independent LD references
Glist is the single public genotype and LD descriptor. Augment it directly with gmat’s signed, disk-backed sparse LD:
Glist <- gbase::gprep(Glist = Glist, task = "sparseld",
                      out_prefix = "reference_ld", r2 = 0.01,
                      max_distance_bp = 1000000)
saveRDS(Glist, "Glist-EUR.rds")
Glist <- readRDS("Glist-EUR.rds")
gbase::verify_ld(Glist) # once after transfer or download
scores <- gbase::ld_scores(Glist)
Glist$sparseLD retains authoritative marker order, alleles, chromosome, position, reference sample count, file paths, checksums and construction settings. ldfiles, idsLD, and rsidsLD identify the same persisted resource, reference samples, and matrix-ordered markers. RDS saves the descriptor, not the external LD files. validate_Glist() checks this identity and alignment without rescanning the CSR; verify_ld() performs the full native structure, checksum, and recorded-score verification after a transfer or when corruption is suspected. Neither check establishes population suitability. Scores are computed from that same resource:
scores <- gbase::ld_scores(Glist, annotations = annotation,
                           corrected = TRUE)
Annotation rows are aligned by exact marker identity. Corrected scores use the selected reference sample count and retain negative corrected contributions. All scores reflect retained sparse pairs; omitted correlations are not reconstructed. Summary harmonization remains separate.

Regional matrices and reusable eigensystems
Select a region using unique marker IDs already in reference order:
R_region <- gbase::ld_region(Glist, markers = region_markers)
eig <- gbase::ld_eigen(Glist, markers = region_markers)
gmat opens the checked resource once per high-level call and reuses one indexed reader across regions; no full CSR is loaded and only the active dense matrix is materialized. gsolve computes the complete symmetric eigensystem using its existing Eigen backend and verifies reconstruction, residual and orthogonality. The result contains descending values, column vectors with marker row names, and numerical diagnostics. Singular or indefinite matrices are not silently repaired: zero and negative eigenvalues remain available to method-specific checks. Thresholded or windowed sparse LD is not necessarily positive semidefinite.
The eigensystem is computed from the checked regional matrix on demand and can be reused across traits or fits for that region. The full decomposition takes quadratic storage and cubic computation; increasing the dimension limit is an explicit choice. Omitted sparse correlations remain zero, the diagonal is one, and no harmonization, clipping or PSD repair occurs.
The gcorr R interface prepares all named regions from one Glist-backed native reader and retains one PreparedRegionalLd per region. HESS, rho-HESS, SUPERGNOVA and LAVA have single-region overloads that reuse a complete checked eigensystem; LDSC and GNOVA already accept prepared gmat score inputs. gsolve can verify imported eigenvalues and vectors against a regional matrix without rerunning the eigensolver. This dense verification is performed once on native import, followed by reuse across fits. The gcorr R interface connects selected methods to these resources, including explicit joint HESS/rho-HESS correction with regional and total uncertainty. It adds no cross-ancestry estimator and also exposes shared LAVA matrices and native conditional inference.
Across these methods, result tables use explicit reference, region, annotation-category and architecture-component labels. Named h2/cov/rg matrices share one layout; method-specific uncertainty, native diagnostics and inconsistent pairwise estimates remain visible. See result conventions.
The interface also exposes SumHer architecture-component and reference-total h2/cov/rg. Multiple traits use the native coordinated marginal and pairwise fits, with joint fixed-weight jackknife covariance when blocks are supplied. Tagging weights are explicit and separate from architecture-weighted scores; no cross-ancestry or full upstream-software parity is implied.
Regional LAVA also accepts explicit binary-trait metadata, reusing Glist allele frequencies for native logistic-Wald reconstruction. Observed and liability h2 remain distinct; binary/mixed pairs use the existing screening and optional bivariate simulation inference. LAVA shares each regional fit across traits and exposes partial correlations, multiple regression, explained variance and supported conditional/omnibus inference.
Native regional execution now supports multiple named references and regions. Each request explicitly assigns a reference to every trait; all traits in that request must agree. Independent requests may use different references. Results retain analysis, region and reference labels, along with method diagnostics or a per-request failure. Execution is sequential and writes no result files. Joint HESS and rho-HESS can reuse prepared regions within one selected reference while retaining their existing disjoint-region and joint uncertainty assumptions. Reference labels are caller-declared identities, not an ancestry validation step.
For continuous-trait regional LAVA correlations, gcorr_lava() accepts an explicit inference list. The native bivariate procedure supplies screened p-values, 95% simulation intervals and Monte Carlo diagnostics while retaining raw point estimates. See the regional inference contract. This adds no new numerical algorithm or statistical calibration claim.

title: Methods
text:
Native colocalisation
gmap provides approximate-Bayes-factor colocalisation for one region and two continuous traits, assuming at most one causal variant per trait and non-overlapping samples. It returns H0-H4 probabilities and explicit prior-sensitivity summaries. The implementation has independent numerical checks and pinned coloc comparisons; these establish numerical agreement, not broad statistical calibration. The gmap::gmap_coloc() route accepts two aligned regional beta/SE tables, explicit phenotype SDs and priors without an LD object. It returns regional probabilities and conditional-H4 marker support, distinct from component-pair colocalisation. See the worked example. GWAS association is implemented separately in glma; Bayesian fine-mapping and posterior-set interpretation are described below.

title: Methods
text:
Native Bayesian inference
The gbayes::gbayes() R workflow exposes single-trait and joint multivariate regression from a prepared individual-level BED Glist or from checked summaries and Glist sparse LD. The BED route uses matched pre-adjusted phenotype columns and native packed-genotype preparation; its joint route can learn residual covariance from observed trait cross-products. BayesC/BayesR support fixed parameters or optional effect-covariance and mixture-weight learning, exact chain seeds, chain-level threading and native posterior summaries. Multiple traits require explicit independent sampling or the common-N shared-LD covariance model. Variable sample sizes are an explicit approximation and, for multivariate fits, require independent sampling and study-size metadata. Shared-LD multivariate sampling covariance can be learned when the response cross-product and likelihood dimension are supplied. Scalar BayesC/BayesR expose fixed, exact in-sample and reference-LD adjusted residual policies. Exact learning uses an explicit response sum of squares, likelihood dimension, scaled inverse-chi-square prior and complete same-sample LD. The reference-LD route uses standardized summary normalization and records its base residual variance, genetic variance and adjusted working variance separately. Latent base-effect covariance is labelled separately from realised genetic covariance. The annotation argument exposes logistic inclusion, continuation-probit pattern/component probabilities and log-linear variance models, with fixed or learned coefficients and native diagnostics. The same interface now binds grouped latent covariance priors and optional native posterior genetic covariance, partition activity/covariance and selected-individual score uncertainty. Heritability normalization requires explicit phenotype variances. Group summaries retain cross-group LD; score uncertainty excludes residual noise. Named study-specific references additionally expose native independent-provider preparation with differing LD, sample sizes and marker subsets. Multiple studies may inform shared effects of one trait within a model of at least two traits. Study identity, trait identity and reference provenance remain distinct. This is not an overlap correction or an automatic ancestry-specific effect model.
gbayes provides single-trait BayesC and BayesR with fixed parameters or explicit learning of residual variance, slab variance and mixture weights. Prepared scores and cross-products can use dense storage, gmat LD operations with explicit marker scaling, or prepared factors with reduced residuals. Factorized execution avoids a dense cross-product matrix. Truncated inputs use explicitly projected scores; residual learning then requires retained-space normalization (dimension and response sum of squares). Results include posterior means, empirical posterior variances, marginal inclusion probabilities and compact per-chain summaries. BayesR also returns marker component probabilities; both methods summarize learned parameters. Residual-variance learning requires compatible phenotype sums of squares and an explicit Gaussian likelihood dimension, not just LD and scores. The gmap() R binding exposes BayesC/BayesR separately across named traits and regions, including optional variance and mixture-weight learning. MCMC learning requires explicit inverse-chi-square or Dirichlet hyperpriors. Residual learning also requires complete in-sample LD, phenotype sum of squares and likelihood dimension; these are never inferred from the reference panel.
The scalar reference-LD recipe has five-repetition qualification for matched continuous-trait BayesC and BayesR analyses, including heritability, effect and score recovery and four-chain diagnostics. Independent scalar calculations, dense/gmat agreement and matched sblr checks support its native implementation. See the qualification record for the exact LD construction, priors and chain lengths. Supplied cross-products must define a valid positive-semidefinite operator; structural checks do not repair or certify arbitrary thresholded LD. A separate five-repetition design qualifies disjoint-block residual learning, the BayesS MAF exponent, shared-LD latent effect and sampling-covariance learning, and strong-LD relocation under their stated contracts. Scalar and multivariate saved states also reproduce uninterrupted chains exactly. Broader annotation models and arbitrary overlap structures remain outside that evidence.

title: Methods
text:
Native regional Bayesian analysis
The Bayesian-enabled gmap::gmap library fits or summarizes one-region BayesC/BayesR models through installed gbayes. It preserves marker alignment, region coordinates, trait/effect units and the complete native posterior. Results include marker rankings and the posterior expected active-marker count, calculated as the sum of marginal PIPs. Existing gbayes priors and learning controls pass through.
These posterior summaries describe marker support. Separate set helpers below interpret marginal PIPs or component assignments. These summaries do not themselves perform colocalisation or estimate regional heritability. The separate gmap_coloc_components() interface consumes multi-effect evidence. Inputs are already aligned. The gmap() R binding returns regional posterior estimates, native set controls and chain diagnostics for named regions and traits, with regional preparation shared across traits. One regional eigensystem supports an ordered retained-positive-mass schedule; the first threshold accepted for every trait is selected and every attempt remains visible. The colocalisation target acquires no Bayesian dependency. Focused checks cover posterior reuse, metadata/ranking semantics and installed interfaces.

title: Methods
text:
Native single-effect inference
gbayes now provides a deterministic single-effect normal model for one prepared marker set. It reuses the normal conditional calculation and accepts the existing dense, LD-backed and factorized inputs. Outputs include marker assignment probabilities, conditional and averaged effect moments, and model evidence against no effect. Residual and effect-prior variances are fixed; marker prior weights can be specified explicitly.
The model assumes exactly one active marker, so assignments sum to one even when evidence is weak. They are not unconditional association probabilities. This is a reusable building block; the separate multi-effect entry point below adds iteration and convergence handling. gmap now consumes assignments for credible sets; multi-signal colocalisation remains separate. There is no R binding. Focused independent numerical integration and installed-interface checks cover the native calculation.

title: Methods
text:
Native multi-effect inference
gbayes also provides single-trait sum-of-single-effects fitting through sequential IBSS updates. It reuses the existing single-effect calculation and dense, LD or factorized operators. Outputs include component assignments, combined effect means, variational variances/PIPs, and an objective trace with explicit convergence or sweep-limit status.
The objective is an evidence lower bound relative to the null likelihood, not an exact model Bayes factor. The approximation factorizes across components; convergence does not guarantee a global optimum or calibrated uncertainty. The maximum component count is supplied, and components may select the same marker. The default fixed-variance route leaves every component active. Optional EM learning estimates a variance for each component and compares it with zero; inactive components contribute no effects or PIPs. Optional residual-variance learning uses expected residual sums of squares with compatible normalization. Inner learning limits and outer convergence are reported explicitly. gmap supplies credible sets only for active components while retaining inactive indices and all component variances. The gmap() R binding exposes this route separately across regions and traits, with optional residual- and effect-variance learning. Residual learning requires complete in-sample LD and explicit phenotype normalization. Small analytic/evidence and operator checks cover the native calculation; full susieR equivalence is not claimed.

title: Methods
text:
Native posterior sets
The optional gmap Bayesian component supports two explicitly labelled routes. Marginal-PIP sets reuse sblr’s LD-neighborhood and approximate multi-signal selection, including incomplete-set handling and alternative lead/removal rules. Their mass is an expected active-marker count, not a probability that at least one causal variant lies in the set. This route consumes BayesC/BayesR PIPs.
Component-based credible sets consume single-/multi-effect assignment rows. They retain each component, report achieved probability coverage and flag exact duplicate memberships. Shared diagnostics include lead-based and full pairwise LD summaries. Low purity is flagged without trimming away coverage. Sparse LD omissions are explicitly recorded; purity is evaluated on the supplied matrix.
These helpers validate probability domains and exact fit/LD marker order, preserve available convergence/likelihood status, and do not refit or align data. Learned zero-variance components are recorded without sets; the raw assignment route still treats every row as a component. Weak fixed-variance components can produce diffuse sets; a complete credible set does not establish a signal. The R binding exposes these controls through control$sets, with explicit set meanings and component eligibility diagnostics.
gmap_sets() converts the nested native result to set-level and marker-level tables without changing those meanings. gmap_bfdr() operates only on fitted marker PIPs: at a supplied threshold it reports the selected count, the expected false-discovery count sum(1 - PIP) and their ratio. A requested BFDR target selects the largest PIP-threshold group below that bound. It does not require LD, retained posterior draws or another model fit, and it is not a frequentist FDR guarantee.
Prior-variance learning is empirical Bayes, not posterior uncertainty over model size or a test proving signal existence. The EM search is local; inactive components are reconsidered from a positive starting variance each sweep. The reusable learned single-effect entry is available independently. Existing fixed-variance entry points retain their previous numerical behavior.

title: Methods
text:
Regional Bayesian R workflow
For an individual-level BayesC/BayesR fit, gmap::gmap_bed(fit, Glist, regions) reuses the saved global posterior. The Glist must carry in-sample sparse LD prepared from exactly the fitted people and markers. Sample order, physical BED offsets, alleles and frequencies are checked. Within-region LD must be complete by default. Native gmap groups the fitted marginal PIPs; the result is neither a regional refit nor a component credible set. This route also accepts a joint-trait BED fit and retains trait labels. See the BED-to-gmap workflow.
gmap::gmap() accepts an aligned Glist and exact sufficient-statistic columns marker, allele1, allele2, score (\(X^T y\)) and marker_ss (\(\operatorname{diag}(X^T X)\)). It fits each named region/trait separately using BayesC, BayesR or multi-effect inference. It does not convert GWAS z scores or beta/SE automatically. The supplied LD and marker scales define the working cross-products; a reference approximation does not become exact cohort LD.
fit <- gmap::gmap(list(height = stat_height, weight = stat_weight), Glist,
            regions = list(locus1 = markers_locus1, locus2 = markers_locus2),
            method = "multi_effect",
            prior = list(residual_variance = 1, effect_variance = .02),
            control = list(effects = 4, estimate_effect_variance = TRUE,
              eigen = list(retained_positive_mass = 1)))
summary(fit)
plot(fit, region = "locus1", trait = "height", quantity = "pip")
Prior values above are illustrative and must match the supplied data scale. Controls and seeds are shared across fits; use separate calls for different priors or independent random streams. Each verified region is decomposed once across traits. The default retained-mass schedule is c(.995, .99, .95). diagnostic_summary records the selected requested/achieved mass, rank and projection change, while eigen_attempts records each attempted threshold. Set control$eigen$retained_positive_mass=1 for the exact full-rank route. Residual-variance learning is restricted to that full-rank route. Component colocalisation also requires a converged full-rank multi-effect fit; use the same explicit setting when the fit will be passed to gmap_coloc_components(). control$sets exposes method-specific native set controls. BayesC/BayesR retain pooled and per-chain PIPs, with native between-chain spread summaries; these are not convergence certificates or Monte Carlo standard errors. Scalar summary BayesC/BayesR in gmap() and gbayes() also expose optional control$ld_swap relocation moves on their dense/sparse and eigen likelihoods. The native gbayes sampler owns neighbour selection and Metropolis-Hastings acceptance. Probability defaults to zero; fit$ld_swap reports proposal counts, not convergence. The existing timing studies used swaps disabled.
For traits analysed in independent samples, the saved fits can be compared:
shared <- gmap::gmap_coloc_components(
  fit, fit, Glist, trait1 = "height", trait2 = "weight", regions = "locus1",
  control = list(complete_region_coverage = TRUE,
                 non_overlapping_samples = TRUE))
summary(shared)
plot(shared)
The two assertions require complete regional coverage and independent trait samples; they must describe the actual analysis. This route requires converged full-likelihood multi-effect fits, uniform marker priors and the same complete LD reference. It consumes stored component evidence without fitting or eigen computation. LD files must remain available for checked purity calculations. H0–H4 probabilities belong to individual component pairs, not the entire region. Inactive, low-purity, incomplete and duplicate components remain labelled; no eligible pairs is not evidence for H0. Summaries and plots of completed results work from saved R objects without accessing LD files.
OLS beta/SE/n preparation is available through gmap_stat(); see below and the worked simulation tutorial. No cross-reference or overlapping-sample colocalisation is exposed.

title: Methods
text:
Linear-regression GWAS input for mapping
gmap::gmap_stat() performs a separate OLS summary conversion in the R layer: for sample phenotype variance \(s_y^2\), it reconstructs \(d_j=(n-1)s_y^2/[(n-2)SE_j^2+\hat\beta_j^2]\) and \(X_j^\mathsf{T}y=d_j\hat\beta_j\). The common-sample, intercept-only, continuous-outcome contract is explicit. LD supplies the off-diagonal cross-products; external LD is approximate. Numerical fitting and sets remain native. See the worked example.

title: Methods
text:
MR through the R interface
gcorr exposes GSMR, GSMR2, IVW, Egger and weighted-median components through gcorr_prepare_mr() and method-specific fitters. Preparation consumes two aligned gbase effect/SE summaries and an explicit signed-LD matrix; it does not accept an LDlist, align alleles or infer ancestry/sample overlap. The serializable result records every selection and LD decision. Focused fitters and gcorr(prepared, method=...) return HEIDI, estimate-unit and method-specific diagnostics. See the MR workflow.

title: Methods
section: Covariance models through the R interface
text:
Covariance models through the R interface
gcorr_covariance() retains labelled continuous genetic covariance and full joint sampling covariance. Focused SEM and GGM functions expose recursive SEM, descriptive partial-correlation networks and fixed-graph GGM. Parameter tables, trait units and estimation metadata remain explicit. Fitted SEM paths and free GGM edges support native joint Wald tests. Coordinated multivariate GNOVA annotation categories and SumHer architecture components can reuse the same models, with cross-group contrasts based on the retained joint jackknife covariance. See the covariance-model workflow.

title: Canonical LMM capability catalog

This is the authoritative catalog of LMM routes and their recorded evidence. Status terms are defined in model architecture. Evidence is indexed in model qualification; reusable machinery and exact reductions are in the primitive registry and model reductions.


This inventory follows the exported constructors, dispatch code and existing test sources; it is not a new numerical qualification run. The single-trait, multitrait, longitudinal, repeatability and direct/maternal tutorial models, plus grouped, AR(1) and exponential residual examples, have been executed with the 10,000-animal pedigree; other rows below still need a comparable user-workflow check. formula and formulas now select the same general gfit() adapter. Use CHOLMOD with selected inversion as the reference configuration for the new sparse-direct model examples. Selecting CHOLMOD alone is insufficient: coordinate tracing can still do many solves. The three pedigree tutorial models already select linear_solver = "sparse_direct", direct_backend = "cholmod", exact_trace_method = "selected_inverse". The source currently differs from that policy:

General pedigree formulas default to sparse direct, CHOLMOD and selected inversion. Explicit alternative backends use coordinate tracing unless the caller requests another trace method; unsupported requests are not repaired.
The four specialized pedigree control constructors default to PCG, automatic backend and coordinate tracing.
Compiled gs_fit_control() defaults to CHOLMOD and selected inversion. Its selected-inversion argument is trace_route, not exact_trace_method.
gs_lmm_control() already defaults to CHOLMOD. Its public signature does not expose the native component PCG/stochastic/adaptive controls; those native capabilities are a separate R-exposure gap.
Dense exact and matrix-free covariance routes are different algorithms; a global CHOLMOD substitution is not applicable to them.

Keep explicit solver choices and clear errors when requested CHOLMOD support is unavailable. Specialized low-level control defaults remain separate. The timing difference observed in the tutorial is not evidence that one backend is universally faster for every model and workload.



Use 10,000 animals/individuals as the default demonstration size for scalable routes, with trait and observation counts stated separately. Tiny deterministic oracle tests remain tiny; dense reference routes and bounded uncertainty targets should not automatically be expanded to 10K dimensions.
Keep this coverage table as the inventory, the existing pedigree tutorial as the introductory example, and reuse build/examples/ for replaceable runtime outputs. Do not create a folder or a dated report for each attempted fit. Promote only selected, reviewed figures and concise results to website sources.
Check each recipe in this order: expressibility through exported R functions, correct model/ID mapping, convergence, result extraction, then agreement with an existing equivalent route or appropriate reference. Passing one example does not requalify every covariance/backend combination.

The combined supplied-precision/structured-residual stochastic illustration was not run. Exact CHOLMOD component capabilities in those rows remain qualified and unchanged.
The optional adaptive component policy preserves those scientific boundaries. It uses deterministic nested probe prefixes and phase-specific PCG tolerances for exploratory, accepted-state, and certification work; the fixed-budget path remains the default. Final convergence is always recomputed with the declared fixed certification prefix and requires score compatibility, deterministic stationarity, and an absolute transformed-parameter uncertainty envelope. Adaptive execution is qualified for the independent-residual identity/ pedigree scope. Use CHOLMOD with selected inversion as the reference configuration for the new sparse-direct model examples. Selecting CHOLMOD alone is insufficient: coordinate tracing can still do many solves. The source currently differs from that policy:

General pedigree formulas default to sparse direct, CHOLMOD and selected inversion. Explicit alternative backends use coordinate tracing unless the caller requests another trace method; unsupported requests are not repaired.
The four specialized pedigree control constructors default to PCG, automatic backend and coordinate tracing.
Compiled gs_fit_control() defaults to CHOLMOD and selected inversion. Its selected-inversion argument is trace_route, not exact_trace_method.
gs_lmm_control() already defaults to CHOLMOD. Its public signature does not expose the native component PCG/stochastic/adaptive controls; those native capabilities are a separate R-exposure gap.
Dense exact and matrix-free covariance routes are different algorithms; a global CHOLMOD substitution is not applicable to them.

Keep explicit solver choices and clear errors when requested CHOLMOD support is unavailable. Specialized low-level control defaults remain separate. The timing difference observed in the tutorial is not evidence that one backend is universally faster for every model and workload.



Use 10,000 animals/individuals as the default demonstration size for scalable routes, with trait and observation counts stated separately. Tiny deterministic oracle tests remain tiny; dense reference routes and bounded uncertainty targets should not automatically be expanded to 10K dimensions.
Keep this coverage table as the inventory, the existing pedigree tutorial as the introductory example, and reuse build/examples/ for replaceable runtime outputs. Do not create a folder or a dated report for each attempted fit. Promote only selected, reviewed figures and concise results to website sources.
Check each recipe in this order: expressibility through exported R functions, correct model/ID mapping, convergence, result extraction, then agreement with an existing equivalent route or appropriate reference. Passing one example does not requalify every covariance/backend combination.

PARDISO selected inversion is unsupported for every route. PARDISO capability metadata reports this explicitly and no fallback is permitted. Longitudinal pedigree coordinate tracing is a bounded moderate-problem PARDISO route; it does not imply that selected inversion is absent globally. The separate selected_solve cells above use documented retained-factor multi-RHS solves; they do not change PARDISO’s selected-inversion classification.
For incomplete multitrait stochastic REML, covariance optimization, optional approximate restricted likelihood, and all-animal BLUP are separate result capabilities. Score/AI convergence and BLUP can succeed when final SLQ exceeds its requested standard-error limit; in that case likelihood is explicitly unavailable and its estimate, uncertainty, and work remain diagnostic only.
The same separation applies to qualified stochastic component REML. Its missing-channel claim means absent canonical scalar records, not imputation or complete-case deletion. The scalable supplied sparse-precision constructor and structured-residual PCG/stochastic paths are retained implementations, but they are not a completed qualified combination. Supplied precision is fixed-state qualified; its stochastic optimizer is not. AR(1) fixed-state evaluation and stochastic optimization are qualified. Continuous exponential coefficient, derivative, trace, AI, and PCG evaluation is fixed-state qualified, whereas its stochastic optimizer ended in explicit score-merit line-search exhaustion. The combined supplied-precision/structured-residual stochastic illustration was not run. Exact CHOLMOD component capabilities in those rows remain qualified and unchanged.
The optional adaptive component policy preserves those scientific boundaries. It uses deterministic nested probe prefixes and phase-specific PCG tolerances for exploratory, accepted-state, and certification work; the fixed-budget path remains the default. Final convergence is always recomputed with the declared fixed certification prefix and requires score compatibility, deterministic stationarity, and an absolute transformed-parameter uncertainty envelope. Adaptive execution is qualified for the independent-residual identity/ pedigree scope. The bounded FA revisit ended with explicit insufficient parameter-step precision, so it does not change the FA row above.

text:
No additional implementation is needed for longitudinal pedigree CHOLMOD selected inversion or PEV/reliability: that public path is already qualified. Potential bounded future work, if prioritized, is limited to catalogued gaps:

A qualification-only closure for an implemented_unqualified combination, such as component active boundaries together with correlated residual blocks, without adding either mechanism again.

title: Scientific model recipes
text:
These definitions preserve useful scientific distinctions from the earlier A-C planning catalog. They are mathematical recipes, not installed syntax, implementation priorities, or qualification claims. Consult the model catalog for each public route and the reductions for established equivalences.
For \(y = X\beta + \sum_k Z_k u_k + e\), each component must declare its external coefficient domain, record incidence and weights, relationship, covariance layout, missingness, and prediction targets. The notation Z describes the mathematics; it does not require a production incidence matrix.









Recipe
Scientific meaning and interpretation




Animal
\(a \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_a^2 A)\); records reference animal coefficients, including pedigree animals without observations


Multitrait animal
Relationship A shared across declared traits with covariance G; observed residual units use R[S,S]; different fixed designs and missing traits require explicit mapping


Repeatability
Independent animal and subject-level identity terms, plus residual; \(h^2 = v_a/(v_a+v_p+v_e)\) and repeatability \(\frac{v_a+v_p}{v_a+v_p+v_e}\)


Common environment
Independent identity component over litter, pen, household, herd, site, or another declared domain; domains need not be nested in pedigree order


Sire
Records reference sire coefficients with covariance \(\sigma_s^2 A_s\); report sire variance explicitly, without silently converting it to additive genetic variance


Direct/maternal
Animal and dam incidence channels share one pedigree relationship and a joint 2-by-2 genetic covariance; all dam references must resolve


Maternal permanent environment
Independent identity component indexed by dam; combining it with direct/maternal genetics gives the full maternal recipe


Trait-specific random effects
Components declare their acting traits and records; absent incidence is structural, distinct from a missing response


Correlated random coefficients
Several declared incidence channels share one relationship K and covariance Q; matching grouping labels alone do not imply correlation


Direct/social
Direct and social genetic channels may correlate, while a social channel has several weighted contributing group mates; self-exclusion, duplicates, weight scale, and member order need explicit contracts


Discrete pedigree GxE
Environment-specific breeding values with covariance \(A\otimes G_E\); a multitrait reduction applies only when incidence and fixed-design mappings match


Random regression/reaction norm
u_i has relationship-by-basis covariance and contributes \(b(t)^{\mathsf T}u_i\) or \(b(E)^{\mathsf T}u_i\); common-grid and irregular records use supplied bases, with explicit prediction rows and extrapolation interpretation



Repeatability and other variance ratios require a valid positive denominator and stated units; their uncertainty support must be assessed separately. For a trajectory, covariance between supplied basis rows is \(b(t)^{\mathsf T}Qb(s)\). Basis rank and external axis order are part of the model, not solver choices.



These families may apply to different domains. A family available in a generic longitudinal API is not thereby available in the component or formula API.







Family
Definition or required distinction




Homogeneous / heterogeneous diagonal
\(\sigma^2 I\) / \(\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_j^2)\); distinguish trait, residual-group, and level-domain variances


Unstructured SPD
\(LL^{\mathsf T}\) with positive diagonal L; log-Cholesky is a parameterization, not another covariance family


Compound symmetry
\(\sigma^2((1-\rho)I+\rho J)\); admissible rho depends on dimension


Heterogeneous compound symmetry
\(D((1-\rho)I+\rho J)D\), where D contains marginal standard deviations


Banded
Ordered levels and a declared bandwidth; specify omitted zeros and a positive-definite parameterization


Antedependence
Structured precision or modified Cholesky, with innovation variances and dependence coefficients; zero dependence reduces to diagonal covariance


Discrete AR(1)
\(\sigma^2\rho^{\lvert t_i-t_j\rvert}\) on integer positions, \(\lvert\rho\rvert<1\); heterogeneous scaling is \(DC_{\mathrm{AR1}}D\)


AR/MA/ARMA
Each order requires its own stationarity/invertibility, ordering, and derivative contract


Continuous exponential
\(\sigma^2\exp(-\phi\lvert t_i-t_j\rvert)\), \(\phi>0\), on irregular finite times; duplicate-time handling must be explicit


Unstructured within-subject residual
A bounded occasion covariance with observed principal submatrices; distinct from a permanent-environment random effect


Factor analytic FA(k)
\(\Lambda\Lambda^{\mathsf T}+\Psi\), positive diagonal specifics; declared rank and loading identification are required; compare derived covariances under permitted sign conventions


Reduced rank
\(\Lambda\Lambda^{\mathsf T}\) is singular when rank is below dimension; it requires an explicit singular precision/determinant/boundary contract


Spatial AR1 by AR1
\(\sigma^2 C_{\mathrm{row}}\otimes C_{\mathrm{col}}\); declare grid order and missing-cell behavior, separately from random row/column effects


General separable covariance
\(S_1\otimes S_2\); both factors need validated ordering and derivatives; \(\log\det(S_1\otimes S_2)=d_2\log\det(S_1)+d_1\log\det(S_2)\)



Support for one positive-interior family does not establish its zero-variance, singular, mixed-family, or optimized boundary extension. Component omission and fixed-parameter reductions remain useful when a chosen route excludes boundaries.

title: Multivariate sparse-pedigree evaluation and REML
text:
Multivariate sparse-pedigree evaluation and REML
gs_multitrait_pedigree_records() stores one row per observed scalar response. Rows sharing an observation-unit label belong to one animal and may contain any nonempty subset of the declared traits. A trait can occur once per unit; missing traits are absent and never imputed. Units are residual-independent, while traits observed together use the corresponding principal submatrix of the full SPD residual covariance R.
ped <- gs_pedigree_data(
  individual = c("child", "sire", "dam"),
  sire = c("sire", NA, NA), dam = c("dam", NA, NA))
records <- gs_multitrait_pedigree_records(
  ped,
  animal = c("sire", "sire", "dam", "child", "child"),
  trait = c("height", "weight", "height", "height", "weight"),
  observation_unit = c("sire", "sire", "dam", "child", "child"),
  phenotype = c(1.2, 2.0, .9, 1.8, 2.7),
  fixed = Matrix::Matrix(cbind(
    height_intercept = c(1, 0, 1, 1, 0),
    weight_intercept = c(0, 1, 0, 0, 1)), sparse = TRUE),
  trait_levels = c("height", "weight"))
start <- gs_multitrait_pedigree_start(records)
control <- gs_multitrait_pedigree_reml_control(
  linear_solver = "sparse_direct", direct_backend = "cholmod",
  exact_trace_method = "selected_inverse",
  maximum_selected_inverse_workspace_bytes = 2 * 1024^3,
  trace_mode = "complete_deterministic",
  maximum_direct_coefficient_dimension = 256,
  max_exact_trace_systems = 256, trace_batch_size = 32,
  requested_threads = 8)
fit <- gs_multitrait_pedigree_fit(
  records, start = start, covariance = "optimized", control = control)
The deterministic start fits the active fixed columns separately by trait and sets both starting covariance matrices to one half of the diagonal residual phenotypic variances. It does not estimate correlations and is not RHE. Explicit SPD G and R override it.
Three capability levels are intentional:

Large-scale fixed SPD G,R: sparse-PCG MME/BLUP, fixed effects, all-animal breeding values, record fitted/residual/Py, and stochastic fixed-parameter REML diagnostics.
Exact-work-limited sparse-direct estimation: one lower-CSC pattern and symbolic PARDISO or CHOLMOD analysis, deterministic coordinate traces in bounded retained-factor batches or one CHOLMOD supernodal selected-inverse derivative-support request per full trace evaluation, exact factor log determinants, and likelihood-monotone log-Cholesky optimization. Preflight reports coefficient dimension, input/factor nonzeros, trace systems, RHS workspace, fill, and factor memory, and enforces the configured limits.
Scalable stochastic estimation: PCG, fixed caller-controlled counter-Rademacher trace/determinant probes and seeds, common probes across accepted and trial states, standard batched AI, and noise-aware log-Cholesky optimization. Raw trace/score SEs are reported diagnostics; step admission and convergence use scale-aware curvature/Newton and standardized-score rules. An unresolved state returns insufficient_stochastic_precision without direct fallback.

The direct accepted state already contains the exact final likelihood. Rejected trials perform no trace or AI work, and final fixed effects and BLUPs reuse the accepted response coefficients without another factorization or solve. The result identifies fixed versus optimized covariance, trace mode, optimizer qualification, exact-work preflight, numerical and stochastic status, starting/final covariances, scores and AI, likelihood and SE, all-animal BLUPs, optional record values, retained-state reuse, observed patterns, sparse storage, PCG work, or direct symbolic/numerical factorization, solve, fill, memory, exact-trace, and thread-domain diagnostics.
Stochastic optimization returns separate optimizer, likelihood, and BLUP statuses. Score/AI convergence promotes the accepted covariance state and allows retained-response all-animal BLUP independently of final SLQ. If the requested log-determinant SE is not met, likelihood_available is false and the typed likelihood status is likelihood_precision_insufficient; the actual estimate, SE, probe/Lanczos configuration, and work remain diagnostic only. Likelihood-dependent model comparisons must require likelihood_available = TRUE. Exact sparse-direct REML is preferred for small or moderate problems within its resource limits, especially when an exact likelihood is required.
The qualified stochastic route retains standard batched AI. The separate augmented-AI experiment, component-LMM stochastic routes, and factor-analytic qualification boundaries are recorded in model qualification.
exact_trace_method = "coordinate" is the unchanged default and works with PARDISO or CHOLMOD. "selected_inverse" requires a resolved CHOLMOD backend and a sufficient maximum_selected_inverse_workspace_bytes limit. Derivative support is compiled once from a deterministic positive-definite planning state; one trace plan, derivative mapping, and selected-inverse workspace are reused across covariance states. It computes the exact inverse values on the coalesced covariance-derivative support, reports request/factor/workspace/peak-memory accounting, and performs zero coordinate trace systems. It does not remove the separately counted AI derivative-response systems. Explicit PARDISO, or automatic resolving to PARDISO, returns not_supported without fallback.
For direct fits, automatic prefers PARDISO. PARDISO retains qualified internal threading; CHOLMOD orchestration and multitrait support work remain 1/1 while selected-inverse dense kernels use their independently requested oneMKL thread count. PCG supports fixed-covariance solves and the stochastic REML route described above; both report zero direct work. An incompatible PARDISO selected-inverse request performs one symbolic capability resolution and then returns not_supported before numerical factorization.
The accepted factor, response, determinant, likelihood, and selected values are retained so BLUP finalization performs zero additional response solves. The shared typed serializer only translates native fields and performs no factorization, solve, trace, likelihood, score, AI, selected inversion, or BLUP work. In direct diagnostics, sparse_direct$requested is the logical direct-route flag; requested_backend and resolved_backend are backend strings.
The combined Windows process loads official Intel libiomp5md and no GNU libgomp; the CHOLMOD-only process loads no OpenMP runtime.
No route constructs dense pedigree, observation covariance, incidence, Kronecker, projection, or MME matrices. Exact covariance boundaries, PARDISO selected inversion, MUMPS, fixed-effect rank repair, general multiple relationship components, longitudinal direct REML through this API, RHE, marker effects, genomic or ssGBLUP models, and serial dependence between observation units are excluded.
Exact conditional PEV/reliability is specified separately in the prediction-error contract, including CHOLMOD selected inversion and bounded PARDISO retained-factor target solves.

title: Sparse-LD preparation contract
text:
gbase::gprep(Glist, task = "sparseld", ...) validates an existing prepared gs_genotypes descriptor, resolves its physical BED rows and marker records, and delegates computation and persistence to gmat. gbase owns the public task, validation, selection, and returned R descriptor. gmat owns the numerical kernel, CSR storage, validation, and LD-score scan. gbits remains the existing packed BED access path. BED remains the genotype store, and neither a dense genotype matrix nor a dense genome-wide LD matrix is constructed.
The input is never prepared implicitly. Unknown tasks and the separate "ldscores" task fail. qgg and sblr are read-only qualification references and are not runtime dependencies.



Reference samples are selected by explicit ids, then Glist$study_ids, then all Glist$ids. Values must be nonempty, unique, nonmissing, and completely resolved. Caller order is preserved in idsLD, provenance, and the exact zero-based source rows passed to gmat.
Markers are selected by explicit rsids, otherwise all prepared markers. Requested IDs must be unique and completely resolved. The physical matrix is always ordered by file and original BIM order; requested order is recorded in provenance. source_marker_indices_0based supplies the original BED record for every marker, so noncontiguous preparation and LD subsets are safe. LD never crosses a chromosome boundary.
Allele frequencies count BIM field 5 (a1). Frequencies from preparation are reused only when the ordered LD samples equal the preparation sample set. Otherwise the existing gbits packed-count primitive recomputes frequencies for the LD reference rows; an all-missing marker fails. This frequency vector is aligned exactly to the CSR marker order. gmat independently obtains the same reference-sample means while standardizing genotypes.



For observed allele-1 dosage g, gmat uses \(p=\operatorname{mean}(g)/2\) and \(z=\frac{g-2p}{\sqrt{2p(1-p)}}\). A missing call is standardized zero, equivalent to mean imputation after centering. Monomorphic and all-missing columns have zero scale and become zero; gsuite rejects an all-missing selected reference marker before computation. Pairwise dot products accumulate in double precision and persisted correlations are signed float32 r. A zero denominator produces \(r=0\).
Only strict-upper off-diagonal entries satisfying \(r^2\geq\texttt{r2}\) are stored, in deterministic row/column order; the unit diagonal is implicit. A base-pair window and marker-index window are inclusive and combined with AND when both are positive. Zero disables one window. Both zero are rejected unless allow_full_ld = TRUE because that evaluates every same-chromosome pair.
Ordinary LD score is computed by scanning the validated persisted CSR: \(1+\sum r^2\) over retained off-diagonal neighbors. The implicit diagonal contributes one, thresholded-out entries do not contribute, and no finite- sample correction is applied. Scores follow rsidsLD exactly.



The canonical gmat format is sparse_ld_csr, format version 1. For prefix P, it owns exactly P.row_ptr.u64.bin, P.col_idx.u32.0based.bin, P.values.f32.bin, P.markers.tsv, and P.meta.txt. The first three contain a strict-upper CSR with zero-based columns and native fixed-width scalar types; the marker sidecar freezes identity and physical source mappings. Exact sizes, row pointers, sorted columns, finite values, dimensions, and marker metadata are validated before publication and on reopen.
Writes use a same-directory staging set. overwrite = FALSE refuses any existing owned target. Explicit overwrite replaces only that five-file set; metadata is published last as the commit marker. Staging and partially published new files are cleaned on failure.
The returned object remains c("gs_genotypes", "Glist"). Its canonical sparseLD member records prefix, format/version, paths, sample/marker counts, nnz, component files, physical one-based rows/cls, aligned AF, marker and sample IDs, zero-based mappings, thresholds/windows, block/thread settings, and provenance. Top-level ldfiles, idsLD, and rsidsLD are the public resource, reference-sample, and ordered-marker identities for that same LD computation; ldscores carries its aligned ordinary scores. Validation requires these views to agree with sparseLD, so they cannot describe a different resource. No external pointer is stored, so saveRDS()/readRDS() is exact and the files can be reopened after reload.
Creation fully validates the published native resource and records checksums and ordinary LD scores. Normal validate_Glist() calls check the serializable descriptor, identity fields, canonical file availability, dimensions, and alignment without hashing or rescanning the complete CSR payload. Use verify_ld() after receiving, copying, or downloading a resource, or when corruption is suspected; it reopens the native resource and verifies its structure and metadata, recorded checksums, and ordinary LD scores. Sparse-LD files are immutable between verification and analysis.
Native consumers open that already-checked identity once per high-level call. The shared gmat reader loads descriptor metadata and row pointers immediately. Regional reads seek directly to selected CSR rows; the first active-column request builds one O(marker count) reverse index that later column windows reuse. Multiple regions, marker sets, traits or chains share the same reader; only the active dense regional matrix or bounded column page is materialized. This keeps repeated full verification out of numerical loops. Consumers do not retain a process-global reader or store an external pointer in Glist, so R serialization and explicit resource ownership remain unchanged.
Independent blocks can be attached after sparse-LD preparation:
blocks <- data.frame(
  block_id = c("1a", "1b"),
  first_marker = c("rs1", "rs101"),
  last_marker = c("rs100", "rs200")
)
Glist <- gbase::define_ld_blocks(Glist, blocks)
The blocks must be ordered, contiguous, exhaustive and confined to one chromosome each. Definition performs one complete native traversal and rejects any retained cross-block correlation. The resulting ldBlocks manifest is tied to the recorded sparse-LD checksums and survives serialization. C++ consumers can then open one session reader and materialize one block at a time; eigensystem truncation and statistical likelihood choices are not stored in Glist.
The core payload layout is readable by the committed sblr CSR reader. The tested qgg 1.1.6 sparse-LD task instead writes fixed-width band files, so compatibility with qgg is numerical rather than a shared persistent format. No converter or sblr adapter is introduced.



Persistent input is the existing \(O(NM/4)\) BED and output is \(O(M + \mathrm{nnz})\). Working memory is bounded by \(O(M+\texttt{source\_N}+\texttt{selected\_N}\,\texttt{block\_size}+\texttt{active\_row\_nnz})\) plus per-row thread-local retained entries. It does not hold \(O(M^2)\) LD or \(O(NM)\) decoded genotypes. Realistic reference LD should be prepared once and reused.
