title: AI-assisted research, methods, software and teaching
text:
What is AI?







Term
Meaning




Artificial intelligence
The broad field of building systems that perform tasks associated with human intelligence


Machine learning and deep learning
Methods that learn patterns from data. Deep learning uses neural networks with many layers


Generative AI
Models that generate text, code, images, audio or other content


AI assistants and agents
Systems built around generative AI that can work with users, files and tools. Agents can carry out multistep tasks



This presentation focuses on AI assistants and agents used for data analysis, method and software development, and teaching.

People use the term AI in different ways. Some think of machine learning or deep neural networks used to analyse data. Others think primarily of generative tools such as ChatGPT.
Machine learning covers methods that learn patterns from data. Deep learning is a form of machine learning based on neural networks with many layers. Modern generative AI is largely based on deep learning, but its purpose is to generate new content rather than only produce predictions.
Assistants interact with users and may have access to files and tools. Agents can use these capabilities to carry out more complex, multistep tasks.
This presentation concerns practical AI-assisted work. Applying machine learning as the scientific method being studied is outside its scope.

title: AI-assisted research, methods, software and teaching
text:
How researchers use generative AI







Activity
Examples




Writing and communication
Draft, revise, translate and shorten text


Literature work
Find relevant papers, summarise them and compare their conclusions


Data analysis
Inspect data, write code, make figures and explain results


Teaching
Develop slides, exercises, examples and explanations


Administration
Prepare emails, meeting notes, plans and reports



Writing and literature review are common entry points. The same technology can also contribute directly to mathematical, analytical and software work.

Many researchers first encounter generative AI as a writing assistant. It can also help identify literature, organise information, write analysis code and develop teaching material.
These uses still require review. Literature searches must be checked against the original sources, and scientific claims must not be accepted simply because the generated text sounds convincing.
My own use extends further into method and software development. That is the main focus of the following slides.

title: AI-assisted research, methods, software and teaching
text:
Areas of AI-assisted work








Area
Example output
Reusable result




Data analysis
An analysis script and report
A reproducible analysis workflow


Method development
A statistical model or algorithm
A clearly defined method with validation evidence


Software development
R and C++ code, interfaces and documentation
Tested and maintainable software components


Teaching
Slides, simulations and worked examples
Editable teaching materials



AI can help with mathematical reasoning, coding, analysis and documentation. Researchers set the scientific direction, review the decisions and determine what evidence is sufficient.

These activities are connected but distinct. A data-analysis question may reveal the need for a new statistical method. The method must then be translated into reliable software before it can be used routinely. A validated implementation can support new analyses and become a teaching example.
AI is particularly useful at the connection between mathematics and software. It can help examine equations, compare algorithms, implement them in R or C++, and prepare numerical checks. Researchers define the scientific problem, review the statistical and computational decisions, and decide what evidence is required.

title: AI-assisted research, methods, software and teaching
text:
Platforms developed with AI assistance







Platform
Purpose




gsuite
Statistical models, numerical computation and user interfaces


gsim
Simulation of genetic data and assessment of methods


gact
Data integration, annotation, analysis and interpretation


gteach
Shared tools and materials for teaching



AI has contributed to developing the platforms themselves. The resulting infrastructure can now support further work with AI assistants.

gtools


These platforms represent substantial outputs from AI-assisted development. The work has included mathematics, numerical algorithms, R and C++ code, interfaces, documentation, simulation, data organisation and teaching tools.
The platforms overlap and should not be assigned exclusively to individual uses. gsuite supports analysis, methods and software development. gsim supports method development and validation. gact supports data analysis and interpretation. qgteach connects research results with teaching.
The important point is cumulative. AI helped develop the infrastructure, and AI assistants can now use and extend what has already been built.

title: AI-assisted research, methods, software and teaching
text:
Using and extending the infrastructure


Use existing capabilities

Inspect the data and available tools
Specify the scientific model
Run and assess the analysis
Save the script and report


Add a missing capability

Identify the limitation
Define the required method or computation
Implement it using existing components
Validate and document the extension


Each completed project can improve the infrastructure available to the next.

From conversation to a reproducible analysis · From a scientific question to a supported model


AI assistants can work with the existing platforms rather than starting each project from scratch. They can inspect the available functionality, run analyses, modify code, add interfaces and prepare documentation.
Researchers remain responsible for defining the scientific problem, reviewing the statistical and computational decisions, and deciding whether the evidence is sufficient.

title: AI-assisted research, methods, software and teaching
text:
Data analysis infrastructure: gact
How can we make data from different sources usable in the same analysis?


Prepare and connect

Detect and validate data structures
Harmonise GWAS summary statistics
Add biological annotations
Record reusable ingestion steps


Analyse and interpret

Connect variants with genes and pathways
Use established statistical methods
Trace results back to their sources
Preserve the complete analysis workflow


The value comes from making data usable together.

gact


gact contains schema detection, normalisation and validation of GWAS summary statistics, ingestion recipes, biological annotation sets and database access. Existing tutorials connect these resources to gene analysis, fine-mapping and pathway analysis, including methods supplied by qgg.
This example concerns data preparation, connection and interpretation. It does not imply that every statistical method belongs within gact or that all four platforms already form one integrated pipeline.

title: AI-assisted research, methods, software and teaching
text:
Simulation for method development: gsim
How well does a method recover known quantities under different scenarios?


Define the scenario

Pedigree and population structure
Genetic architecture and effects
Phenotypes and environmental variation
Quantities that the method should recover


Assess the method

Compare estimates with known truth
Examine uncertainty and failures
Change the scenario and repeat
Identify where the method struggles


Simulation helps us develop, compare and refine methods under conditions where the truth is known.

gsim


gsim provides simulation infrastructure rather than owning every benchmark. It supports pedigrees, genotype and phenotype simulation, multiple genetic architectures and retained simulation truth. Study designs and evaluation metrics belong in the assessment workflow, for example sblrbench.
Our 10,000-animal pedigree examples use simulation to compare estimates and breeding values with known quantities. Replicated scenarios assess statistical behaviour. Independent small numerical references still provide a separate check of the implementation.

Development connects statistical ideas to efficient and usable software.

gsuite


Read the layers from bottom to top. Development includes numerical algorithms, native C++, shared libraries, reusable model components and the R interface. CHOLMOD and PARDISO are established external solvers that we build on. Our selected inverse uses retained CHOLMOD factors. The YAMS analogy concerns computing needed inverse entries, not a YAMS dependency.
greml owns model computations and gsolve owns solvers. The R interface exposes supported combinations. A Python interface remains a possible future addition and is therefore not presented here as a current capability.

text:
The libraries behind gsuite








Repository
Main responsibility




gsuite
R interface: models, computational tasks and results


greml
Mixed models, REML estimation and prediction


gsolve
Numerical solvers, factor reuse and selected inverse calculations


gmat
Matrix operations, genotype panels and linkage disequilibrium


gbits
Compact genotype storage and operations on packed data


gcorr
Genetic correlation calculations


gscore
Genetic scoring and prediction


gbayes
Bayesian regression models




gsolve connects our model computations to established numerical libraries:
CHOLMOD / SuiteSparse and PARDISO → sparse matrix factorisation and linear solves.

This is a responsibility map, not a complete dependency graph. gsuite exposes selected capabilities through its R interface. gsim is a separate R package for simulation.
CHOLMOD and PARDISO are external libraries, not software developed by us. gsolve provides interfaces that allow supported model computations to use these sparse numerical backends. Other dense and iterative routes also exist.
Our selected-inverse implementation builds on retained CHOLMOD supernodal factors. It calculates required inverse entries without forming the full dense inverse. It does not use PARDISO for selected inversion.
AI-assisted development includes the algorithms and infrastructure around these external libraries, their integration, and the statistical and R layers.

title: AI-assisted research, methods, software and teaching
section: Reusable computational building blocks in gsuite
text:
Reusable computational building blocks in gsuite





Model specification leads to sparse mixed-model equations, factorization and solves, reuse of numerical quantities, and a REML update. The update returns to assembly for the next iteration.



Reused quantities

MME solutions and quadratic forms
Log determinants from factorizations
Selected inverse entries for trace terms
Derivative solves and cross-products

REML calculations

Restricted log likelihood
Score: first derivatives
Information: second-order curvature
Average Information for parameter updates


Reuse the same building blocks for estimation, prediction and uncertainty.

Architecture · Numerical foundation


The model specification supplies the design matrices and covariance components. From these, we assemble the mixed-model coefficient matrix and right-hand side. In the standard notation, the coefficient matrix contains terms formed from X, Z, inverse residual covariance and inverse random-effect covariance.
The sparse factorization supports several calculations. We use it to solve the mixed-model equations and obtain quadratic forms. The factorization also provides the coefficient-matrix log determinant. The covariance components provide the other determinant terms required by the restricted likelihood.
Selected inverse entries provide the trace terms needed by the direct sparse route. Derivative solves and cross-products contribute to the score and information calculations.
The score contains the first derivatives of the restricted likelihood. Observed and expected information describe second-order curvature. The Average Information matrix provides an efficient curvature calculation for updating the covariance parameters.
After each update, we rebuild the parameter-dependent parts and repeat the calculation. At the final covariance estimates, the same solver infrastructure supports prediction and uncertainty calculations.
Within the ecosystem, gsuite provides the R-facing model specification, greml owns the mixed-model and REML calculations, and gsolve provides factorization and solver operations. This slide describes the sparse direct route. Other backends may use different numerical building blocks.

title: AI-assisted research, methods, software and teaching
section: Mathematical core of the same REML calculation
text:
Mathematical core of the same REML calculation


Mixed model
\[
y=X\beta+Zu+e,\qquad u\sim N(0,G),\quad e\sim N(0,R)
\]
Mixed-model equations
\[
C(\theta)
\begin{bmatrix}\widehat\beta\\\widehat u\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}X^\top R^{-1}y\\Z^\top R^{-1}y\end{bmatrix}
\]
\[
C(\theta)=
\begin{bmatrix}
X^\top R^{-1}X & X^\top R^{-1}Z\\
Z^\top R^{-1}X & Z^\top R^{-1}Z+G^{-1}
\end{bmatrix}
\]
Determinants for REML
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\log|V|+\log|X^\top V^{-1}X|\\
&\qquad=\log|R|+\log|G|+\log|C|
\end{aligned}
\]

REML quantities
\[
\begin{aligned}
V &= ZGZ^\top+R\\
P &= V^{-1}-V^{-1}X(X^\top V^{-1}X)^{-1}X^\top V^{-1}
\end{aligned}
\]
\[
\begin{aligned}
-2\ell_R(\theta) &= \mathrm{constant}+\log|V|\\
&\quad+\log|X^\top V^{-1}X|+y^\top Py
\end{aligned}
\]
For \(V_i=\partial V/\partial\theta_i\),
\[
s_i=\frac12\left[y^\top PV_iPy-\operatorname{tr}(PV_i)\right]
\]
\[
\mathcal I_O=-\frac{\partial^2\ell_R}{\partial\theta\,\partial\theta^\top}
\]
\[
\mathcal I_{AI,ij}=\frac12 y^\top PV_iPV_jPy
\]

Solves, selected inverse entries and derivative blocks supply these quantities.

Independent \(u,e\); positive-definite \(G,R\); full-rank \(X\). AI form shown for covariance components entering \(V\) linearly.
Architecture · Numerical foundation


The covariance parameters are collected in theta. They determine the residual covariance R, the random-effect covariance G, the marginal covariance V and the mixed-model coefficient matrix C.
The mixed-model equations provide estimates and predictions without forming the dense marginal covariance matrix V. The determinant identity expresses the two marginal REML determinant terms through R, G and the sparse mixed-model coefficient matrix C.
The restricted likelihood combines these determinant terms with the quadratic form y transpose P y.
For each parameter, V sub i is the derivative of V with respect to that parameter. The score is the first derivative of the restricted likelihood. It contains a quadratic term and a trace term.
The observed information is the negative second derivative of the likelihood. The Average Information matrix provides the curvature used for parameter updates. For variance components that enter V linearly, its familiar form is one half y transpose P V sub i P V sub j P y.
The implementation does not need to construct the dense P matrix. Sparse MME solves, selected inverse entries and derivative calculations provide the required quantities.
For nonlinear covariance parameterisations, transformation and chain-rule terms must also be included. The equations shown here describe the core variance-component formulation.

section: gsuite versus DMU: agreement and runtime
text:
gsuite versus DMU: agreement and runtime




Numerical agreement
50,000 animals
Maximum covariance-estimate difference below \(4.3\times10^{-8}\).
Prediction correlations essentially 1 on 1,000 preselected animals.
Competitive runtime on these three tested models.


gsuite 0.29.0 and DMU 5.6. Each bar represents one execution. The work boundaries differ: gsuite fitting versus DMU preprocessing and fitting.


Results, scope and provenance


The numerical results provide evidence for these frozen direct pedigree REML models. Covariance agreement covers the saved parameters. Prediction correlations exceed 0.999999999998 on the predeclared first 1,000 pedigree-coded animals, not all 50,000. Likelihood constants remain unreconciled. Timings are descriptive single runs with different work boundaries, so this is not a general speed claim or qualification of all current gsuite routes.

title: AI-assisted research, methods, software and teaching
text:
Where will AI lead us?


What is likely to change

Writing, coding and analysis will become faster
More groups will develop advanced methods and software
AI assistants will perform increasingly complex tasks
Research roles and expectations will change


Questions for our programme

Which expertise and resources will distinguish us?
How should we combine AI with our data and infrastructure?
Which capabilities should we develop and share?
How should training, review and responsibility change?


What should we change now to remain scientifically distinctive as AI becomes part of research?

AI is already part of research, and its capabilities will continue to develop. Routine use of writing assistants or code generation will become common. The strategic question concerns how this changes our research and what will remain distinctive.
Scientific questions, domain knowledge, trusted data, critical evaluation and responsibility will remain important. Our shared platforms provide one possible advantage because they capture expertise in infrastructure that researchers and AI assistants can use and extend.
We should discuss which capabilities we need, how our roles may change, and where we should invest to remain scientifically strong.

title: AI-assisted research, methods, software and teaching
section: From a computational need to a component
text:
From a computational need to a component
Need: Obtain required inverse entries without forming a full dense inverse.







Step
What we work through with AI




Build small references
Dense inverse and scalar Takahashi calculations in C++


Implement the efficient algorithm
Selected inversion using retained CHOLMOD factors


Compare in native tests
Check requested entries against both references


Check computational behaviour
Factor reuse, thread agreement and retained solves


Integrate and assess
Supported model computations and the R workflow



Reference and production calculations are both native C++.

The development pattern is to establish a small reference, implement the efficient algorithm, compare them, and then check broader computational and user workflows. This describes the documented validation structure rather than asserting the exact historical order of every implementation step. gsolve/docs/testing.md and tests/test_supernodal_selected_inverse.cpp document and implement two small C++ references: a dense inverse and a separate scalar Takahashi recurrence. Requested entries from the production supernodal route are compared with both. The scalar reference is test-only, not an installed production fallback. Additional assertions check repeated factorisation, thread agreement, and preservation of retained solves and log-determinants. CHOLMOD is external; our production route uses its retained supernodal factors without forming the full dense inverse. PARDISO is not used for this selected inversion. These are test contracts, not a claim that every current test passes.

title: AI-assisted research, methods, software and teaching
text:
Different checks answer different questions







Check
Question it addresses




Mathematics and special cases
Does the formulation represent the intended model?


Small native reference versus production algorithm
Do separate computational approaches agree?


Repeated simulation with known truth
How well does the method recover quantities across scenarios?


Comparison with other software
Do results agree for matched models and settings?


Complete user workflow
Can the interface produce an interpretable, reproducible result?



Independence comes from a separate computational approach, not a different programming language.

These checks complement one another. Both reference and production code can be C++. greml retains small dense, analytical and finite-difference checks in native tests; gmat uses explicit dense correlation and LD calculations; gbits compares optimised implementations with scalar references. Their testing.md guides describe the assertions and reference limitations. Not every comparison has the same degree of independence: two wrappers over the same engine do not provide an independent numerical reference. Agreement between programs requires matching models, conventions and settings. Simulation can assess bias, uncertainty and prediction, but the generating model and studied scenarios limit what we learn. Runtime comparisons require explicit work boundaries. Define tolerances and acceptance criteria before interpreting results, and record the model, route and scale covered by the evidence.

title: AI-assisted research, methods, software and teaching
text:
Where human judgement enters


Scientific decisions

Which question matters?
Which assumptions fit the study?
Which quantities should we estimate?
What can the results support?


Development decisions

Which approximations are acceptable?
What should be implemented or reused?
Which checks are sufficient?
When is a result ready to share?


AI can help examine each decision. We remain responsible for accepting it.

Human judgement is present throughout the process, not only in a final review. The researcher contributes study knowledge and statistical reasoning; software developers contribute computational and engineering judgement. AI can propose alternatives, expose assumptions, implement choices and assemble checks. Important decisions should remain visible in model definitions, code review, documentation and the interpretation of the evidence.

title: AI-assisted research, methods, software and teaching
text:
What remains after the conversation?


A reusable analysis or method

Model definition and assumptions
Code and an executable example
Tests and numerical evidence


Enough information to revisit it

Data identity, settings and versions
Results and documented limitations
Explanations and teaching material


The next researcher should be able to understand and use the work without reading the chat.

Conversation helps us develop the work, but it is not a substitute for its reproducible outputs. Keep the relevant data provenance, source revisions, settings and random seeds alongside results. Documentation should describe the final implementation and its limitations. Store reviewed evidence rather than every temporary experiment. This is what lets progress in one project benefit another, with or without the same assistant.

text:

LDSC, GNOVA, SumHer


Regional

Implemented capabilities


This is a concrete example of developing methods with an assistant. The starting point was existing software, including an LDSC core and sparse LD machinery. The question above is a summary of the initiating discussion, not a verbatim quote.
These are implementations of established method families, with bounded supported options. They are not claims of complete parity with every original package. The common interface preserves different meanings of annotation components, category totals and regional quantities, and method-specific uncertainty.

title: AI-assisted research, methods, software and teaching
section: How the researcher and assistant worked
text:
How the researcher and assistant worked








Step
Researcher
Assistant




Define the next capability

Implement and check
Review assumptions and challenge results
Write native code; compare small numerical oracles

Short, reviewed steps: specify → implement → test → discuss → commit.
The checks included independent calculations, selected upstream comparisons, R/native agreement and simulated data with known truth.

The conversation repeatedly narrowed scope: native libraries first, reuse existing components, keep the interface simple, and do not equate successful execution with statistical validity. The researcher chose the next milestone and reviewed the result before committing. The assistant investigated failures and updated code, tests and documentation.
Evidence was collected as the work progressed. For example, native uncertainty evaluations exposed undercoverage in some settings. Those limits were recorded, not removed by presenting only passing examples. Numerical oracles were small, independent reference calculations, distinct from the production algorithms.

title: AI-assisted research, methods, software and teaching
text:
The simulations also reveal differences

All 1,380 expected point estimates were available. The SUPERGNOVA shift gives a specific result to investigate.

20-dataset comparison, settings and uncertainty


Each dataset has two continuous traits, 10,000 disjoint GWAS individuals per trait, 4,000 independent reference individuals and 20 regions. Each error is relative to its own realized population truth. The left panel shows h2 for trait A. The right panel averages regional covariance errors within each dataset; it does not treat the 400 regions as independent replicates. All points are shown.
Under this design, LDSC and SumHer were almost identical. GNOVA was more variable. HESS and LAVA had small mean regional errors; SUPERGNOVA had mean error -0.001219 and regional RMSE 0.004099, compared with about 0.002 for HESS/LAVA. The cause is not established by this small comparison. Component selection, finite reference LD and assumptions deserve focused investigation. Earlier native records also examined SUPERGNOVA selection sensitivity; this is a new connected workflow observation, not the first discovery of a possible limitation.
One HESS regional SE was unavailable because its estimated matrices failed the uncertainty requirements. LAVA covariance SEs were unavailable for this call. Twenty datasets do not establish general calibration or rank the methods.

title: AI-assisted research, methods, software and teaching
section: What could become a research contribution?
text:
What could become a research contribution?







Status
Concrete example




Reusable infrastructure, implemented
Shared LD resources, named covariance results and common numerical components


Native extension, implemented
Annotation-specific genetic regression and partial correlations from GNOVA covariance estimates


Research question to evaluate
Do conditional genetic relationships differ between annotations?



Existing methods can become building blocks for new questions.
Statistical novelty still needs a literature comparison and evidence. Shared code alone is not a new statistical method.

The native annotation extension is documented in gcorr/docs/annotation-multivariate.md and its reliability study. It reuses named genetic covariance matrices for regression and partial correlations, with paired-delete uncertainty. Numerical checks include larger conditioning sets and overlapping categories; statistical validation remains bounded. This extension is not being claimed as exposed by the current gsuite annotation R interface.
Overlapping annotation totals are not independent components and must not be summed. Conditioning describes genetic association, not a causal effect. Weak components, nearly singular predictor covariance and uncertainty calibration remain substantive issues. Any publishable novelty must be distinguished from existing methods and evaluated, rather than inferred from a common interface.
The demonstrated contribution is a reusable implementation and evaluation framework, developed through scientific direction and assistant-supported work.

title: AI-assisted research, methods, software and teaching
text:
What is AI?







Term
Meaning




Artificial intelligence
The broad field of building systems that perform tasks associated with human intelligence


Machine learning and deep learning
Methods that learn patterns from data. Deep learning uses neural networks with many layers


Generative AI
Models that generate text, code, images, audio or other content


AI assistants and agents
Systems built around generative AI that can work with users, files and tools. Agents can carry out multistep tasks



This presentation focuses on AI assistants and agents used for data analysis, method and software development, and teaching.

People use the term AI in different ways. Some think of machine learning or deep neural networks used to analyse data. Others think primarily of generative tools such as ChatGPT.
Machine learning covers methods that learn patterns from data. Deep learning is a form of machine learning based on neural networks with many layers. Modern generative AI is largely based on deep learning, but its purpose is to generate new content rather than only produce predictions.
Assistants interact with users and may have access to files and tools. Agents can use these capabilities to carry out more complex, multistep tasks.
This presentation concerns practical AI-assisted work. Applying machine learning as the scientific method being studied is outside its scope.

title: AI-assisted research, methods, software and teaching
text:
How researchers use generative AI







Activity
Examples




Writing and communication
Draft, revise, translate and shorten text


Literature work
Find relevant papers, summarise them and compare their conclusions


Data analysis
Inspect data, write code, make figures and explain results


Teaching
Develop slides, exercises, examples and explanations


Administration
Prepare emails, meeting notes, plans and reports



Writing and literature review are common entry points. The same technology can also contribute directly to mathematical, analytical and software work.

Many researchers first encounter generative AI as a writing assistant. It can also help identify literature, organise information, write analysis code and develop teaching material.
These uses still require review. Literature searches must be checked against the original sources, and scientific claims must not be accepted simply because the generated text sounds convincing.
The following slides focus on applications in method and software development.

title: AI-assisted research, methods, software and teaching
text:
Areas of AI-assisted work








Area
Example output
Reusable result




Data analysis
An analysis script and report
A reproducible analysis workflow


Method development
A statistical model or algorithm
A clearly defined method with validation evidence


Software development
R and C++ code, interfaces and documentation
Tested and maintainable software components


Teaching
Slides, simulations and worked examples
Editable teaching materials



AI can help with mathematical reasoning, coding, analysis and documentation. Researchers set the scientific direction, review the decisions and determine what evidence is sufficient.

These activities are connected but distinct. A data-analysis question may reveal the need for a new statistical method. The method must then be translated into reliable software before it can be used routinely. A validated implementation can support new analyses and become a teaching example.
AI is particularly useful at the connection between mathematics and software. It can help examine equations, compare algorithms, implement them in R or C++, and prepare numerical checks. Researchers define the scientific problem, review the statistical and computational decisions, and decide what evidence is required.

title: AI-assisted research, methods, software and teaching
text:
Platforms developed with AI assistance







Platform
Purpose




gsuite
Statistical models, numerical computation and user interfaces


gsim
Simulation of genetic data and assessment of methods


gact
Data integration, annotation, analysis and interpretation


gteach
Shared tools and materials for teaching



AI has contributed to developing the platforms themselves. The resulting infrastructure can now support further work with AI assistants.

gtools


These platforms represent substantial outputs from AI-assisted development. The work has included mathematics, numerical algorithms, R and C++ code, interfaces, documentation, simulation, data organisation and teaching tools.
The platforms overlap and should not be assigned exclusively to individual uses. gsuite supports analysis, methods and software development. gsim supports method development and validation. gact supports data analysis and interpretation. qgteach connects research results with teaching.
The important point is cumulative. AI helped develop the infrastructure, and AI assistants can now use and extend what has already been built.

title: AI-assisted research, methods, software and teaching
section: From numerical algorithms to an analysis package
text:
From numerical algorithms to an analysis package







Layer
Components in and around gsuite




Numerical computation
Sparse solves and the inverse entries needed for model calculations


Native C++ and shared libraries
Solver interfaces, reuse of calculations and diagnostics


Reusable model components
Covariance models, estimation, prediction and computational tasks


R interface
Model specification and results through gfit() and gvc()



The solver infrastructure uses established numerical libraries: CHOLMOD / SuiteSparse and PARDISO.

Architecture · Numerical foundation


Read the table from top to bottom, following the development from algorithms to the user interface. gsuite is the R-facing package; the numerical and statistical components live in focused libraries behind it.
CHOLMOD and PARDISO are external libraries. The gsolve selected-inverse implementation uses retained CHOLMOD factors. It computes needed inverse entries without forming the full dense inverse; PARDISO is not used for that selected-inverse route. The work also includes the surrounding solver infrastructure, reuse, model computations and R integration.
A Python interface remains a possible future addition, not a current claim. The technical deck contains the repository map and equations.

title: AI-assisted research, methods, software and teaching
section: From a scientific question to a model
text:
From a scientific question to a model


Each extension can add capabilities that other models can reuse.


From a scientific question to a supported model


The gsuite ecosystem is a collection of reusable computational building blocks. A scientific question determines the model and method, which determine the components required. Existing components may already provide what is needed. Otherwise, development adds the missing components to the collection.
Availability does not establish that a particular combination is supported. The assembled model still needs statistical and numerical validation, including reference calculations and checks of assumptions, convergence and predictions. AI can help identify, combine, implement and check components. Researchers and developers define the scientific meaning and decide what evidence is sufficient. Code that runs becomes a supported model only after its statistical meaning and numerical behaviour have been checked.

title: AI-assisted research, methods, software and teaching
section: A shared collection of building blocks
text:
A shared collection of building blocks


Existing capabilities can be combined and extended to support new models and methods.


These are conceptual groups, not a repository dependency graph or a claim that every combination is currently supported. gsuite provides the R interface; related libraries provide reusable model and numerical components.
Bayesian and non-Bayesian methods can share data handling, model structures, matrix operations and solves. They also require different inference machinery. Bayesian building blocks already exist in sblr. The plan is to organise these capabilities into gbayes and integrate them with gsuite. This is primarily about making existing machinery reusable across the ecosystem, rather than developing Bayesian methods from scratch. Each new integration and model combination still requires appropriate checks.
Reusable components make focused extensions possible. The amount of new work depends on the model, and an extension may require substantial algorithmic work. The value is cumulative: checked components remain available for later methods.

title: AI-assisted research, methods, software and teaching
text:
Developing gsuite with AI


Mathematics and design

Discuss the model and its assumptions
Derive the required computations
Compare algorithms and special cases
Decide what to implement or reuse


Implementation and review

Work directly with the R and C++ code
Compile and run focused checks
Inspect failures and revise the approach
Retain reviewed code and documentation


AI assistance connects statistical ideas with their implementation.

ChatGPT supported discussion of statistical models, mathematics and software design. Codex supported work directly in the repositories. The assistant can examine the code, make a focused change, build it, run checks and explain the result.
This has made it possible to work through several layers in the same conversation. The developer remains the editor: defining the purpose, questioning assumptions, reviewing decisions and deciding what evidence is sufficient.
A concrete computational example was obtaining selected inverse entries from retained sparse factors. The task connects a mathematical requirement in REML with an algorithm, a native implementation and a reusable solver capability.

title: AI-assisted research, methods, software and teaching
text:
Checking the calculations







Check
Concrete example from the work




Small reference calculations
Compare the efficient selected inverse with dense and scalar references in C++


Computational behaviour
Check factor reuse, thread agreement and retained solves


Independent software comparison
Compare matched pedigree models with DMU on 50,000 animals


User workflow
Fit models through R and inspect summaries, predictions and diagnostics



In the saved DMU comparison, covariance estimates differed by less than \(4.3\times10^{-8}\).

Historical comparison: gsuite 0.29.0 and DMU 5.6; three frozen pedigree models. Results and scope


Both the small references and the efficient selected-inverse algorithm are native C++. The references include a dense inverse and a separate scalar Takahashi calculation. Independence comes from the different computational approaches, not from using different programming languages.
The saved DMU evidence covers single-trait, multitrait and longitudinal models. The numerical agreement is concrete evidence for those versions, models and settings. It does not qualify every current capability. The following slide shows historical runtime evidence. Individual desktop timings varied markedly in later reruns.
Checks must continue as the software changes. A recent current-version multitrait rerun reached estimates close to the historical endpoint but failed its line-search requirement. That remains a failure to investigate, not a successful current-version benchmark. Running code and supported models are not the same acceptance state.

title: AI-assisted research, methods, software and teaching
section: A pedigree analysis as a conversation
text:
A pedigree analysis as a conversation
How much genetic variation is present in body weight, and how accurately can breeding values be predicted?


Work through the analysis

Check pedigree, observations and missing values
Discuss fixed effects and genetic effects
Fit the model and check convergence
Inspect estimates and predictions
Save the R script, figures and report


Keep the model explicit
fit <- gfit(
  formula = BW ~ sex + cohort + herd + (1 | id),
  data = data,
  pedigree = pedigree,
  task = "reml",
  control = fit_control
)
summary(fit)
Ordinary R data frames; a model that can be reviewed and rerun.


Analysis with an assistant · Worked example: 10,000 pedigree animals


This code follows the single-trait pedigree tutorial. The data frames and fit_control are prepared in that tutorial; the slide is an excerpt, not a standalone analysis script. The saved example has 10,000 pedigree animals, with 8,588 animals observed.
The assistant can help inspect identifiers, missingness and covariates, explain the model and run the code. Researchers review which effects belong in the analysis and what the resulting estimates mean. The report should include variance estimates, fit status and diagnostic plots, not just a fitted object.
Simulation truth supports the teaching example. Real data require scientific interpretation and sensitivity checks; a plausible plot does not establish that the model assumptions are correct.

title: AI-assisted research, methods, software and teaching
section: A concrete case: GWAS summary statistics
text:
A concrete case: GWAS summary statistics
The question: can existing building blocks support a family of methods for heritability and genetic correlation?







Analysis
Implemented method families




Genome-wide and annotation-based
LDSC, GNOVA, SumHer


Regional
HESS/rho-HESS, SUPERGNOVA, LAVA


Conditional relationships
LAVA regression and partial genetic correlations



Native calculations in gcorr, reusable LD resources in gmat, numerical components in gsolve, and a common gsuite R interface.
The outcome includes working examples, diagnostics and documented limits.

Implemented capabilities


This is a concrete example of developing methods with an assistant. The starting point was existing software, including an LDSC core and sparse LD machinery. The question above is a summary of the initiating discussion, not a verbatim quote.
These are implementations of established method families, with bounded supported options. They are not claims of complete parity with every original package. The common interface preserves different meanings of annotation components, category totals and regional quantities, and method-specific uncertainty.

title: AI-assisted research, methods, software and teaching
section: How the researcher and assistant worked
text:
How the researcher and assistant worked








Step
Researcher
Assistant




Define the next capability
Set the scientific question and scope
Inspect equations and existing components


Implement and check
Review assumptions and challenge results
Write native code; compare small numerical oracles


Connect and evaluate
Decide what is supported and what needs investigation
Add the R interface, examples and simulations



Short, reviewed steps: specify → implement → test → discuss → commit.
The checks included independent calculations, selected upstream comparisons, R/native agreement and simulated data with known truth.

The conversation repeatedly narrowed scope: native libraries first, reuse existing components, keep the interface simple, and do not equate successful execution with statistical validity. The researcher chose the next milestone and reviewed the result before committing. The assistant investigated failures and updated code, tests and documentation.
Evidence was collected as the work progressed. For example, native uncertainty evaluations exposed undercoverage in some settings. Those limits were recorded, not removed by presenting only passing examples. Numerical oracles were small, independent reference calculations, distinct from the production algorithms.

title: AI-assisted research, methods, software and teaching
text:
The simulations also reveal differences

All 1,380 expected point estimates were available. The SUPERGNOVA shift gives a specific result to investigate.

20-dataset comparison, settings and uncertainty


Each dataset has two continuous traits, 10,000 disjoint GWAS individuals per trait, 4,000 independent reference individuals and 20 regions. Each error is relative to its own realized population truth. The left panel shows h2 for trait A. The right panel averages regional covariance errors within each dataset; it does not treat the 400 regions as independent replicates. All points are shown.
Under this design, LDSC and SumHer were almost identical. GNOVA was more variable. HESS and LAVA had small mean regional errors; SUPERGNOVA had mean error -0.001219 and regional RMSE 0.004099, compared with about 0.002 for HESS/LAVA. The cause is not established by this small comparison. Component selection, finite reference LD and assumptions deserve focused investigation. Earlier native records also examined SUPERGNOVA selection sensitivity; this is a new connected workflow observation, not the first discovery of a possible limitation.
One HESS regional SE was unavailable because its estimated matrices failed the uncertainty requirements. LAVA covariance SEs were unavailable for this call. Twenty datasets do not establish general calibration or rank the methods.

title: AI-assisted research, methods, software and teaching
section: What could become a research contribution?
text:
What could become a research contribution?







Status
Concrete example




Reusable infrastructure, implemented
Shared LD resources, named covariance results and common numerical components


Native extension, implemented
Annotation-specific genetic regression and partial correlations from GNOVA covariance estimates


Research question to evaluate
Do conditional genetic relationships differ between annotations?



Existing methods can become building blocks for new questions.
Statistical novelty still needs a literature comparison and evidence. Shared code alone is not a new statistical method.

The native annotation extension is documented in gcorr/docs/annotation-multivariate.md and its reliability study. It reuses named genetic covariance matrices for regression and partial correlations, with paired-delete uncertainty. Numerical checks include larger conditioning sets and overlapping categories; statistical validation remains bounded. This extension is not being claimed as exposed by the current gsuite annotation R interface.
Overlapping annotation totals are not independent components and must not be summed. Conditioning describes genetic association, not a causal effect. Weak components, nearly singular predictor covariance and uncertainty calibration remain substantive issues. Any publishable novelty must be distinguished from existing methods and evaluated, rather than inferred from a common interface.
The demonstrated contribution is a reusable implementation and evaluation framework, developed through scientific direction and assistant-supported work.

title: AI-assisted research, methods, software and teaching
text:
Where is AI taking research?


What is likely to change

Writing, coding and analysis will become faster
More groups will develop advanced methods and software
AI assistants will perform increasingly complex tasks
Research roles and expectations will change


Questions for the programme

Which expertise and resources will distinguish the programme?
How can AI be combined with the available data and infrastructure?
Which capabilities should be developed and shared?
How should training, review and responsibility change?


What needs to change now for the programme to remain scientifically distinctive as AI becomes part of research?

AI is already part of research, and its capabilities will continue to develop. Routine use of writing assistants or code generation will become common. The strategic question concerns how this changes research and what will remain distinctive.
Scientific questions, domain knowledge, trusted data, critical evaluation and responsibility will remain important. Shared platforms provide one possible advantage because they capture expertise in infrastructure that researchers and AI assistants can use and extend.
Discussion can focus on the capabilities required, changing research roles, and investments that support scientific strength.
The gsuite experience suggests connecting applied research and development through manageable scientific questions. Each project can leave reusable analyses, checked components and documented evidence for later work. Scientific quality, review effort and maintenance matter alongside time saved.

The input is an ordinary data frame with qgg-style names. When a Glist reference is available, gbase::checkStat() performs marker mapping, allele alignment and explicit QC. A task package never imports gsuite.

statistics <- data.frame(rsids = markers, chr = "1", pos = 1:20,

title: Genetic-correlation workflow
text:
Fit a focused method
ld_scores <- setNames(seq(1, 2, length.out = 20), markers)
blocks <- setNames(rep(paste0("b", 1:5), each = 4), markers)

fit <- gcorr_ldsc(statistics, ld_scores, blocks,
  marker_count = 50000)
fit$estimates
Use gcorr_gnova() or gcorr_sumher() when their explicit score and annotation inputs are available. Regional workflows pass a sparse-LD Glist and named marker regions to gcorr_prepare_regions(), then call a focused HESS, SUPERGNOVA, LAVA or HDL-L function. See the complete method contract.

title: Bayesian genomic regression
text:
The main interface is gbayes::gbayes():
stat + Glist selects a summary-statistics likelihood. data + Glist selects an individual-level BED likelihood. A named list of checked summary frames or several named phenotype columns selects the multivariate route. Unsupported method/data combinations fail explicitly.

title: Bayesian genomic regression
text:
Prepare genotypes and summaries
Single-trait summary BayesC/BayesR also accepts familiar iteration and prior arguments:
fit <- gbayes::gbayes(Glist=Glist, stat=stat, method="bayesC",
  algorithm="mcmc", nit=100, nburn=0, seed=10)
head(fit$stat)       # bm: native posterior mean; dm: PIP
head(fit$post)      # ve, vg, vb, pi, pip on the fitted likelihood scale
head(fit$conv)      # native R-hat, ESS, MCSE and diagnostic statuses
Familiar calls default to one chain, 100 sweeps, zero burn-in, h2=.5, BayesC active probability .001, and learned slab/residual variances and mixture weights. nit/nburn/nthin/nrun/seed, pi/gamma/vb/ve, and updateB/updateE/updatePi adapt to native settings. Explicit conflicting aliases and nested settings are rejected; existing advanced calls retain their defaults. Familiar adaptation is limited to single-trait summaries.
Summary bm remains in standardized native genotype/phenotype units. The standalone reference-LD residual policy defaults to adjustment .9; it differs from qgg’s marker-specific adjustment. No independent genetic-variance draw is recreated. post$vg instead averages the joint-effect quadratic b' C b / n from retained draws, reusing the fitted residual. It is unavailable with variable sample sizes or a distinct explicit posterior reference. pi is total non-null mixture probability and pip is summed marker PIP (expected active count); pi0, pi1, … retain component weights. conv exposes rhat_*, ess_*, mcse_* and status_* columns, rather than qgg Geweke z scores. Original native posterior and diagnostic fields remain available. Single-chain output does not establish convergence or posterior equivalence. Use gmap::getCredibleSets(Glist, fit, sets) to interpret saved marginal PIPs with full BED LD without refitting.
Scalar summary BayesC/BayesR support optional LD swaps on sparse-LD and block-eigen routes, with the same controls as regional gmap():
fit <- gbayes::gbayes(Glist=Glist, stat=stat, method="bayesC",
  algorithm="mcmc", nit=1000, nburn=100, nrun=4, seed=10,
  control=list(ld_swap=list(probability=.05, minimum_r2=.8,
    maximum_friends=50L, moves=1L)))
fit$ld_swap
Native Metropolis-Hastings proposals relocate an active effect to an inactive LD neighbour. probability selects sweeps for up to moves proposals; minimum_r2 and maximum_friends bound candidate neighbours. Neighbours use the fitted cross-products, including retained eigen truncation. fit$ld_swap reports pooled attempted/accepted counts and the acceptance rate; fit$chains retains per-chain counts. Counts include burn-in and no attempts gives an NA rate. They measure proposal activity, not convergence. Individual BED fits do not support these swaps. For sparse LD, neighbour preparation scans the existing stored correlations once and shares the list across chains. It does not recompute LD from genotypes or rebuild the list at every sweep.
Probability defaults to zero; zero moves also disables swaps and neighbour preparation. Finding neighbours adds preparation cost, especially with eigen operators. Existing manuscript timings used swaps disabled and remain unchanged; improved mixing or elapsed time has not been established by those timings.
BayesC and BayesR also accept algorithm="mcmc-eigen". Declare exhaustive contiguous LD blocks using gbase::define_ld_blocks(Glist, blocks); block edges must have no retained cross-block LD. The verified decomposition is prepared once per block and reused by every chain. This route uses the retained block-diagonal summary likelihood, defaults to positive eigenvalue mass .995, and learns a global residual variance in the retained response/rank space:
eigen_fit <- gbayes::gbayes(stat, Glist, method="bayesR",
  algorithm="mcmc-eigen", nit=1000, nburn=100, nrun=4, seed=10,
  control=list(eigen_control=list(retained_positive_mass=.995)))
eigen_fit$diagnostics$block_eigen
Use updateE=FALSE for fixed residual variance. Reference-LD adjustment and caller-supplied full-space normalization cannot be combined with this route. SBayesRC remains a separate annotated model with block-specific residual scales. The eigen option is not a promise of lower elapsed time: preparation and retained rank affect the cost. The existing manuscript timings describe the earlier dense/sparse MCMC version and have not been replaced by these interface changes.
gbase::gprep() owns the qgg-style Glist contract. Sparse LD is added to the same object rather than creating another public descriptor.
Glist <- gbase::gprep(
  bedfiles = c("chr1.bed", "chr2.bed")
)

Glist <- gbase::gprep(
  Glist = Glist,
  task = "sparseld",
  out_prefix = "reference/ld"
)

stat <- gbase::checkStat(Glist = Glist, stat = reported_statistics)
checkStat() returns an ordinary data frame with qgg-style names. It performs marker, coordinate and allele alignment but does not introduce a summary class, infer sample sizes or manufacture study frequencies. For the Gaussian summary likelihood, gbayes() requires finite b, seb and positive n; the package performs the documented standardized-effect conversion internally.

title: Bayesian genomic regression
text:
Scalar BayesC and BayesR
fit <- gbayes::gbayes(
  stat,
  Glist,
  method = "bayesr",
  prior = list(
    residual_variance = 1,
    effect_variance = 0.05,
    weights = c(0.8, 0.15, 0.05),
    variance_multipliers = c(0, 0.1, 1)
  ),
  control = list(
    burnin = 500,
    sampling_sweeps = 1000,
    seeds = c(11, 29)
  ),
  trait = "height"
)
For individual-level fitting, phenotype rows are matched by ID and may be in a different order from the selected Glist samples.
fit <- gbayes::gbayes(
  data = phenotypes,
  Glist = Glist,
  trait = "height",
  method = "bayesc",
  prior = list(
    residual_variance = 1,
    effect_variance = 0.05,
    inclusion_probability = 0.01
  )
)
Both routes support fixed or learned effect variance and mixture weights, explicit residual policies, compact posterior summaries, annotations and exact serialized continuation. Individual fits use native BED coding and return portable allele-labelled fit$weights.

title: Bayesian genomic regression
text:
Annotation-informed block-eigen regression
method = "sbayesrc" fits a single checked summary trait with an annotation-informed BayesR prior. The Glist must contain a verified independent block partition. Each LD block is loaded and decomposed once per fit, and the prepared immutable factors are shared by all chains.
Glist <- gbase::define_ld_blocks(
  Glist,
  data.frame(
    block_id = block_table$block_id,
    first_marker = block_table$first_marker,
    last_marker = block_table$last_marker
  )
)

component_design <- as.matrix(annotation_table[fitted_markers, , drop = FALSE])

fit <- gbayes::gbayes(
  stat,
  Glist,
  method = "sbayesrc",
  annotation = list(component = list(design = component_design)),
  control = list(
    eigen_control = list(retained_positive_mass = 0.995),
    block_eigen_residual = list(mode = "all_mix")
  )
)
The block residual update is defined on retained response coordinates: each block uses the squared retained response norm and retained rank. This is an explicit reduced-space likelihood and is not an assertion of identical normalization to GCTB or another SBayesRC implementation. Set retained_positive_mass = 1 to retain every positive eigenvalue. On a full-rank block-diagonal reference with fixed block residuals, this route reduces to the ordinary bayesr sufficient-statistic fit.
fit$diagnostics$block_eigen records block loads, eigensystem decompositions, retained ranks, discarded positive mass and peak dense-block memory. The factors remain native working state; the returned fit is serializable and continuation restores sampler state without serializing dense eigenvectors.

title: Bayesian genomic regression
text:
Additional summary engines
The same dispatcher provides focused single-trait summary methods:
point_normal <- gbayes::gbayes(stat, Glist, method = "point_normal")
shrinkage <- gbayes::gbayes(stat, Glist, method = "continuous_shrinkage")
variational <- gbayes::gbayes(stat, Glist, method = "variational")
mixture <- gbayes::gbayes(stat, Glist, method = "mixture_variational")
These retain method-specific controls and outputs. They do not silently inherit all BayesC/BayesR sampling, learning or annotation features.

title: Bayesian genomic regression
text:
Multivariate and study-specific fits
Named phenotype columns fit a joint individual-level model:
joint <- gbayes::gbayes(
  data = phenotypes,
  Glist = Glist,
  trait = c("height", "weight"),
  method = "bayesr",
  prior = list(
    effect_covariance = effect_covariance,
    residual_covariance = residual_covariance
  )
)
For summaries, stat may be a named trait list with one shared Glist sparse-LD reference, or a named study list paired with a named list of study-specific Glist references. Study identity remains distinct from trait identity. Local LD operators are preserved; no synthetic union LD matrix is created. Independent and shared-LD sampling assumptions are declared through sampling.

title: Bayesian genomic regression
text:
Annotations and continuation
BayesC supports inclusion and variance annotations. BayesR supports component and variance annotations. BayesS scaling uses the same checked variance-model boundary. Multivariate fits additionally support pattern annotations.
Pass a previous fit, or its $continuation member, back through continuation. The model-defining inputs, marker order, prior, annotations and transition controls must remain identical. Continuation restores native chain states and performs zero additional burn-in.

title: Bayesian genomic regression
text:
Posterior genetic quantities
An explicitly aligned sparse-LD Glist can define the reference population for posterior genetic covariance and correlation. Heritability additionally requires an explicit phenotype variance; no denominator is inferred.
groups <- setNames(marker_groups, fitted_marker_ids)

fit <- gbayes::gbayes(
  stat,
  Glist,
  method = "bayesr",
  posterior = list(
    reference = Glist,
    partition = groups,
    phenotype_variance = c(height = 1)
  )
)
fit$quantities separates genetic covariance/correlation, heritability, reporting partitions, predictions and per-chain quantities. Partition groups are reporting objects and are independent of covariance-group priors.

title: Bayesian genomic regression
text:
Predict selected individuals with uncertainty
Posterior score uncertainty uses an existing target Glist. Its active markers may be a strict subset of fitted markers and may span any number of BED components. Components and markers retain Glist order; requested individuals retain the supplied ID order.
target <- gbase::gprep(
  bedfiles = c("target-chr1.bed", "target-chr2.bed"),
  ids = selected_ids,
  rsids = selected_markers
)

fit <- gbayes::gbayes(
  stat,
  Glist,
  method = "bayesr",
  posterior = list(
    prediction = list(
      Glist = target,
      ids = selected_ids,
      target_set = "validation",
      retain_draws = FALSE
    )
  )
)
The package validates exact fitted-marker availability, coordinates and counted alleles. Component projections use the public gscore::summary interface and are summed into one score. Coverage records fitted, used and omitted markers and the number of active BED components. Reported score covariance is posterior effect uncertainty, not phenotype predictive variance.

title: Bayesian genomic regression
text:
Apply portable posterior weights
When genotype coding is identified, fit$weights is directly consumable by gscore(). This includes block-eigen SBayesRC fits; scoring uses the portable posterior mean weights and does not need the fitted eigensystems:
prediction <- gscore::gscore(fit$weights, target)
For pathway or other marker-set scores, pass a uniquely named list of marker IDs. The target Glist resolves their BED locations and the native scorer handles overlapping or cross-file sets in one pass:
prediction <- gscore::gscore(
  fit$weights, target,
  sets = marker_sets,
  include_total = TRUE
)
Weight learning remains with gbayes; score application remains with gscore. Raw association effects are not automatically Bayesian weights, and conventional clumping and thresholding remains gscore::clump_threshold().

title: Bayesian genomic regression
text:
Regional interpretation
gmap::gmap_bed() can consume a saved individual-BED gbayes_fit together with sparse LD prepared from the same Glist samples and physical marker selection:
mapped <- gmap::gmap_bed(fit, Glist, regions)
This interprets global marginal PIPs by region without refitting. Marginal-PIP groups are not component credible sets.
gmap_bed() is specific to individual-BED fits because it verifies the fitted sample selection, BED files and in-sample LD identity. A summary SBayesRC fit remains a whole-reference gbayes_fit; regional BayesC/BayesR or multi-effect models are fitted through gmap() with their own explicit regional likelihood.

title: Bayesian genomic regression
text:
Qualification status
The package passed its complete source check with no errors or warnings, focused deterministic tests, an exact Windows DLL-closure and SHA-256 audit, and clean binary loading. The two source-check NOTEs concern installed DLL size and the conservative compiled-code scan of the bundled native DLL closure.

title: Mendelian randomisation with prepared instruments
text:
MR uses two aligned ordinary effect/standard-error data frames and a signed-LD matrix labelled in the same candidate order. It does not accept an LDlist, harmonize alleles, infer ancestry or infer sample overlap.
library(gbase)
library(gcorr)

prepared <- gcorr_prepare_mr(
  statistics = list(exposure = exposure_summary, outcome = outcome_summary),
  signed_ld = candidate_ld,
  exposure = "exposure", outcome = "outcome",
  reference_sample_size = 5000,
  ancestry = c(exposure = "EUR", outcome = "EUR"),
  reference_ancestry = "EUR",
  effect_units = c(exposure = "SD", outcome = "SD"),
  non_overlapping_samples = TRUE,
  preparation = "gsmr2")
Preparation records every candidate decision and every retained LD-pair decision. The result is serializable and contains no native pointer. GSMR uses an LD r-squared default of 0.1; GSMR2 preparation uses 0.05 and derives exposure p-values from effects and standard errors.

text:
