title: Mendelian randomisation with prepared instruments
text:
Focused estimators
gsmr <- gcorr_gsmr(prepared)
gsmr2 <- gcorr_gsmr2(prepared)
ivw <- gcorr_mr_ivw(prepared)
egger <- gcorr_mr_egger(prepared)
median <- gcorr_mr_weighted_median(prepared,
  bootstrap_replicates = 1000, seed = 19)
The thin dispatcher provides the same selection without a task contract:
gcorr(prepared, method = "gsmr")
gcorr(prepared, method = "weighted_median", seed = 19)
GSMR and GSMR2 apply their distinct HEIDI procedures unless explicitly disabled. IVW, Egger and weighted median use the prepared set before HEIDI and require approximately independent instruments. Weighted median always requires an explicit seed. Reverse-direction analysis must prepare again from the original candidate summaries.
Effects retain outcome units per exposure unit. Instrument strength, HEIDI or agreement across estimators does not establish the exclusion restriction. The interface supports univariable, explicitly non-overlapping-sample analyses; it does not provide multivariable or overlapping-sample MR.

title: Gene-set and pathway analysis
text:
gsea() connects prepared gene-level evidence to the native gsea library. The same named sets and explicit gene background support several questions:
The last two choices also accept several traits fitted jointly. Bayesian PIPs are probabilities under the specified model and priors; they are not p-values. Attach gsea and use its re-exported vegas() for the separate marker-set association test below. The implementation and native integration remain in glma; users do not need to attach both packages. Use gbase::checkStat() when summary statistics need mapping or harmonisation first. Gene-ID conversion and allele harmonization remain explicit external preparation. The capability overview describes the separate native gene-evidence operations.

title: Gene-set and pathway analysis
section: From GWAS summary statistics to pathways
text:
From GWAS summary statistics to pathways
Download the complete GWAS-to-pathway example. Run it with installed gsuite, gsea and gsim packages from the repository root:
source("tools/examples/gwas_pathways.R")
The script simulates two continuous traits in 10,000 individuals, with 240 markers assigned to 80 artificial genes across four artificial chromosomes. It prepares LD, computes ordinary GWAS Z statistics, derives gene evidence and runs pathway analyses. Genotypes are only needed to construct this demonstration; vegas() itself consumes ordinary checked summary-statistics data frames and the sparse-LD resource attached to a Glist. Outputs stay together in build/examples/gwas-pathways/: a saved workflow, one pathway table, one figure and the reference files.
The analysis boundary is explicit:
library(gsea)

evidence <- vegas(
  statistics, Glist, sets = genes,
  metadata = metadata,
  control = list(tail_method = "controlled_series"),
  threads = 4, verbose = TRUE
)

input <- gsea_input(evidence)

fit <- gsea(input$stat, sets, method = "preranked",
            control = list(seed = 31, replicates = 999, adjustment = "BH"))
fit$pathways
plot(fit, trait = "trait_A")
Each statistics entry is an ordinary data frame in complete sparse-LD marker and allele order, using qgg-style names such as rsids, ea, nea, stat, b, and seb. gbase::checkStat() can establish that order and orientation from a Glist. Z-score, effect/standard-error and score/information forms are accepted. A named list supplies traits; native set preparation is reused across them. When the same reference and gene definitions serve multiple analyses, retain that work explicitly:
prepared_genes <- prepare_vegas(Glist, genes, threads = 4)
evidence_A <- vegas(statistics_A, prepared = prepared_genes)
evidence_B <- vegas(statistics_B, prepared = prepared_genes)
The prepared object is an ordinary R object and can be saved with saveRDS(). sets = genes supplies the marker membership for each gene, for example list(gene1=c("m1","m2"), gene2=c("m3","m4")). Nonnegative quadratic weights are supplied separately through weights. The same vegas() interface accepts regions or other marker sets. Its set column is mapped explicitly to the gene-labelled schema expected by gsea() by gsea_input() as shown above. The adapter rejects unavailable p-values and inconsistent traits. The helper verifies identities and allele coding but does not harmonize them.
sets alone defines the regions. Native code opens one validated sparse-LD reader and prepares eigenvalue spectra in bounded parallel batches across genes. Trait evaluation reuses those spectra and does not reread LD. The default maximum is 2,048 markers per gene.
The returned evidence$stat includes the standardized quadratic gene score, p_value, tail diagnostics, marker count and SNP-wise mean metadata. VEGAS does not construct cross-gene covariance. ORA and preranked enrichment can consume the gene statistics directly. Competitive, MAGMA and Bayesian pathway models require a separately prepared, labelled gene covariance; marker-set membership is not treated as evidence of independence.
MAGMA’s sample-size and MAC adjustments additionally require explicit metadata columns gene, sample_size, and mean_minor_allele_count in gene order. A named trait list can provide different GWAS metadata per trait. The example calculates these from its GWAS individuals. The LD-reference sample count is provenance and is never substituted for GWAS sample size. Weighted genes do not acquire unit-weight SNP-wise mean metadata automatically.
Unavailable native tails remain visible through p_available, unavailable_reason, tail_error_bound and tail_terms. They are not silently replaced or filtered. The MAGMA route rejects nonfinite or endpoint gene p-values. A score-based model can be selected explicitly, but answers a different question. Singular gene dependence also remains an error in downstream GLS.
The script plots gene evidence together with ORA and preranked pathway results. Pathway A contains effects in both traits; pathway B contains effects only in trait B; pathway C contains none. This is one reproducible functional example, not a calibration study. Covariance-based pathway methods remain available through their explicit sampling contract, but are not included in this direct VEGAS handoff.

title: Gene-set and pathway analysis
text:
A small gene-level example
Download the runnable R example. It contains all six methods and uses 120 artificial genes and three overlapping pathways. This is an interface demonstration, not a comparative calibration study.
library(gsuite)
set.seed(2401)
genes <- paste0("gene", seq_len(120))
sets <- list(pathway_A=genes[1:25], pathway_B=genes[21:45],
             pathway_C=genes[71:95])
X <- vapply(sets, function(s) as.numeric(genes %in% s), numeric(120))
noise <- matrix(rnorm(240),120,2)
stat <- list(
  trait_A=data.frame(gene=genes, score=2*X[,1]+noise[,1]),
  trait_B=data.frame(gene=genes, score=1.5*X[,1]+X[,2]+
                      .3*noise[,1]+sqrt(.91)*noise[,2])
)
stat is a data frame for one trait or a named list for several traits. Every frame must contain the same unique character gene IDs in the same order. All genes in the declared background remain in the analysis, including genes outside every set. Unknown or duplicate set members are errors. Set overlap is allowed. For competitive and Bayesian regression, a labelled numeric feature matrix can replace binary set membership.

title: Gene-set and pathway analysis
section: Selected genes or a ranked list
text:
Selected genes or a ranked list
ora <- gsea(transform(stat$trait_A, selected=score>2), sets, "ora",
            control=list(adjustment="BH"))
ranked <- gsea(stat$trait_A, sets, "preranked",
               control=list(replicates=999, seed=2401, adjustment="BH"))
ranked$pathways
ranked$details$trait$leading_edge
plot(ranked)
ORA requires a logical selected column over the complete background; the selection rule is the caller’s decision. Preranked GSEA uses a finite score, a stable decreasing ranking and whole-background gene-label permutations. It does not correct for LD or perform phenotype permutations. Excluded sets and unavailable directional inference remain in the result with diagnostics. adjustment="BH" or "BY" adjusts the tested p-values, not pooled NES values as in Broad GSEA’s FDR calculation. Defaults are no adjustment, exponent 1, set sizes 1–500, seed 1, 999 permutations and one thread.

title: Gene-set and pathway analysis
text:
Competitive regression
fit <- gsea(stat, sets, "competitive",
             sampling=list(gene_covariance="independent"),
             control=list(adjustment="BH"))
fit$pathways
summary(fit)
plot(fit, trait="trait_A")
Classical methods analyse traits separately, with adjustment within each trait. Competitive regression fits pathways jointly by default; joint=FALSE fits each pathway separately with the same covariates and background. Covariates are a numeric matrix with gene row names or a data frame with gene and numeric columns; an intercept is added internally. Encode factors explicitly.
Regression always requires sampling$gene_covariance. Supply "independent" only when that working assumption is intended, or provide a labelled covariance matrix / named list of labelled blocks that partition the complete background. Block labels are used explicitly to map to gene order. Blocks must be symmetric positive definite; singular designs fail rather than silently drop columns. Student-t inference is a working approximation for non-Gaussian gene scores.

title: Gene-set and pathway analysis
text:
The bounded MAGMA route
gene_p <- transform(stat$trait_A,
  p_value=pnorm(score,lower.tail=FALSE), marker_count=10,
  effective_parameters=8, sample_size=10000, mean_minor_allele_count=2000)
magma <- gsea(gene_p, sets, "magma",
               sampling=list(gene_covariance="independent"),
               control=list(adjustment="BH"))
magma$pathways
magma$preparation$trait
These artificial p-values illustrate the API. Real analyses require calibrated gene-level evidence. Native preprocessing applies the documented probit transformation, clipping and gene-property corrections; the default adjusts the outcome for internal covariates before fitting each pathway separately. Constant internal covariates are reported. correct_size, correct_density, correct_sample_size and correct_mac default to TRUE; their positive input columns are required whenever enabled. truncate and residualize_internal also default to TRUE; bounds are lower_z_bound=-3, upper_z_sd=6 and covariate_sd_bound=5. External custom covariates use competitive instead.
For this method, gene dependence means quadratic-score correlation, with nonnegative entries and unit diagonal. The native workflow applies the recorded working-correlation power (default 1.1). This is not exact covariance of the transformed probit scores. It is a defined subset of MAGMA’s workflow, not full MAGMA equivalence. SNP-to-gene tests, allele alignment and reference preparation are separate native operations and are not hidden inside this call.

title: Gene-set and pathway analysis
text:
PoPS-style gene ranking
pops() is separate from pathway testing. It learns a joint feature model of gene evidence and predicts every gene from a fit that excluded the gene’s chromosome. Feature selection, nuisance adjustment and ridge-penalty selection are therefore repeated for every chromosome.
genes <- paste0("gene", seq_len(60))
chromosome <- rep(as.character(1:3), each = 20)
features <- cbind(
  expression = seq(-2, 2, length.out = 60),
  constraint = rep(c(-1, 1), 30),
  distance = cos(seq_len(60) / 6)
)
rownames(features) <- genes

gene_stat <- data.frame(
  gene = genes,
  chromosome = chromosome,
  score = 1.5 * features[, "expression"] + sin(seq_len(60) / 4)
)

ranking <- pops(
  gene_stat,
  features,
  sampling = list(gene_covariance = "independent"),
  control_features = "expression"
)

ranking$predictions[order(ranking$predictions$genome_rank), ]
ranking$folds
ranking$features
plot(ranking)
Use gene_covariance="independent" only when that assumption is intended. For correlated gene evidence, pass named covariance blocks using the same sampling contract as gsea(); every block must stay within one chromosome. The input score may come from a checked MAGMA-style gene analysis, gsea::vegas(), or another checked gene-level method, but pops() does not perform SNP-to-gene mapping or infer chromosome labels.
The result is a feature-based priority score with genome-wide and within-chromosome ranks. It is not a p-value, causal probability or locus definition, and the function does not automatically choose a top gene per locus. The fit retains the penalty, effective degrees of freedom, selected features and coefficients for every held-out chromosome.

title: Gene-set and pathway analysis
text:
Joint Bayesian pathways
Omega <- matrix(c(1,.3,.3,1),2,dimnames=list(names(stat),names(stat)))
G <- diag(2);dimnames(G)<-dimnames(Omega)
fit <- gsea(stat, sets, "bayesr",
  sampling=list(gene_covariance="independent",trait_covariance=Omega),
  prior=list(effect_covariance=G),
  control=list(burnin=100,sampling_sweeps=1000,seeds=c(11,29)))
fit$pathways                 # trait-specific effects and PIPs
fit$joint                    # probability of activity in any trait
fit$parameters$joint         # prepared-scale parameter summaries
fit$diagnostics$joint        # conditioning, threads and chain PIP spread
plot(fit, trait="trait_A")
saveRDS(fit, "pathway-fit.rds")
Bayesian models fit all pathways jointly and adjust both response and features for the shared nuisance design. They support overlapping pathways and proper priors when the number of features exceeds the number of genes; highly dependent sets can still make individual PIPs difficult to interpret.
For one trait, supply prior=list(residual_variance=1,effect_variance=1) with values chosen for the prepared score scale. BayesC defaults to inclusion probability 0.5. Scalar BayesR defaults to weights (0.7,0.1,0.1,0.1) and variance multipliers (0,0.01,0.1,1). Optional scalar learning flags are estimate_effect_variance, estimate_residual_variance and estimate_weights. The corresponding priors are effect_variance_prior=list(df=...,scale=...), residual_variance_prior=list(df=...,scale=...) and positive weight_prior counts.
Joint fits require a labelled effect_covariance prior and a separate, fixed residual trait_covariance on original response units. The latter describes remaining gene-score dependence between traits, not pathway-effect covariance. All traits share genes, features, covariates and gene dependence. The native likelihood uses a separable gene-by-trait covariance model. It does not infer sample overlap or substitute a genetic-correlation matrix for residual covariance.
By default, joint models enumerate activity patterns across 2–12 traits. For larger trait sets, explicitly provide restricted binary patterns with labelled trait columns, distinct rows and the null row first; the native maximum is 64 traits. A restricted pattern set changes the model. pattern_weights default to equal probabilities. Joint BayesC has one positive component scale, 1; BayesR uses (0.01,0.1,1) with equal conditional component weights. The null is represented by the null pattern, not a zero component scale.
Joint learning is optional: estimate_covariance requires covariance_prior=list(df=...,scale=...) (an inverse-Wishart scale matrix); estimate_pattern_weights requires positive pattern_prior counts; and BayesR’s estimate_component_weights requires positive component_prior counts. The residual trait covariance stays fixed.

title: Gene-set and pathway analysis
text:
Results, units and bounds

pathways retains method-specific statistics; summary() also returns parameters, diagnostics and provenance. plot() requires a trait choice when several are present. No automatic significance or PIP cutoff is applied.
Bayesian pathway means and variances use original response/feature units. Priors, native chain traces and parameter summaries use prepared coordinates. preparation records response and feature scales and nuisance rank.
scale_response and scale_features default to TRUE. Chain defaults are 100 burn-in sweeps, 1,000 sampling sweeps, thinning 1, seeds (1,2) and one thread. retain_diagnostics=TRUE retains parameter traces. Joint retain_pattern_probabilities=TRUE additionally stores pathway-by-pattern probabilities. Chain PIP spread is not an ESS or R-hat convergence check.
Regression defaults bound features (255 classical / 4,096 Bayesian), user covariates (128), each covariance block (2,048 genes) and preparation payload (512 MiB). Bayesian preparation checks its native payload estimate; the R classical check bounds the feature matrix, not total process memory. Joint sampler storage has a separate 256 MiB memory_limit_bytes estimate.
Competitive fits permit at most 256 coefficients by default and require reciprocal condition at least 1e-10; both controls are configurable. The bounded MAGMA route retains those native limits. No dense whole-genome covariance is formed when explicitly partitioned blocks are supplied.

The focused R checks compare ORA to the hypergeometric calculation, GLS to a dense R reference, and unadjusted MAGMA preprocessing to the corresponding competitive fit. Bayesian checks cover chains, units, labels, joint probabilities, learning and serialization. The GWAS adapter additionally checks quadratic moments and dependence against a direct R calculation, equal-eigenvalue chi-square tails, explicit block assumptions, unavailable tails and the connected pathway fits. These integration checks complement the small native oracles; they do not establish broad genomic calibration or full package qualification.

title: One simulated dataset across six genomic modules
text:
Completed example and supported recipes



All six modules ran on the same simulated dataset. Pathway analyses use the documented saddlepoint route, which returned all requested gene statistics. The connected 50K-marker BayesC and BayesR fits use declared fixed parameter values. Parameter learning is checked in a separate matched-reference study; see the qualification record for its settings and numerical scope.

title: One simulated dataset across six genomic modules
text:
What this example demonstrates
Start with a simulated population, run GWAS, then reuse its summary statistics and LD for Bayesian regression, genetic correlation, fine-mapping, scoring and pathway analysis. Genetic correlation uses the gcorr R package; the other calls use their current task-package or umbrella interfaces.
This connected example covers glma, gbayes, gcorr, gmap, gscore and gsea. It checks selected calculations and demonstrates representative methods at this scale. It does not establish calibration of every supported method or option. The library-specific qualification pages report a separate fixed set of ten simulations using the same design.

title: One simulated dataset across six genomic modules
text:
One population, explicit sample groups







Setting
Value




Individuals / markers
10,000 / 50,000


Traits
Three continuous traits: A, B and C


Target heritabilities
0.30, 0.40 and 0.35


Genomic layout
500 independent artificial regions of 100 markers


GWAS samples
Three disjoint groups of 3,000; one per trait


Scoring test sample
1,000 individuals excluded from GWAS and LD preparation


LD reference
The pooled 9,000 GWAS individuals


Annotation
1,000 artificial genes; enriched, background and mixed pathway sets


Replicates
One detailed example and an earlier set of ten fixed simulations



The genotype generator has known within-region population LD. It writes one marker at a time to a packed BED file. gsim then generates phenotypes from explicit effects, using bounded reads from the prepared Glist. Neither a full genotype matrix nor a 50,000-by-50,000 LD matrix is created.
The LD reference retains all within-region correlations and treats regions as independent. It shares individuals with the GWAS samples; it is not an independent external panel. Summary-based fits therefore use a pooled-LD approximation to each study’s cross-products. The artificial chromosomes, genes and pathways have no biological interpretation.

title: One simulated dataset across six genomic modules
text:
The connected workflow
These excerpts show the current supported model calls. The retained results use the sample selection, truth construction and effect units defined in the shared design.
# Association: one selected GWAS group and its phenotype.
association <- glma::glma(y, Glist, method = "linear", threads = 1)

# Prepare aligned summaries separately from fitting.
prepared <- gbase::checkStat(stat, Glist)

# Genome-wide genetic correlation from prepared public inputs.
correlation <- gcorr::gcorr(statistics, ld_scores = ld_scores,
                            blocks = blocks, method = "ldsc",
                            overlap_intercept = 0)

# Bayesian regression: fixed declared parameters, four posterior chains.
bayesian <- gbayes::gbayes(statistics$A, Glist, method = "bayesc",
                  prior = prior, control = control)

# Regional mapping after explicit OLS sufficient-statistic preparation.
mapping_stat <- gmap::gmap_stat(statistics, LD_Glist,
                               phenotype_variance = phenotype_variance)
mapping <- gmap::gmap(mapping_stat, LD_Glist, regions = regions,
                method = "multi_effect", prior = prior, control = control)

# Apply allele-labelled weights with explicit coding to held-out individuals.
prediction <- gscore::gscore(weights, test_Glist)

# Aggregate marker evidence, then analyse pathways of genes.
evidence <- glma::vegas(statistics, LD_Glist, sets = genes,
                 metadata = metadata,
                 control = list(tail_method = "saddlepoint"))
gene_stat <- lapply(evidence$stat, function(x) transform(x, gene = set))
pathways <- gsea(gene_stat, pathway_sets, method = "preranked")
The prior and control placeholders differ between Bayesian regression and regional mapping. They are explicit in the script. No universal prior scale is assumed across methods.

title: One simulated dataset across six genomic modules
text:
Results

GWAS: which signals were detected?



Manhattan plots for three linear GWAS scans. Orange triangles mark variants with a nonzero simulated effect for the plotted trait; grey points have zero direct effect. The first 80 enriched artificial regions have a pale blue background.


Each panel shows all 50,000 markers from glma, with a dashed reference line at \(p=0.05/50{,}000=10^{-6}\) for that trait. Positions follow the 500 artificial regions, not human chromosomes. A causal variant need not reach this threshold: most effects are small and each GWAS uses 3,000 individuals. Conversely, a grey marker can be associated through LD with a causal variant; grey significant points are not automatically false-positive associations.
The association summary reports the numbers of causal markers and threshold crossings separately. Each trait has 984 causal markers; 985 distinct markers affect at least one trait. There are three threshold crossings for A, three for B and two for C; all are directly causal in this draw. The 15 direct comparisons with R ordinary least squares remain the independent numerical check of these scans.



Estimated versus true marginal GWAS effects for the three traits, on the raw-dosage scale.


The target here is the marginal effect, \(R_{\mathrm{pop}}B\), which includes LD with other causal variants. The diagonal represents equality. Direct causal effects \(B\) are a different target and are used for the Bayesian comparison below.


Heritability and genetic correlation



Heritability estimates with jackknife uncertainty and true versus estimated genetic correlations. Dashed lines show population truth; LDSC+ann includes the enriched annotation.

The baseline fits underestimate heritability in this draw. Effects are concentrated in the first 80 regions, which also occupy the lower-LD end of the generator. The annotation-aware model represents this heterogeneity and gives estimates closer to truth here. This contrast is about model assumptions; it does not rank software implementations or establish bias across repetitions. SumHer uses ordinary LD scores as tagging weights and one baseline architecture component, explaining its near-identical results to baseline LDSC in this setup.
The uncertainty bars show estimate plus/minus 1.96 jackknife standard errors, using the 500 regions as blocks. They are illustrative normal approximations, not an interval-coverage evaluation. Correlations are imprecise with 3,000 individuals per trait: baseline LDSC gives B/C rg = 1.095 (SE 0.331), and annotation-aware LDSC gives 1.052 (SE 0.228), versus truth 0.726. These out-of-range estimates remain visible; they are not clipped to one.
HESS, SUPERGNOVA and LAVA also returned the requested covariances in 20 predetermined regions. HESS standard errors were unavailable for 40 of the 60 trait-pair/region results because its plug-in genetic/residual matrices did not meet the positive-semidefinite requirement. SUPERGNOVA returned all 60 standard errors. The exercised LAVA covariance route does not return standard errors. Finite point estimates do not remove those uncertainty limitations.



Regional genetic covariance estimates against population truth, and LDSC annotation heritabilities.


Each regional panel contains 20 predetermined regions and three trait pairs. Covariances use phenotype-standardized units. The annotation panel compares the enriched and background contributions to total heritability; the categories are disjoint and exhaustive. Points for regions and traits from the same dataset are dependent. Download the labelled truth comparisons.


Bayesian regression: a supported reference-LD recipe
The scalar BayesC and BayesR workflow was qualified separately across five simulations. Each fit used standardized summary statistics from 3,000 individuals and sparse LD from an independent, matched reference of 9,000 individuals. LD retained a 1,000-marker window with \(r^2=0.001\).
The fit learns residual variance, marker-effect variance and mixture probabilities. The reference-LD residual update is
\[
V_e^{\mathrm{work}}=V_e+0.9V_g,
\qquad
V_g=b^{\mathsf T}R_{\mathrm{ref}}b.
\]
Priors specify an expected nonzero proportion of 0.02. BayesR uses variance multipliers \((0,0.01,0.1,1)\) and active-component proportions \((0.012,0.006,0.002)\). Mixture probabilities use an explicit Dirichlet strength of 5,000. Four chains use 500 burn-in sweeps and retain 700 BayesC or 5,000 BayesR sweeps.
fit <- gbayes::gbayes(statistics, Glist, method = "bayesc", trait = "trait",
  prior = prior,
  control = list(
    residual_policy = "reference_ld",
    residual_adjustment = 0.9,
    estimate_effect_variance = TRUE,
    estimate_weights = TRUE,
    burnin = 500,
    sampling_sweeps = 700,
    seeds = c(101, 102, 103, 104),
    threads = 4
  ),
  posterior = list(reference = LD_Glist,
                   phenotype_variance = c(trait = 1)))

The exact settings, acceptance criteria and downloadable results are in the qualification record.


Regional mapping and colocalisation
The two regions were selected before fitting. Region 1 contains a shared causal variant; region 2 contains distinct causal variants for A and B. The fitted multi-effect model uses one component, matching this deliberately simple regional truth. ABF colocalisation uses the same complete regional summaries from disjoint samples and its at-most-one-causal-variant-per-trait assumption.
All four regional fits converged. ABF H4 is effectively one for the shared signal, and H3 is effectively one for the distinct signals in this draw. The credible-set summary records set size, completeness, LD checks and whether the known causal marker is included for each region and trait. All four sets contain one marker, the true causal variant, and pass the recorded LD checks.



Regional inclusion probabilities and shared versus distinct causal signals. H3 denotes distinct causal variants and H4 a shared variant.




Pathways
glma::vegas() aggregates marker evidence into 1,000 artificial genes, processing each gene region once for all three traits. The supported workflow uses the saddlepoint tail calculation for all 3,000 gene-by-trait statistics. Every statistic was returned in the detailed example, with no moment-matching fallback.
The retained analysis artifacts also compare ORA, preranked GSEA, competitive regression, the bounded MAGMA route and a scalar Bayesian pathway model. The current direct VEGAS handoff covers ORA and preranked analysis; the covariance- based methods require a separately prepared gene covariance. The enriched pathway covers the simulated enriched regions; the mixed pathway samples genes across the genome, and the background pathway covers regions with lower causal-marker probability. Background does not mean zero genetic effects.



Pathway evidence from the bounded MAGMA route for three traits, and Bayesian pathway inclusion probabilities for trait A. Gene p-values use the saddlepoint approximation.


The enriched pathway has nominal bounded-MAGMA p-values of 0.0086, 0.00077 and 0.0018 for A, B and C. Its Bayesian PIP for trait A is 0.9995, compared with 0.0705 for background and 0.0315 for mixed. ORA, preranked GSEA and competitive regression also show the strongest evidence for the enriched set in this draw. Pathway p-values here are unadjusted; the different methods use different null hypotheses, so their magnitudes do not rank method quality.
P-values and posterior inclusion probabilities answer different questions and are shown on separate scales. One simulated dataset cannot establish pathway false-discovery control, credible-set coverage or comparative power.



Four frequentist pathway summaries for trait A alongside the separate Bayesian PIP scale.

title: One simulated dataset across six genomic modules
text:
Earlier connected results across simulations
Ten datasets repeat the same 10,000-individual, 50,000-marker design. Genotypes, marker effects and phenotypes are regenerated each time. The regions, annotations, sample split, priors, chain lengths and working-noise scale are fixed before these runs. The detailed example above is excluded from the aggregate. No seeds are selected or replaced based on their results.
All ten runs completed. Mean population heritability for trait A was 0.300. These repetitions provide the connected checks for correlation, regional mapping and pathway analysis. The separate five-repetition Bayesian qualification above is the maintained evidence for the supported parameter-learning recipe.
Baseline LDSC, GNOVA and SumHer underestimate heritability on average in this nonuniform architecture. Annotation-aware LDSC changes the mean estimates to 0.310, 0.439 and 0.394 for A, B and C, against mean truths of 0.300, 0.398 and 0.349. Accounting for enrichment reduces systematic underestimation here but can overshoot; it does not improve every trait’s RMSE.



Heritability estimation errors by trait and method, and mean genetic-correlation error across three trait pairs for each simulation.


Each point represents one simulation; short black lines show means. Zero is the estimation-error target. Genetic-correlation errors are first averaged over the three pairs within a simulation, so the pairs are not presented as independent repetitions. Download accuracy summaries.
All 40 component credible sets contain their simulated causal variant; each set contains one marker. Colocalisation assigns probability effectively one to the appropriate shared- or distinct-causal hypothesis in these easy regions. The mean Bayesian pathway PIP is 0.894 for the enriched set, compared with 0.054 for background and 0.038 for mixed. The downloadable tables retain variation across datasets and the other pathway methods.
Across the ten runs, HESS supplies standard errors for 189 of 600 regional covariances, SUPERGNOVA for 600 of 600, and the exercised LAVA route for none. Six annotation-category correlations are undefined because an estimated component heritability is nonpositive. The supported saddlepoint gene-tail route returns all 30,000 gene/trait p-values; 11 use its recorded moment-matching fallback. These availability and fallback flags remain in the downloadable tables.
With only ten simulations, one outcome changes a proportion by ten percentage points. These results are descriptive checks under one non-null design, not precise calibration, a null false-positive assessment or general method rankings. The run status lists every planned seed and its outcome. The linked aggregate tables retain the labelled truth comparisons and numerical availability used above.

title: One simulated dataset across six genomic modules
text:
Inspect the recorded results
Download the compact result tables: correlation estimates, pathways, numerical availability, gene-tail comparison and stage timings. Additional downloads: GWAS summary, Bayesian qualification summary and Bayesian repetition results.
Read the qualification record for the scientific targets, check definitions and untested capabilities. The existing smaller replicated comparison is a separate simulation design; its results are not pooled with this example.

title: One genomic dataset, seven R packages
text: These tutorials follow one connected analysis. gbase prepares a PLINK BED/BIM/FAM panel and a reusable LD reference. The other packages perform association testing, Bayesian regression, genetic correlation, fine-mapping, scoring and gene-level analysis. The pages show actual tables and figures from one seeded simulation, along with the R calls that produced them.

title: One genomic dataset, seven R packages
text:
The simulated study







Component
Design




Genotypes
20,000 individuals and 50,000 biallelic markers across 500 artificial chromosome labels, one per 100-marker region


Traits
Three quantitative traits, A, B and C


GWAS
Three disjoint groups of 6,000 individuals, one group per trait


LD reference
The first 18,000 individuals; 500 independent 100-marker regions


Prediction
The remaining 2,000 individuals, excluded from GWAS and LD preparation


Gene sets
1,000 artificial genes, two nonoverlapping marker sets per region


Pathways
Three gene collections labelled enriched, background and mixed



The simulation uses deliberately strong signals and simple independent LD regions to make the outputs readable. Effect sizes, p-values and run times are properties of this one simulated dataset. They do not establish calibration or performance on real cohorts.

title: One genomic dataset, seven R packages
text:
Reproduce the complete run
Install the seven source packages and gsim. Download the complete R driver, place it in a new working directory and run:
Rscript run.R --threads=4
The driver creates the PLINK files and phenotypes, computes LD once, and runs all seven package workflows. It saves stage objects under build/benchmarks/genomic-20k-50k-4cores/ and small result tables under benchmarks/genomic_20k_50k/results/. This is a substantial simulation; allow disk space for the packed genotypes and LD files. The tutorial plots and tables were generated from its saved four-thread stage objects. Package installation and compilation are outside the driver.
To inspect a saved stage without repeating the analysis:
cache <- file.path("build", "benchmarks", "genomic-20k-50k-4cores")
stage <- function(name) {
  readRDS(file.path(cache, paste0(name, ".rds")))$value
}

reference_Glist <- stage("sparse_ld_and_scores")
statistics <- stage("gwas_and_checkstat")$statistics
bayes_fit <- stage("bayesian_regression")

base_cache <- file.path("build", "benchmarks", "genomic-20k-50k")
simulation_cache <- if (file.exists(file.path(cache, "data_simulation.rds")))
  cache else base_cache
simulation <- readRDS(file.path(simulation_cache,
  "data_simulation.rds"))$value
prefix <- simulation$prefix
Y <- simulation$simulation$Y
rownames(Y) <- sprintf("id%05d", seq_len(nrow(Y)))

marker_ids <- sprintf("m%05d", 1:50000)
regions <- split(marker_ids,
  rep(sprintf("region%03d", 1:500), each = 100))
gene_sets <- list()
for (r in seq_along(regions)) {
  cut <- 20L + r %% 60L
  gene_sets[[sprintf("gene%04d", 2L * r - 1L)]] <- regions[[r]][1:cut]
  gene_sets[[sprintf("gene%04d", 2L * r)]] <- regions[[r]][(cut + 1L):100L]
}
regions and gene_sets are named marker vectors; pathway_sets in the gsea tutorial contains gene names. These are different units: a gene set identifies markers in the Glist, while a pathway identifies genes already summarized by VEGAS. In an ordinary study, replace prefix, Y, the sample IDs and set definitions with your own data.

title: Association analysis with glma
text: glma scans individual-level genotypes in a Glist. It supports quantitative linear scans, conditional scans, binary logistic scans and two leave-one- chromosome-out (LOCO) background models. Its vegas() function then combines aligned marker evidence within named marker sets using reference LD. This page follows the shared simulation, where each of three traits has a separate 6,000-person GWAS cohort. First run the loading block in that overview to define prefix, Y, simulation, reference_Glist and gene_sets; the snippets below can then be run in order.

title: Association analysis with glma
text:
Scan the quantitative traits
The phenotype is named by individual ID, so glma() can match its rows to the selected Glist sample order. A named matrix can scan several traits in the same cohort; this simulation instead uses disjoint cohorts and fits one trait at a time.
library(gbase)
library(glma)

gwas_ids <- list(
  A = sprintf("id%05d", 1:6000),
  B = sprintf("id%05d", 6001:12000),
  C = sprintf("id%05d", 12001:18000)
)

fits <- setNames(vector("list", 3), names(gwas_ids))
for (trait in names(gwas_ids)) {
  study <- gprep(bedfiles = paste0(prefix, ".bed"),
    ids = gwas_ids[[trait]], nthreads = 4)
  phenotype <- setNames(Y[, trait], rownames(Y))
  fits[[trait]] <- glma(phenotype, study,
    method = "linear", threads = 4, block_size = 128)
}

head(fits$A$associations[c("marker", "a1", "a2", "beta", "se",
  "statistic", "p", "status")])
beta is the effect per allele-1 dosage; se and p describe its single-marker test. status distinguishes tested markers from unavailable fits. In this simulated run, large signals were planted at markers including m00050, m00125 and m00175; nearby LD can produce secondary peaks.

title: Association analysis with glma
text:
Prepare the shared summary tables
Use gbase::checkStat() to orient the scan results to the LD reference. The driver also supplies chr, pos and allele labels from the same reference metadata before alignment:
metadata <- reference_Glist$sparseLD$marker_metadata
statistics <- lapply(names(fits), function(trait) {
  a <- fits[[trait]]$associations
  raw <- data.frame(
    rsids = a$marker, chr = metadata$chromosome,
    pos = metadata$base_pair_position,
    ea = metadata$allele1, nea = metadata$allele2,
    b = a$beta, seb = a$se, p = a$p,
    n = length(gwas_ids[[trait]])
  )
  checkStat(reference_Glist, raw,
    excludeMAF = NULL, excludeMAFDIFF = NULL, excludeINFO = NULL,
    excludeCGAT = FALSE, excludeINDEL = FALSE, excludeDUPS = TRUE,
    excludeMHC = FALSE, excludeMISS = NULL, excludeHWE = NULL)
})
names(statistics) <- names(fits)
The resulting named list is the common input for gcorr, gbayes, gmap and gene aggregation below.

title: Association analysis with glma
text:
Test genes with VEGAS
Each gene is a vector of marker names. vegas() finds them in the Glist and processes all traits while each gene’s LD is available. The saved run used 1,000 artificial genes and a saddlepoint tail calculation.
gene_metadata <- setNames(lapply(names(statistics), function(trait) {
  data.frame(
    set = names(gene_sets),
    sample_size = length(gwas_ids[[trait]]),
    mean_minor_allele_count = vapply(gene_sets, function(markers) {
      p <- simulation$frequencies[match(markers, marker_ids)]
      mean(2 * length(gwas_ids[[trait]]) * pmin(p, 1 - p))
    }, numeric(1))
  )
}), names(statistics))

gene_results <- vegas(statistics, reference_Glist,
  sets = gene_sets, metadata = gene_metadata,
  control = list(tail_method = "saddlepoint"), threads = 4)

head(gene_results$stat$A[c("set", "marker_count", "score",
  "p_value", "p_available")])
The result contains one gene-level table per trait. p_available must be checked before gsea::gsea_input() converts VEGAS output to a gene-statistics table. The leading trait A genes in the saved run were:

title: Association analysis with glma
text:
Other association routes








Question
Public call
Important input or output distinction




Does a marker add signal after a known marker?
glma(..., method = "linear", condition_on = index)
index is a 1-based position in selected Glist marker order.


Is a binary outcome associated?
glma(binary, study, method = "logistic")
Outcome is coded 0/1; beta is a log-odds effect and failures have status.


Is there signal after a polygenic background?
glma(..., method = "infinitesimal_loco")
Produces calibrated score tests with explicit background diagnostics.


Does a selected prior improve the LOCO background?
glma(..., method = "prior_selected_loco")
Records prior selection, refits and effect estimates.



For example, a conditional scan in the same cohort is:
study_A <- gprep(bedfiles = paste0(prefix, ".bed"),
  ids = gwas_ids$A, nthreads = 4)
phenotype_A <- setNames(Y[, "A"], rownames(Y))
lead_index <- match("m00050", unlist(study_A$rsids, use.names = FALSE))
conditional <- glma(phenotype_A, study_A, method = "linear",
  condition_on = lead_index, threads = 4)
head(conditional$associations)
The simulation assigns a separate artificial chromosome label to each 100-marker region. Those labels do not represent real chromosome-scale backgrounds, so this dataset is not a meaningful LOCO example. The full glma guide works through binary, conditional and LOCO examples with a suitable small panel.

title: Heritability and genetic correlation with gcorr
text: gcorr works with aligned summary statistics. The convenient ldsc() route uses LD scores and reference metadata already held by a gbase Glist. Other public functions provide GNOVA, SumHer, regional covariance methods, covariance models and Mendelian randomisation when their additional inputs are available. This page uses the three disjoint GWAS cohorts from the shared simulation. Run the overview’s loading block first for statistics, reference_Glist and regions.

title: Heritability and genetic correlation with gcorr
text:
Estimate genome-wide quantities
statistics is a named list of aligned A, B and C tables from glma. The traits use the same reference markers in the same order. The disjoint GWAS cohorts justify a zero cross-trait overlap intercept in this simulated example; that assumption must be reconsidered for overlapping cohorts.
library(gcorr)

ordinary <- ldsc(statistics, reference_Glist,
  what = "rg", block_count = 200L,
  overlap_intercept = 0,
  marginal_intercept = "fixed_one")

ordinary$estimates
ordinary$h2
ordinary$rg

title: Heritability and genetic correlation with gcorr
section: Attribute heritability to a marker group
text:
Attribute heritability to a marker group
The first 80 artificial regions form an enriched annotation. Standard stratified LDSC computes an annotation LD-score column; at any marker it includes LD to annotated markers, including LD that crosses the annotation boundary. The residual column covers the remaining marker membership.
enriched_markers <- unlist(regions[1:80], use.names = FALSE)

partitioned <- ldsc(statistics, reference_Glist,
  sets = list(enriched = enriched_markers),
  residual = TRUE, set_model = "stratified",
  what = "rg", block_count = 200L,
  overlap_intercept = 0,
  marginal_intercept = "fixed_one")

subset(partitioned$estimates,
  trait1 == "A" & is.na(trait2) &
    quantity %in% c("h2", "enrichment"))
The trait A rows from this fit show a total h2 of about 0.36, with about 0.267 attributed to the enriched category. enrichment compares a category’s heritability share with its marker share. It is a model-based estimate, not a count of causal variants.

title: Heritability and genetic correlation with gcorr
section: Work at regional or covariance level
text:
Work at regional or covariance level
One prepared regional LD object can be reused across methods and trait pairs. The preparation loads the requested regions and verifies their complete eigensystems once in the current R session:
prepared_regions <- gcorr_prepare_regions(reference_Glist,
  regions = regions[1:20])

regional_h2 <- gcorr_hess(statistics$A, prepared_regions,
  maximum_components = 0, minimum_eigenvalue = 0)
regional_h2$estimates
This call illustrates HESS; regional results were not part of the displayed LDSC table. Regional methods require method-specific sample overlap, eigenvalue and inference choices.








Analysis

title: Polygenic scoring with gscore
text: gscore applies allele-labelled marker weights to selected people in a gbase Glist. It can produce total scores, scores for named marker sets and several weight columns in one pass. It also constructs clumping-and-thresholding (C+T) weights from aligned GWAS statistics and stored sparse LD. The shared simulation holds out 2,000 individuals for this example. Run the overview loading block first for prefix, Y, bayes_fit, gene_sets, statistics and reference_Glist.

title: Polygenic scoring with gscore
text:
Apply BayesC weights
The gbayes fit provides standardized, portable weights for trait A. The target Glist selects only the held-out people from the same PLINK files. sets contain marker names; the Glist resolves their BED locations and the scorer accumulates their contributions while reading the target panel.
library(gbase)
library(gscore)

holdout_ids <- sprintf("id%05d", 18001:20000)
test_Glist <- gprep(bedfiles = paste0(prefix, ".bed"),
  ids = holdout_ids, nthreads = 4)

prediction <- gscore(bayes_fit$weights, test_Glist,
  sets = gene_sets[1:20], include_total = TRUE,
  coding = "standardized", scale_scores = FALSE,
  control = list(threads = 4))

dim(prediction$scores)
colnames(prediction$scores)[1:6]
The score matrix has 2,000 rows in selected individual order. Its A column is the total BayesC score; the remaining columns are the requested gene contributions. Since scale_scores = FALSE, scores are not standardized again across the target cohort.

text:
Evaluate the held-out score
Join scores to outcomes by individual ID, rather than relying on row position. Here the same trait A score is correlated with all three simulated outcomes; the B and C rows are cross-trait associations, not separately fitted B or C prediction models.
observed <- Y[rownames(prediction$scores), , drop = FALSE]
trait_A_score <- prediction$scores[, "A"]
vapply(colnames(observed), function(trait)
  cor(trait_A_score, observed[, trait]), numeric(1))

title: Polygenic scoring with gscore
section: Construct another score from GWAS evidence
text:
Construct another score from GWAS evidence
clump_threshold() chooses markers by GWAS p-value, LD and distance. It needs an LD resource retaining every pair its requested window could inspect. The main tutorial reference has a 100-variant construction limit, so it cannot be used for a 250 kb C+T window even on this artificial panel. Construct a separate clumping reference with no variant-count limit and a base-pair window at least as wide as the clumping rule:
dir.create("analysis", showWarnings = FALSE)
ct_reference <- gprep(bedfiles = paste0(prefix, ".bed"),
  ids = sprintf("id%05d", 1:18000), nthreads = 4)
ct_reference <- gprep(Glist = ct_reference, task = "sparseld",
  out_prefix = "analysis/clumping-LD",
  max_distance_bp = 250000, max_distance_variants = 0,
  r2 = 0.1, block_size = 128, nthreads = 4)

ct_weights <- clump_threshold(statistics$A, ct_reference,
  p_threshold = 5e-8, r2_threshold = 0.1,
  window_bp = 250000)

ct_prediction <- gscore(ct_weights, test_Glist,
  coding = "standardized", scale_scores = FALSE,
  control = list(threads = 4))
This C+T call is a supported alternative; the displayed scatter and correlations use BayesC weights only. C+T needs the aligned b, seb, p and n fields. Save ct_reference with its LD files for reuse; the clumping resource does not need to be recomputed for each trait.

title: Earlier connected genomic evidence and Bayesian parameter learning
text:
This records the earlier connected genomic simulation and separate Bayesian parameter-learning qualifications. The shared genomic simulation has a newer fixed set of ten draws and separate pages for each library. Results from these runs are not pooled with the newer set. Development history, failed runs and exploratory diagnostics are deliberately excluded.


The workflow connects glma, gcorr, gbayes, gscore, gmap and gsea through the gsuite R interfaces. One detailed dataset provides figures and worked results. Ten independently simulated datasets repeat the same fixed design for a small descriptive qualification.
The qualification asks whether the modules can share prepared genomic data, summary statistics and LD resources; whether requested analyses complete; and whether their outputs behave sensibly relative to known simulation truth. A separate five-repetition design qualifies the supported BayesC and BayesR reference-LD recipe. The results are descriptive checks rather than a ranking of competing methods.




10,000 unrelated simulated individuals and 50,000 biallelic markers.
500 independent 100-marker regions with within-region correlation ranging from 0.2 to 0.8.
Three continuous traits with target heritabilities 0.30, 0.40 and 0.35.
Effects enriched in the first 80 regions.
Region 1 contains a shared causal variant for two traits; region 2 contains distinct causal variants.
Three disjoint GWAS samples of 3,000 individuals and 1,000 held-out individuals for prediction.
A pooled LD reference constructed from the 9,000 GWAS individuals. It retains every pair within each simulated region with \(r^2=0\) and no cross-region LD.

Population truth is calculated from the simulated effects and the known population LD, rather than from the observed reference matrix.











Component
Exercised capability
Outcome




glma
Three 50,000-marker linear GWAS scans
All marker fits completed; 150 selected marker/trait comparisons across the ten repetitions agreed with R OLS within \(10^{-9}\)


gcorr
LDSC, GNOVA, SumHer, annotation-aware LDSC, HESS, SUPERGNOVA and LAVA
Point estimates completed; truth comparisons, unavailable uncertainty and out-of-range correlations remain visible


gbayes
BayesC and BayesR using sparse reference LD
The supported parameter-learning recipe passed all heritability, effect-recovery, prediction and chain-diagnostic criteria across five simulations


gscore
Ridge, BayesC and BayesR scoring
Held-out scoring completed; truth-effect scoring agreed with simulated genetic values within numerical tolerance


gmap
Regional multi-effect mapping and ABF colocalisation
The deliberately simple shared and distinct causal signals were recovered in all repetitions


gstat and gsea
Gene statistics, ORA, preranked GSEA, competitive regression, bounded MAGMA and Bayesian pathway analysis
All requested gene and pathway statistics completed through the documented saddlepoint gene-tail route



All ten planned repetitions completed. Seeds were fixed in advance and no failed simulation was replaced. Native operation-local thread counts were one.





Use the scalar BayesC and BayesR reference-LD workflow as follows:

Standardize the continuous phenotype and dosage scale, align summary statistics to the LD reference, and retain the allele labels.
Use a matched reference population. The qualification uses 3,000 GWAS individuals and an independent reference of 9,000 individuals.
Construct sparse LD with a 1,000-marker window and \(r^2=0.001\).
Use residual_policy = "reference_ld" and residual_adjustment = 0.9.
Set priors to the intended architecture. Here the expected nonzero proportion is 0.02. BayesR uses variance multipliers \((0,0.01,0.1,1)\) and active-component proportions \((0.012,0.006,0.002)\). Mixture weights use an explicit Dirichlet strength of 5,000.
Run four chains. Use 500 burn-in sweeps, followed by 700 retained sweeps for BayesC or 5,000 for BayesR. Require maximum R-hat at most 1.05 and minimum bulk ESS at least 100 for the reported scalar parameters.

The sampler learns residual variance, marker-effect variance and mixture probabilities. It returns posterior marker effects, PIPs, parameter traces and joint-draw reference heritability. Posterior-mean effects can be passed to gscore() without changing marker order or allele orientation.



Five fixed simulations use 3,000 study individuals, 2,000 markers, 40 causal markers and target heritability 0.30. BayesC is evaluated under a homogeneous normal-effect architecture. BayesR is evaluated under its matching three-component variance mixture. Each simulation receives a separately generated reference panel from the same genotype population. No failed draw was replaced.

Small fixed-seed native checks also show that the BayesC and BayesR transitions agree with the corresponding installed sblr calculations to numerical precision. With complete same-sample LD, posterior mean effects correlate 0.9975 for BayesC and 0.9994 for BayesR with individual-level sblr effects. These checks connect the supported R workflow to its native implementation.



A second fixed five-repetition qualification covers four advanced transitions under their intended data contracts. Block residual learning uses two disjoint summary-likelihood blocks with separate response normalizations. BayesS uses 600 markers, 300 nonzero effects and a known MAF exponent. The multivariate design uses three continuous traits measured on the same 1,800 individuals, complete shared LD, and the observed response cross-product required to learn sampling covariance. The relocation design uses 20 strongly correlated marker pairs.

title: Earlier connected genomic evidence and Bayesian parameter learning
text:
The workflow connects glma, gcorr, gbayes, gscore, gmap and gsea through the gsuite R interfaces. One detailed dataset provides figures and worked results. Ten independently simulated datasets repeat the same fixed design for a small descriptive qualification.
The qualification asks whether the modules can share prepared genomic data, summary statistics and LD resources; whether requested analyses complete; and whether their outputs behave sensibly relative to known simulation truth. A separate five-repetition design qualifies the supported BayesC and BayesR reference-LD recipe. The results are descriptive checks rather than a ranking of competing methods.

title: Earlier connected genomic evidence and Bayesian parameter learning
text:
10,000 unrelated simulated individuals and 50,000 biallelic markers.
500 independent 100-marker regions with within-region correlation ranging from 0.2 to 0.8.
Three continuous traits with target heritabilities 0.30, 0.40 and 0.35.
Effects enriched in the first 80 regions.
Region 1 contains a shared causal variant for two traits; region 2 contains distinct causal variants.
Three disjoint GWAS samples of 3,000 individuals and 1,000 held-out individuals for prediction.
A pooled LD reference constructed from the 9,000 GWAS individuals. It retains every pair within each simulated region with \(r^2=0\) and no cross-region LD.

Population truth is calculated from the simulated effects and the known population LD, rather than from the observed reference matrix.

title: Earlier connected genomic evidence and Bayesian parameter learning
text:
Use the scalar BayesC and BayesR reference-LD workflow as follows:

Standardize the continuous phenotype and dosage scale, align summary statistics to the LD reference, and retain the allele labels.
Use a matched reference population. The qualification uses 3,000 GWAS individuals and an independent reference of 9,000 individuals.
Construct sparse LD with a 1,000-marker window and \(r^2=0.001\).
Use residual_policy = "reference_ld" and residual_adjustment = 0.9.
Set priors to the intended architecture. Here the expected nonzero proportion is 0.02. BayesR uses variance multipliers \((0,0.01,0.1,1)\) and active-component proportions \((0.012,0.006,0.002)\). Mixture weights use an explicit Dirichlet strength of 5,000.
Run four chains. Use 500 burn-in sweeps, followed by 700 retained sweeps for BayesC or 5,000 for BayesR. Require maximum R-hat at most 1.05 and minimum bulk ESS at least 100 for the reported scalar parameters.

The sampler learns residual variance, marker-effect variance and mixture probabilities. It returns posterior marker effects, PIPs, parameter traces and joint-draw reference heritability. Posterior-mean effects can be passed to gscore() without changing marker order or allele orientation.



Five fixed simulations use 3,000 study individuals, 2,000 markers, 40 causal markers and target heritability 0.30. BayesC is evaluated under a homogeneous normal-effect architecture. BayesR is evaluated under its matching three-component variance mixture. Each simulation receives a separately generated reference panel from the same genotype population. No failed draw was replaced.

The 50K-marker connected fits hold residual variance, effect scale and mixture weights fixed at declared values. They estimate marker effects and their posterior genetic summaries. Separate evidence covers parameter learning with a matched independent LD reference. The interval counts above describe conditional posterior intervals, not calibrated frequentist coverage.
Effect recovery · Posterior diagnostics



The bounded block-eigen validation uses 512 markers, verified independent LD blocks and summary effects generated from the same reference. It confirms one native block load and eigensystem decomposition per block, square peak dense-block storage, and the exact full-positive-rank reduction to ordinary BayesR under matched controls.
For this synthetic spectrum, 99.5% retained positive mass kept 504 of 512 coordinates, so retained-factor memory fell by only 1.6%. Its LD-weighted posterior difference from the full fit was within the independent-seed Monte Carlo baseline. These results validate execution and diagnostics only; they do not establish a generally optimal retention threshold, population-scale speed, or external SBayesRC equivalence.
